name: How Effectively Did the Nazis Control Germany, 1933–45?

parts.problemMd:
The Nazis built a police state to remove opposition.

What was the role of the SD?
parts.solutionMd:
The SD was the Nazi intelligence service, created by Heinrich Himmler in 1931 and placed under the command of Reinhard Heydrich [1]. Its job was to gather information on anyone suspected of opposing the Nazi Party [1]. Those it watched included members of other political parties, government officials, minority groups such as Jewish people, Jehovah's Witnesses and Freemasons, and even members of the Nazi Party itself [1]. From 1934 it was the only police agency allowed to collect and manage intelligence, and it went on doing this work throughout the war [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point, up to a maximum of 4.
> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the Gestapo instead. The Gestapo made the arrests and carried out the interrogations; the SD gathered the intelligence that told them whom to target.
> - Describing the SS instead. The SS was the parent organisation that oversaw both the SD and the Gestapo, so writing about black uniforms and racial purity does not answer this question.
> - Writing only that 'they spied on people'. Naming who was watched, or who ran the organisation, is what turns that into a creditable point.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Heydrich and the SD compiled the list of SA members used during the Night of the Long Knives in 1934.
> - The organisation grew rapidly, from 33 members in 1932 to around 850 in 1934 and 4,000 by 1939.
> - Its work fed directly into the wider police state, since the SS acted on the information the SD supplied.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Name Himmler and Heydrich. Examiners look for precision, and the two organisations are easy to muddle without them.
> - Keep each point in its own sentence so they can be counted.
> - The clearest way to show you understand the SD is to contrast it with the Gestapo in a single phrase: the SD found out, the Gestapo acted.

parts.problemMd:
The Nazis built a police state to remove opposition.

Why did the Nazis change the legal system in Germany?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was to make repression look lawful [R]. A government that simply had its opponents beaten in the street looks like a gang, but a government that convicts them in a courtroom looks legitimate. By keeping judges, trials and verdicts in place while making sure of the outcome, the Nazis could remove their enemies under the appearance that justice was being done. This mattered because it made persecution easier for ordinary Germans to accept and harder for other countries to criticise, since on paper Germany still had courts of law [E].

A second reason was to guarantee the result of every case [R]. Trial by jury was abolished so that verdicts rested with judges alone, and those judges had to join the National Socialist League for the Maintenance of the Law or lose their posts, with lawyers similarly required to join the German Lawyers Front. From 1936 judges even wore the swastika. On top of this the People's Court was created to try treason, sitting in secret with judges chosen for their loyalty and with the right of appeal removed. The effect is clear from the figures: eight political opponents were executed between 1930 and 1932, but 534 between 1934 and 1939 [E].

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 6 marks are awarded for explaining two reasons.
> - Explaining one reason is worth 4 marks, rising to 5 marks where the explanation is supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Listing the changes rather than explaining the purpose behind them. Naming the People's Court is a description; saying what it allowed the Nazis to do is an explanation.
> - Writing about the Gestapo and the concentration camps at length. They are part of the police state but they are not the legal system, and an answer that drifts there stops answering the question.
> - Treating the courts as simply irrelevant to the Nazis. The point is the opposite: the Nazis kept the courts precisely because a legal conviction was more useful to them than an obvious act of violence.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Jewish judges and lawyers were removed from the profession, which changed who was left to sit in judgement.
> - The number of offences carrying the death penalty was greatly increased, so more opponents could be dealt with through the courts.
> - Cases were frequently decided before they were heard, which is why the conviction rate rose so sharply.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two explained reasons is the target, and each should end in what the Nazis gained.
> - A strong line of argument is to ask why a dictatorship would bother with courts at all. Answering that gets you straight to the purpose.
> - The execution figures are the sharpest evidence available here. Moving from eight to 534 shows the change had a measurable effect, and that kind of specific detail lifts Level 3 from 4 marks to 5.

parts.problemMd:
The Nazis built a police state to remove opposition.

Which was more important to Nazi control of Germany: the Gestapo or the willingness of ordinary Germans to inform on each other? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
There is a strong case for the Gestapo [R]. Set up by Goering to combat all attempts to threaten the state and led by Heydrich from 1934, it had powers no ordinary police force has. Its officers wore plain clothes so nobody knew who they were, they tapped telephones, and they could arrest, question and torture a suspect and then send them straight to a concentration camp under protective custody without any trial. Around 160,000 people were arrested for political crimes in 1939 alone. The Gestapo also deliberately let details of conditions in the camps leak out, so the fear did the work even where the officers were not present [E].

Against that, the arithmetic does not support the idea of the Gestapo as an all-seeing machine [R]. Cities the size of Hamburg and Frankfurt had only 40 to 50 Gestapo agents each, which is nowhere near enough to watch a population. The figures on where cases actually came from make the point plainly: only about 10 per cent of political crimes were discovered by the Gestapo themselves, while around 80 per cent were reported by ordinary citizens. A neighbour, a colleague or a family member was far more likely to end someone's freedom than a secret policeman was [E].

Informing also reached where no police force could [R]. The Gestapo could not sit at a family dinner table or stand in a workplace canteen, but a relative or workmate could, and Germans did denounce friends and family. That is why so many people conformed: the danger was not a man in a leather coat but the possibility that anyone listening might repeat what you had said [E].

Overall the willingness of Germans to inform was the more important of the two [A]. The Gestapo's own records show it was finding only a small fraction of cases itself, and no organisation of 40 agents could have controlled a city without help. But the two cannot be separated completely, because it was the Gestapo's reputation that made informing feel like the safe choice. The honest conclusion is that the Gestapo supplied the fear and ordinary Germans supplied the information, and of the two it was the informers who did the greater part of the actual work of control [A].

**[10 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 10 marks require you to explain both sides and then support a valid judgement on which was more important.
> - Explaining both sides without a supported judgement is worth 7-9 marks. Seven marks are given for one explanation on each side, with one further mark for each additional explanation on either side.
> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.
> - Identifying or describing valid points without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 10 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the Gestapo in detail and mentioning informers only in passing. A comparison needs both sides developed, and an answer that covers only one is capped at 6 marks.
> - Bringing in the SS, the SD and the concentration camps as additional factors. They are relevant background, but the question offers two specific options and the marks come from weighing those.
> - Concluding that 'both were important'. That avoids the question. Choose one and justify the choice.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Gestapo membership grew from 6,500 in 1937 to 20,000 in 1939 and 32,000 by 1944, so it was expanding, but never to a size that could match the population.
> - People informed for ordinary human reasons as well as political ones, including settling grudges with neighbours or removing a rival at work, which meant denunciation spread far beyond genuine opposition.
> - The system worked partly because nobody could tell how many informers there were, so the uncertainty was as effective as the reality.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - The statistics are what win this question. Ten per cent of cases found by the Gestapo against 80 per cent reported by citizens is the single most powerful piece of evidence you can deploy.
> - Handle both options properly before you judge, and make sure the judgement names a winner.
> - A sophisticated move, and one examiners reward, is to show that the two are connected: the Gestapo's reputation is what made informing attractive. Just be sure you still come down on one side.

parts.problemMd: Write an account of Himmler’s role in Nazi Germany
parts.solutionMd:
Himmler joined the Nazi Party in the early 1920s and became very important in the party. He served in different capacities even before it came to power. He was Nazi propaganda leader from 1923 to 1929 and took up the leadership of the SS in 1929, a role he continued playing for a long time [E].

After Hitler came to power in 1933, Himmler rose in the hierarchy. He was made the head of the political police in Bavaria and the police president in Munich. As head of the SS, which began as a small paramilitary bodyguard, Himmler planned to transform it into an elite, feared and powerful organisation that was totally loyal to Hitler [E]. He expanded the size of the SS and allocated more responsibilities to make it a major tool of Nazi control. The SS took responsibility for security, policing and racial policy [E].

Himmler aimed at developing the Nazi police state. In 1936 he controlled both the SS and the Gestapo as Chief of German Police. This gave him complete authority over the entire security system of Nazi Germany. The Gestapo was allowed to arrest anyone who could be disloyal to the regime, for example Jews, Roma and Sinti, and other political opponents including communists and liberals. The Gestapo would arrest any potential threat, interrogate them, and send them to concentration camps without trial. The running of these camps was also taken over by the SS to eliminate opposition and spread fear [E].

Himmler drafted and structured the Nazis' racial policies. He was obsessed with the idea of racial purity and enforced it by persecuting Jews, Roma and other groups the regime called undesirable. He also encouraged Aryan breeding programmes. He set up the first Nazi concentration camp, Dachau, in 1933 [R]. After 1941 he started organising the Holocaust with the creation of extermination camps such as Auschwitz. In 1943 he became Minister for the Interior and started overseeing the 'Final Solution', a plan to exterminate Jews from Europe, and also directed forced labour in the camps [E]. The SS were allowed to conduct mass shootings and to enact the Final Solution [E].

Himmler's role also extended to the Nazi war effort. Under his command the Waffen-SS, the armed wing of the SS, grew into a powerful military force that fought alongside the regular army [R]. Towards the end of the Second World War, when the defeat of the Nazis became clear, he tried to negotiate secretly with the Allies. This did not sit well with Hitler, and he was stripped of all his roles [E].

In conclusion, Himmler's role in Nazi Germany was crucial, making him one of the most important figures in maintaining Nazi power. He built the SS into a powerful organisation that was loyal to Nazi ideology and to Hitler personally. It helped enforce Nazi rule, crush opposition and carry out racial policies, which culminated in the Holocaust [E].

**[15 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - You will be awarded 11-15 marks if your response is clear and detailed, goes beyond description, and contains a logical explanation of events. It should directly answer the question throughout and show an understanding of the significance of events and the connections between them.
> - You will receive 6-10 marks if your response covers some accurate knowledge but is not always detailed. Explanation may be uneven or only partly clear. There is some focus on the question, but the answer may drift into description.
> - You will be awarded 1-5 marks if your response contains very little knowledge. It could be mostly vague, general or inaccurate. Events are described briefly with no clear explanation.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 11-15 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating Himmler's biography instead of his role in the Nazi Party.
> - Confusing Himmler with other high-profile Nazis, such as Reinhard Heydrich or Hermann Goering.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Himmler played a vital role in building up the SS. When he took over in 1929 there were only 280 members. He transformed it into the most feared organisation in Nazi Germany, with over 250,000 members by 1939.
> - Himmler focused on strict uniform standards to reflect racial purity and discipline. He also believed the black SS uniform was a symbol of power and superiority.
> - Reinhard Heydrich, his deputy, organised the Wannsee Conference in 1942 on Himmler's instructions, where the 'Final Solution' was planned. Himmler later took responsibility for executing the extermination programme.
> - Himmler started the Lebensborn programme, which encouraged SS men the regime considered racially pure to father children with Aryan women in order to increase the population.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Focus on the period after 1923, when Himmler joined the Nazi Party.
> - Ensure that you organise events in chronological order.
> - Use accurate knowledge to explain a logical sequence of causes and effects.
> - Focus on the precise wording, such as cause, effect, success, importance or failure, and explain accordingly.
> - Support every point with specific facts such as names, dates, events, treaties and places.
> - Avoid vague generalisations and focus on precision.
> - Do not give a judgement without explanation.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of the SS to Nazi rule
parts.solutionMd:
The SS was undoubtedly one of the most important organisations in maintaining Nazi rule in Germany. However, it is an overgeneralisation to consider it the only reason why the Nazis maintained control [R]. The SS was immensely loyal to Hitler and enforced terror and racial policy to maintain Nazi control. However, other factors, such as Hitler's charismatic personality, propaganda, and economic recovery after 1933, also played vital roles [E].

The SS implemented Nazi racial policies and enforced measures against Jewish people, Roma and other minority groups. This racial policing included control over the daily lives of people and strict monitoring of marriage, reproduction and behaviour in the community [A]. After 1941 the SS organised the Final Solution and ran the extermination camps, such as Auschwitz and Treblinka, where millions of non-Aryan people were murdered. By carrying out this genocide the SS fulfilled Hitler's ideological aims of racial purity in Germany, and also terrorised society into submission [A]. Racial policy supported a unifying ideology that separated so-called true Germans from outsiders. By targeting minorities, especially Jews, the Nazis fostered a sense of belonging and superiority among Aryan Germans. The persecution of minorities also weakened those groups and diminished the possibility of organised resistance [E].

After Himmler became Chief of German Police, he gave the SS full authority to arrest, interrogate and imprison political opponents without trial. Their armed wing, the Waffen-SS, became a powerful military force and acted like a parallel army. They were extremely loyal to Hitler and to Nazi ideology [A]. That is why it was natural for Hitler to trust them unconditionally, as they ensured his power was protected even within the army. The climate of fear created by the Gestapo and the concentration camp system made open opposition to Nazi rule almost impossible, securing Hitler's control [A].

However, the SS cannot fully explain Nazi rule by itself, because other factors also contributed. Propaganda built widespread support for the regime and created an atmosphere in which Germans accepted it willingly. Nazi propaganda promoted militarism, German nationalism and a sense of pride through speeches, radio, films, posters, school textbooks and rallies such as those at Nuremberg, where Nazi ideology was reiterated and spread among the German people [A].

Similarly, economic recovery after 1933 reduced unemployment [E]. The new economic plan focused on public works and rearmament, which generated jobs. The promise of stability that Hitler had made during the election campaign was fulfilled, and this added to his popularity. For ordinary people, these day-to-day improvements in living standards were more important than the activities of the SS [A].

Finally, Hitler's charismatic personality helped him inspire people and gain their loyalty. His speeches and his role as Führer bound the system together. His policies and their implementation made him popular, and people looked up to him as the saviour of Germany [E].

To conclude, the SS played an extremely crucial role in the consolidation of Nazi rule. It provided Hitler with a loyal military force, created a police state in Germany, and enforced his racial policies. However, other factors cannot be neglected. Economic success led to improvements in living standards and attracted people towards Nazism, and propaganda ensured mass support for the regime. The SS was therefore part of a wider system of power that used terror, persuasion and popularity together to maintain Nazi rule [A].

**[25 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> - Analysis - [A]

> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.

> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.

> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Describing what the SS was instead of explaining its importance to Nazi control.
> - Confusing the SA's role with the SS's. Writing that the SS was responsible for street fighting in the 1920s describes the SA.
> - Attributing secret police surveillance to the SS rather than the Gestapo.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The SS became so powerful in the 1930s that it came to be known as a state within the Nazi state. It ran its own courts, schools and industries. To maintain the racial purity of the group, membership was strictly scrutinised: applicants had to undergo physical tests and prove their Aryan ancestry back to 1750.
> - The SS uniforms were black and carried a death's head symbol, chosen to project fear and authority.
> - The SS used slave labour from concentration camps in its businesses, which included armaments, construction and even furniture.
> - SS members swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler, not to Germany.
> - The SS, which started as a small bodyguard unit, grew into a powerful organisation under Himmler's leadership, dominating policing and security and maintaining the police state.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Do not just describe events; always explain their impact.
> - Use the correct chronology to explain events and their consequences.
> - Weigh your arguments and conclude which factor was most significant.

parts.problemMd: Write an account of Nazi policies towards the Christian churches in Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Germany in 1933 was a heavily Christian country, divided mainly between Protestants and Catholics, and this presented the Nazis with a problem. Church teaching contradicted Nazi belief at almost every point: the churches placed God rather than Hitler at the head of authority, taught that all races were equal, favoured peace over war, and held that the strong should help the weak rather than dominate them [R].

Hitler's response was not to attack the churches outright. Destroying them was risky, since Christianity had more followers than the Nazi Party and many Christians had voted for Hitler, and the two sides did share an emphasis on the family. Controlling the churches also offered a way of controlling the population. Hitler therefore began by seeking to make them work with the Nazi government [R].

The Catholic Church posed particular difficulties, because Catholics were loyal to the Pope, had supported the Catholic Centre Party, and ran their own schools teaching beliefs at odds with Nazi ones. In July 1933 Hitler signed an agreement with the Pope known as the Concordat. Catholics were to be allowed to worship freely and keep their schools; in return, Catholic priests would stay out of politics and swear loyalty to the regime [R].

The Nazis broke the agreement almost from the start. Around 400 priests were sent to Dachau concentration camp. Catholic schools were taken under Nazi control or closed altogether, Catholic youth organisations such as the Catholic Youth League were banned, and monasteries were shut down. By 1937 the Concordat had collapsed, and the Pope issued a statement, 'With Burning Anxiety', condemning the regime and describing Hitler as a mad prophet [R].

Policy towards the Protestant churches took a different form. Many Protestants had supported the Nazis by 1933, because the party promised protection against the communists, who were hostile to religion altogether. The Nazis used that goodwill to merge the Protestant churches into a single body, the Reich Church, under Ludwig Müller as Reich Bishop. Around 2,000 individual churches joined. The swastika was displayed in some of them, and Jewish people were forbidden to be baptised [R].

Protestant resistance followed. Pastor Martin Niemöller refused to accept Nazi interference and founded the Pastors' Emergency League, and out of this came the Confessing Church in 1934, which around 6,000 churches joined. Nazi policy towards the churches therefore ended in neither destruction nor control: the Catholic agreement had broken down by 1937, and the attempt to absorb the Protestant churches had produced an organised rival that most Protestant congregations preferred [R].

**[15 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> 
> Accuracy, coverage and sequence earn the marks, not explanation.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **11-15 marks:** the account includes the main events and developments and directly addresses the question. It is consistently supported by accurate historical knowledge and is logically sequenced.
> - **6-10 marks:** the account describes some events and developments relevant to the question. It is mostly supported by accurate historical knowledge and is structured in its approach.
> - **1-5 marks:** limited relevance to the question. Some accurate historical knowledge. Points are generally unconnected.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 11-15 marks include:
> 
> - Writing only about Catholics. The Concordat is the best-known part of the story, but an answer that never reaches the Reich Church or the Confessing Church has covered half the topic. Examiners specifically look for both denominations.
> - Confusing the Reich Church with the Confessing Church. The Reich Church was the Nazi-controlled body under Müller; the Confessing Church was the opposition to it.
> - Drifting into the persecution of Jewish people. That is religious persecution of a different kind and belongs to a different question.
> - Listing Nazi beliefs about Christianity without saying what the regime actually did. The question asks for policies and actions.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The Concordat brought Hitler an early diplomatic success, since a foreign power had signed an agreement with his government within months of his coming to power.
> - The papal statement of 1937 is often known by its German title, Mit brennender Sorge, and was read aloud from Catholic pulpits across Germany.
> - Niemöller was later imprisoned in a concentration camp, showing how the regime dealt with clergy who would not conform.
> - Some Nazis favoured replacing Christianity altogether with a revived Germanic paganism, though this never became official policy.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Split your answer between Catholics and Protestants. It is the clearest possible structure and it guarantees you meet the examiner's expectation of covering both.
> - Note that policy changed over time, moving from cooperation in 1933 to open conflict by 1937. Showing that development is what makes an account logically sequenced.
> - Dates and names carry the marks here: July 1933 for the Concordat, 1937 for its collapse, Ludwig Müller, Martin Niemöller, and the 1934 founding of the Confessing Church.
> - The figures are worth memorising, since 400 priests at Dachau, 2,000 Reich churches and 6,000 Confessing churches are exactly the kind of specific support the top level rewards.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of Nazi propaganda on the German people.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is the near-monopoly the Nazis established over everyday information.** In 1933 the party controlled around three per cent of German newspapers; by 1939 it controlled most of them, having closed roughly 1600 in 1935 alone, while the party's own daily, Der Völkischer Beobachter, reached 1.1 million readers by 1941. Radio was pushed just as hard. Goebbels censored most stations after 1933, employers were required to place radios in workplaces, and the cheap Volksempfänger or People's Receiver was introduced in 1933 to put a set in every home. The impact was that an ordinary German's routine sources of news all carried the same message, so Nazi claims were rarely met by a competing account [E].

**The second facet is the emotional effect of spectacle.** Rallies were held at Nuremberg every year from 1933 to 1938 on grounds designed by Albert Speer. The 1934 rally drew 200,000 people and used 152 searchlights to create the Cathedral of Light, and Leni Riefenstahl's film Triumph of the Will carried the scene to Germans who had not attended. This worked differently from the newspapers: it offered belonging and a sense of national revival rather than argument, and deliberately contrasted Nazi order with the disorder of the Weimar years. Rallies also advertised the strength of the army, in open breach of the military terms of the Treaty of Versailles [E].

**The third facet is the removal of alternatives through control of culture.** The Reich Chamber of Culture, created in 1933, ran separate chambers for creative art, music, literature and film, and membership was compulsory. Around 42,000 artists were admitted; those refused were forbidden to teach, produce or sell art. In 1936 over 12,000 paintings and sculptures were taken out of galleries, some 2500 writers were banned, and in May 1933 students in Berlin burned 20,000 books, with burnings taking place in 34 cities. The impact here is easy to underestimate, because it was not about what Germans were told but about what they were prevented from encountering at all [E].

**The fourth facet is propaganda aimed outwards as well as inwards.** The 1936 Berlin Olympics were staged to demonstrate the strength and modernity of Nazi Germany to the world, and Riefenstahl's Olympia followed in 1938. But this facet also shows the limits of the method, because Jesse Owens won four gold medals and finished as the most successful athlete of the games, publicly contradicting the claim of Aryan superiority that the occasion had been designed to prove [E].

**The fifth facet is that propaganda never worked alone.** The rules of the Reich Chamber of Culture were enforced by the SS and the Gestapo, and Gestapo officers visited artists' studios to inspect what was being produced. This makes the impact genuinely hard to measure: when people conformed, it is not possible to separate those who had been persuaded from those who were simply afraid. Nor was conformity complete, since around 6000 congregations joined the Confessing Church rather than the Nazi-run Reich Church [E].

**Judgement.** The most important impact was not persuasion but monopoly [A]. The rallies and the Olympics are the most visible achievements and the hardest to assess, because enthusiasm at a rally may be genuine belief or may be theatre. What can be measured is the change from three per cent of newspapers to almost all of them, and 12,000 works removed from galleries: by the late 1930s a German who wanted a different account of events had very few places left to find one.

That matters because it made the regime's other instruments effective [A]. Terror requires people not to know how widespread the arrests are; a foreign policy of rearmament requires that the Treaty of Versailles be remembered as an injustice. Propaganda supplied those conditions. Jesse Owens is the useful qualification, however: propaganda controlled what Germans read and heard, but it could not control events, and when reality contradicted the message in public the message lost [A].

**[25 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the methods instead of assessing the effects. A tour through newspapers, radio, rallies and film is recall; every method named has to be turned into a claim about what it did to people.
> - Assuming propaganda simply worked. The strongest answers acknowledge that conformity under a police state is not proof of belief.
> - Ignoring censorship. Propaganda is as much about what was removed as about what was broadcast, and answers that only cover the positive message miss half the impact.
> - Producing a list of facts with no ranking. Level 5 needs a judgement on which impact mattered most, not a summary of all of them.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Goebbels held that the best propaganda works invisibly, which suggests the intended impact was to make Nazi assumptions feel like common sense rather than like political argument.
> - The People's Receiver was built with a deliberately short range, so it could pick up German stations but not foreign broadcasts.
> - Music policy shows the same pattern of promotion and exclusion, with Wagner, Beethoven and Bach promoted while Jewish composers were censored and a monument to Mendelssohn was removed in 1936.
> - The Nazi Party made around 1300 films, and newsreels of German achievements were shown before feature films, so audiences received propaganda even when seeking entertainment.
> - Continued youth nonconformity, and the survival of private grumbling, indicate that saturation did not guarantee belief.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Distinguish between what propaganda promoted and what it suppressed. Treating these as two separate facets is the quickest way to show range.
> - Impact means effect on people, so keep asking what a given measure changed about what Germans knew, felt or did.

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis turned Germany into a police state.**

What was the role of the Gestapo?
parts.solutionMd:
The Gestapo was the Nazi secret police, created by Hermann Goering to 'investigate and combat all attempts to threaten the state', and led by Reinhard Heydrich from 1934 [1]. Its members wore plain clothes so that they could not be easily identified [1]. They tapped phones, spied on opponents, and arrested, questioned and tortured suspects, with around 160,000 people arrested for political crimes in 1939 [1]. They could send people straight to a concentration camp using protective custody, and deliberately released information about camp conditions in order to spread fear [1].

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis wanted to display the strength of the new Germany.**

Describe how the Nazis used rallies.
parts.solutionMd:
Rallies became more frequent after Hitler was declared Fuhrer in 1934, and were used to create a sense of unity and to celebrate occasions such as Hitler's birthday [1]. They advertised the strength of the German army, which broke the military restrictions of the Treaty of Versailles [1]. Nuremberg was chosen to host annual rallies from 1933 to 1938, with the grounds designed by Hitler's favourite architect, Albert Speer [1]. The 1934 Nuremberg rally was attended by 200,000 people and used 152 searchlights as pillars of light, known as the 'Cathedral of Light', and was filmed by Leni Riefenstahl as Triumph of the Will [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Persecution of Jewish people began as soon as the Nazis took power.**

parts.solutionMd:
In March 1933 the Nazi Party announced a boycott of Jewish businesses and professions such as doctors and lawyers, and in April Jewish civil servants and teachers were sacked [1]. parts.problemMd:
**Most opposition to the Nazis in Germany was private rather than public.**

Why was there little active opposition to the Nazi regime?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the strongest opposition had already been destroyed. By July 1933 all political parties except the NSDAP and all trade unions had been banned, and the Night of the Long Knives removed opposition inside the Nazi Party itself [R]. The SS, the SD and the Gestapo then ran a police state in which around 160,000 people were arrested for political crimes in 1939, and details of conditions in camps such as Dachau were deliberately leaked [R]. This mattered because ordinary citizens reported 80% of political crimes while the Gestapo uncovered only 10%: nobody knew which neighbour would inform, so opposition had to stay private to be survivable [E].

A second reason was that many Germans had reasons to be satisfied. Four million people joined the Nazi Party between 1933 and 1939, unemployment fell, women were rewarded for having children, and young people joined the Nazi youth groups [R]. Censorship banned criticism, propaganda built a cult of personality around Hitler, and the return of the Saar in 1935 showed the Treaty of Versailles being reversed [R]. This explains the lack of opposition because resistance requires believing something better is possible, and for many Germans the regime appeared to be delivering what the Weimar Republic had not [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis targeted several minority groups within Germany.**

Why did the Nazis persecute minority groups?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that persecution followed directly from Nazi racial beliefs. The Nazis believed in eugenics and racial hygiene, holding that Aryans should reproduce only with Aryans and that the 'undesirable' should be prevented from having children [R]. In Mein Kampf Hitler set out a racial hierarchy with Aryans at the top, Slavs as Untermenschen or sub-humans, and Jewish and Black people at the bottom, and he blamed Germany's defeat in the First World War on the 'pollution' of the Aryan race [R]. This explains the persecution because if a nation's strength depended on its racial purity, then removing those the Nazis classed as impure was not cruelty but policy [E].

A second reason was that minorities were useful as scapegoats. Anti-semitism had been common across Europe for centuries and was strong in Germany, and Jewish people were blamed both for the surrender of 1918 and for the two economic depressions [R]. The Nazis claimed that Roma did not work or pay enough taxes, that 'asocials' were a drain on the economy, and that disabled people were a burden on society [R]. This mattered because it gave Germans a single visible explanation for complicated problems, and blaming a minority united the majority behind the regime [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Goebbels became Minister for People's Enlightenment and Propaganda in 1933.**

Why was Goebbels important to Nazi control of Germany?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Goebbels controlled what Germans were able to know. As Minister for People's Enlightenment and Propaganda from 1933 he told journalists what they could publish, closed around 1,600 newspapers in 1935, and increased Nazi control of the press from 3% of newspapers in 1933 to most of them by 1939 [R]. He censored most radio stations and introduced the Volksempfanger in 1933, a receiver costing 35 Reichsmarks, about a week's wages, and deliberately short-range so foreign stations could not be picked up [R]. This mattered because a German who could not read an independent newspaper or hear a foreign broadcast had no way of testing what the government told them [E].

A second reason was that he made the regime look powerful and legitimate. Rallies were held annually at Nuremberg from 1933 to 1938, the 1934 rally drew 200,000 people and used 152 searchlights to create the 'Cathedral of Light', and Leni Riefenstahl filmed it as Triumph of the Will [R]. The party made 1,300 films, and the 1936 Berlin Olympics displayed swastikas throughout the largest stadium in the world [R]. This was important because terror can produce silence but not enthusiasm, and Goebbels' work was what turned obedience into the appearance of genuine national unity [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis ruled Germany from 1933 until 1945.**

'Most Germans supported the Nazi regime.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Nazis had real popular support and an enormous apparatus of terror at the same time. The difficulty is that neither fact explains the other away [R].

The evidence of support is substantial. Four million people joined the Nazi Party between 1933 and 1939, unemployment fell, women were rewarded for marrying and having children, and young people joined the Nazi youth groups in large numbers [R]. After Hindenburg's death 90% of the public voted in favour of Hitler becoming Fuhrer [R]. Many were willing to accept a regime that was reversing the Treaty of Versailles and had ended the chaos of the Depression [E].

Many Germans went further than acceptance. The Gestapo uncovered only around 10% of political crimes, while 80% were reported by ordinary citizens, and towns such as Hamburg and Frankfurt had only 40 to 50 Gestapo agents [R]. Germans also took part in the boycotts of 1933 and in Kristallnacht in 1938 [R]. A police state that thin on the ground only works because the population is willing to do its work for it [A].

However, the regime still needed force. The SS grew from 52,000 in 1933 to 290,000 by 1939, Dachau opened in 1933, and executions rose from eight between 1930 and 1932 to 534 between 1934 and 1939 [R]. A government confident of its support does not need that machinery [A].

Opposition also came from every part of society. The Confessing Church was joined by 6,000 churches, Cardinal Galen publicly exposed the T-4 programme in 1941, over 700 Edelweiss Pirates were arrested in 1942, the White Rose leaders Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in 1943, and 4,900 Germans were executed after the July 1944 plot [R]. Resistance reached even into the army [E].

The statement is true to a large extent, and the T-4 programme proves why. Public outrage forced the government to end it officially in 1941, which shows that Germans could stop a Nazi policy when enough of them objected [A]. That is the decisive point: if opposition worked when it was attempted, then the absence of opposition to everything else cannot be explained by terror alone. Most Germans supported or were prepared to accept most of what the regime did [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Goebbels aimed to control every aspect of German cultural life.**

How effectively did the Nazis control culture and the media? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Nazis were extremely successful at removing every alternative source of information. They were markedly less successful at making Germans believe what replaced it [R].

Control of the press and radio was almost total. Around 1,600 newspapers were closed in 1935, Nazi control rose from 3% of newspapers in 1933 to most of them by 1939, and Nazi papers dominated what Germans could read [R]. The Volksempfanger radio of 1933 cost 35 Reichsmarks, was deliberately short-range so foreign stations could not be received, and made up 75% of all radio sales in 1934 [R]. Employers were required to put radios in workplaces, so Nazi broadcasting reached Germans who had never chosen to listen [E].

The arts were reorganised just as thoroughly. The Reich Chamber of Culture was created in 1933, and anyone refused membership was forbidden to teach, produce or sell their work [R]. Over 12,000 paintings were removed from galleries in 1936, around 2,500 writers were banned, students burned 20,000 books in Berlin in May 1933, and the party produced 1,300 films [R]. An artist or author who would not conform simply could not work [A].

However, Germans found ways around the controls. The Swing Youth listened to banned jazz, the White Rose published anti-Nazi leaflets from Munich University in 1943, and anti-Nazi jokes were common despite the risk of denunciation [R]. Removing alternatives did not remove the appetite for them [A].

Controlling information also failed to control opinion. Cardinal Galen revealed the T-4 killings in 1941 and public outrage forced the programme to end officially, despite everything Goebbels controlled [R]. At the 1936 Olympics, the regime's own showcase, Jesse Owens won four gold medals and became the most successful athlete of the games, contradicting Nazi racial claims in front of the world [E].

Nazi control of culture and the media was therefore highly effective but not complete. As censorship it worked almost perfectly: by 1939 an ordinary German had little access to any account the regime had not approved [A]. As persuasion it worked less well, because the groups most exposed to it, the young, produced the most visible cultural resistance. The Nazis could decide what Germans heard; they could not fully decide what Germans thought about it [A].

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis used both fear and persuasion to govern Germany.**

Which was more important to Nazi control of Germany: terror or propaganda? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Terror explains why Germans did not speak against the regime. Propaganda explains why so many of them did not want to [R].

The apparatus of terror was real and it grew. The SS expanded from 52,000 members in 1933 to 290,000 by 1939, the Gestapo from 6,500 in 1937 to 20,000, and the SD gathered intelligence on party members and minority groups [R]. Dachau opened in 1933 as the first concentration camp, and the Gestapo could send people there directly through protective custody [R]. Around 160,000 people were arrested for political crimes in 1939 [E].

The courts made that terror legal. Trial by jury was abolished so judges alone decided cases, and the People's Court heard treason cases in secret with no right of appeal [R]. Executions rose from eight between 1930 and 1932 to 534 between 1934 and 1939 [R]. Opposition therefore risked not just arrest but death, through a system that looked lawful [A]. Even so, the machinery of terror was thinly spread: Hamburg and Frankfurt had only 40 to 50 Gestapo agents each, and the Gestapo itself uncovered just 10% of political crimes, relying on ordinary citizens to report the other 80% [R].

Propaganda, however, reached everyone rather than a minority. Goebbels closed 1,600 newspapers in 1935 and took Nazi control of the press from 3% in 1933 to most of it by 1939, while the cheap, short-range Volksempfanger made up 75% of radio sales in 1934 [R]. Rallies at Nuremberg drew 200,000 people, and the party made 1,300 films [R]. A German might never meet the Gestapo, but could not avoid the radio [E].

It also produced belief rather than mere silence. Four million people joined the Nazi Party between 1933 and 1939, and 90% voted for Hitler to become Fuhrer in 1934 [R]. Propaganda created a cult of personality that terror could never have generated [A].

Propaganda was more important, and the Gestapo's own thin staffing, set out above, shows why. A police force with only 40 to 50 agents in cities the size of Hamburg and Frankfurt, uncovering just 10% of political crimes itself, could not have terrorised a nation of 60 million by itself [A]. It worked because Germans believed it was everywhere and were willing to inform on each other, and that belief was manufactured. Terror did the arresting, but propaganda supplied both the informers and the fear [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the persecution of minority groups in Nazi Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Nazi persecution followed from a set of racial beliefs. The Nazis held to eugenics and racial hygiene, believing that Aryan Germans should reproduce only with other Aryans and that the 'undesirable' should be prevented from having children [R]. In Mein Kampf Hitler set out a racial hierarchy in which Aryans were superior, the Slavs of Eastern Europe were Untermenschen or sub-humans, and Jewish and Black people were placed lowest of all [R]. Different groups were then given different justifications: the Nazis claimed that Roma did not work or pay enough taxes, that homosexuals lowered moral standards because they could not form a traditional family, that 'asocials' were a drain on the economy, and that disabled people were a burden on society [D].

The Roma were persecuted from the very beginning. There were around 26,000 Roma in Germany in the early 1930s, and in 1933 they were arrested as social nuisances and sent to concentration camps [R]. From 1935 some were banned from marrying other Germans, and in 1936 some were forced to live in special camps with poor living conditions [R]. In 1938 Roma were banned from travelling in groups and lost their German citizenship if they failed a racial characteristics test, and in 1939 orders were given to remove all Roma from Germany [R].

Homosexuals and disabled people were targeted through the law. Stronger laws against homosexuality were introduced in 1935, around 4,000 men were imprisoned by 1936 and around 8,000 by 1938, and in total around 100,000 people were arrested, of whom 10,000 were sent to concentration camps and made to wear a pink triangle [R]. For disabled people the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring was passed in 1933, and by 1939 around 400,000 people had been sterilised [R]. The T-4 programme began in 1939 and killed disabled people using carbon monoxide, with the Einsatzgruppen developing techniques later used in the Final Solution [R]. Public outrage forced the official end of T-4 in 1941, although it continued secretly and killed an estimated 250,000 people [D].

Persecution widened sharply during the war. 'Asocials' were arrested by the Gestapo and the SS, sent to concentration camps and made to wear black triangles, and many died from exhaustion, beatings and executions [R]. From 1939 Jewish people were evicted into sealed ghettos, from 1941 all were forced to wear the Star of David and forbidden to leave the country, and between 1941 and 1942 the Einsatzgruppen rounded up and killed Jewish people and Slavs in Eastern Europe [R]. The Wannsee Conference of January 1942 agreed the 'Final Solution', and six extermination camps were built, the most notorious being Auschwitz-Birkenau [R]. By 1945 around 11 million people had died as victims of Nazi persecution, including roughly 6 million Jewish people [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of opposition to the Nazi regime.
parts.solutionMd:
Political opposition was driven underground almost immediately. Trade unions were banned in 1933, but some continued illegally, encouraging workers to report sick or damage factory machinery and distributing leaflets calling for strikes [R]. The Social Democrats campaigned against the Nazis from abroad, while Communists and other left-wing groups met in secret and circulated pamphlets, anti-Nazi newspapers and jokes about Hitler [R]. Ordinary Germans also resisted in small ways, telling anti-Nazi jokes despite the risk of denunciation, or refusing to give the straight-armed salute or say 'Heil Hitler' [D].

The Churches produced some of the most public opposition. After the Concordat with the Pope failed, the Nazis shut Catholic schools and sent around 400 priests to Dachau, and in 1937 Pope Pius XI denounced the Nazis as anti-Christian [R]. Pastor Martin Niemoller resisted Nazi control of the Protestant Church by founding the Pastors' Emergency League, and the Confessing Church created in 1934 was joined by 6,000 churches [R]. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who helped create the Confessing Church, was banned from preaching by the Gestapo in 1937, helped Jewish people escape Germany, and was executed in 1945 for conspiring to assassinate Hitler [R]. Paul Schneider spoke out against Goebbels, was imprisoned in 1937 and executed in 1939 [R]. Cardinal Galen had criticised the Nazis since 1934 and in 1941 revealed the killing of disabled people, and Goebbels chose not to execute him for fear that the population of Munster 'could be regarded as lost to the war effort' [D].

Young people formed the most visible cultural resistance. The Swing Youth listened to the jazz music Hitler had banned, and the Edelweiss Pirates resisted the Hitler Youth both passively and violently, going on camping trips and singing folk songs [R]. Over 700 Edelweiss Pirates were arrested in 1942, and after members in Cologne killed the local Gestapo chief in 1944, twelve of them were publicly hanged [R]. The White Rose group was formed at Munich University in 1943 and opposed the government through leaflets and marches, and its leaders Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested and executed by guillotine in 1943 [R].

Opposition also reached the conservative elite and the army. Officers such as General Ludwig Beck secretly communicated with the British, while businessmen and members of the upper classes met in secret in groups such as the Kreisau Circle [R]. Admiral Canaris, who feared a repeat of the failure of the Schlieffen Plan, tried to persuade senior officers to join a coup against Hitler, and was arrested and executed in 1944 [R]. In July 1944, during Operation Valkyrie, the army officer Claus von Stauffenberg carried a briefcase containing a bomb into the Wolf's Lair headquarters at Rastenburg [R]. Hitler survived because the briefcase had been placed behind the heavy wooden leg of the conference table, and afterwards he ordered the execution of 4,900 Germans [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which Nazi Germany was a totalitarian state.
parts.solutionMd:
Totalitarianism means a government with complete control over its citizens. Nazi Germany came closer to it than any previous German state, and the question is whether 'complete' is the right word [R].

The first facet is the machinery of the police state, which was genuinely comprehensive. The SS grew from 52,000 members in 1933 to 290,000 by 1939 and 800,000 by 1944, the Gestapo from 6,500 in 1937 to 20,000 by 1939, and the SD, created in 1931, became the only agency collecting intelligence from 1934 [R]. Dachau opened in 1933, the Gestapo could send people there directly through protective custody, and around 160,000 people were arrested for political crimes in 1939 [R]. This supports the claim because there was no area of life the regime could not reach: the SD gathered information on Nazi Party members as well as on opponents, so even loyalty was monitored [E].

The second facet is that the law offered no protection. Trial by jury was abolished so that judges alone decided cases, judges had to join the National Socialist League for the Maintenance of the Law or be dismissed, and from 1936 they wore the swastika [R]. The People's Court heard treason cases in secret with no right of appeal, and executions rose from eight between 1930 and 1932 to 534 between 1934 and 1939 [R]. A state that controls the courts as well as the police has removed the last institution capable of restraining it [A].

The third facet is control of what Germans could know and think. Around 1,600 newspapers were closed in 1935 and Nazi control of the press rose from 3% in 1933 to most of it by 1939, while the deliberately short-range Volksempfanger made up 75% of radio sales in 1934 [R]. The Reich Chamber of Culture, created in 1933, meant that artists, musicians, writers and film-makers refused membership could not work at all, and 2,500 writers were banned [R]. Religion was brought under the same control: Hitler signed a Concordat with the Pope in July 1933 under which Catholic priests agreed not to interfere in politics, while Ludwig Muller was installed as Reich Bishop of a unified Protestant Reich Church which around 2,000 individual churches joined, some displaying the swastika [R]. Many Germans also agreed with the regime, since four million joined the Party between 1933 and 1939 and 90% voted for Hitler to become Fuhrer [E].

However, the regime never eliminated opposition. The Confessing Church was joined by 6,000 churches, over 700 Edelweiss Pirates were arrested in 1942, the White Rose published leaflets from Munich University in 1943, and the July 1944 plot came from inside the army itself [R]. Cardinal Galen criticised the Nazis publicly from 1934 and was never executed, because Goebbels feared losing Munster to the war effort [A]. A truly totalitarian state does not have to calculate whether it can afford to punish a critic [A]. The Concordat also collapsed: by 1937 the Pope had issued 'With Burning Anxiety', calling Hitler a 'mad prophet', and the Confessing Church had been founded in direct opposition to the Reich Church [R].

More tellingly, public opinion could still change policy. Outrage at the T-4 programme forced the government to end it officially in 1941, and although the killing continued in secret, the Nazis had been obliged to retreat publicly [R]. The regime also relied on its citizens rather than commanding them: the Gestapo uncovered only 10% of political crimes while ordinary Germans reported 80%, and towns as large as Hamburg and Frankfurt had only 40 to 50 agents [R]. That is not the profile of a state in complete control; it is the profile of one that had made itself popular enough to be policed voluntarily [E].

Nazi Germany was a totalitarian state to a large extent, but its control rested on consent as much as on command. In every formal respect the claim holds: there was one party, no independent courts, no free press and no legal protection from arrest [A]. Yet the T-4 retreat, the survival of Cardinal Galen and the thinness of the Gestapo all point the same way, towards a regime that governed with the cooperation of most Germans rather than against them. The Nazis achieved totalitarian power but never total control, and the difference was made up by a population largely willing to be governed [A].

> - You will receive 16-20 marks if your essay presents more than one facet with explanations supporting them, and attempts a judgement which is only partially supported.
> - You will be awarded 11-15 marks if your essay presents one or more facets but explains only one of them, and any judgement is unsupported.

> - You will be awarded 1-5 marks if your essay presents general knowledge of the topic, describes or identifies some points with limited focus, and makes no real attempt at judgement.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 25 marks include:
> 
> - Never defining totalitarianism. The whole question turns on what 'complete control' would require, so the definition has to be stated.
> - Describing the SS, SD and Gestapo in turn without ever testing the claim in the question.
> - Listing opposition groups without asking whether any of them limited what the regime could do.
> - Treating the existence of opposition as proof that Germany was not totalitarian. Opposition existed in every dictatorship, and the argument has to be about whether it constrained the state.
> - Reaching a judgement in the final sentence that the essay has not argued for.
>

>

> 
> - Nazi policies towards women, young people, the Churches and culture were all intended to strengthen state control of private life.
> - Local government was abolished in January 1934, when the regional Lander parliaments were replaced with Nazi governors.
> - Many Germans conformed rather than believed, and did nothing to protect minority groups, which supports the case for effective control.
> - Youth groups such as the Swing Youth and Edelweiss Pirates challenged Nazi ideology directly, which suggests control over the young was incomplete.
> - Opposition existed within the army, and Admiral Canaris tried to organise a coup, so even the armed forces were not fully controlled.
> - Candidates may argue that Nazi Germany became more totalitarian over time, since control tightened between 1933 and 1939 and then again during the war.
> - A strong judgement may distinguish between totalitarian ambition, which the Nazis certainly had, and totalitarian achievement, which is harder to demonstrate.

> - Set out your line of argument and keep it consistent to the conclusion. Avoid 'in this essay I will'; frame the facets instead.

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which opposition threatened the Nazi regime.
parts.solutionMd:
Opposition to the Nazis existed in every part of German society, from schoolchildren to generals. Whether any of it threatened the regime is a different question from whether it existed [R].

The first facet is political and workplace opposition, which was persistent but powerless. Trade unions were banned in 1933, yet some operated illegally, encouraging workers to report sick or damage machinery and distributing leaflets calling for strikes, while the Social Democrats campaigned from abroad and Communists circulated pamphlets and anti-Nazi newspapers [R]. This mattered very little to the regime's survival, because the organisations that could have coordinated resistance had been destroyed: by July 1933 every party except the NSDAP was banned, and the Night of the Long Knives had removed opposition inside the party itself [E]. Censorship and propaganda then removed any means of reaching a wider audience, while the police state made discovery likely, since ordinary citizens reported 80% of political crimes [R].

The second facet is youth opposition, which was culturally visible but politically slight. The Swing Youth listened to banned jazz, the Edelweiss Pirates went camping and sang folk songs in deliberate contrast to the Hitler Youth, and the White Rose group published anti-Nazi leaflets from Munich University in 1943 [R]. The state's response shows how seriously it took them: over 700 Edelweiss Pirates were arrested in 1942, twelve were publicly hanged after members in Cologne killed the local Gestapo chief in 1944, and Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed by guillotine in 1943 [R]. Yet none of this could remove a government, and the executions were possible precisely because the groups were small enough to destroy [A].

The third facet is the Churches, which came closest to forcing the regime to change course. Pastor Martin Niemoller founded the Pastors' Emergency League and the Confessing Church of 1934 was joined by 6,000 churches, while the Nazis sent around 400 priests to Dachau and Pope Pius XI denounced them as anti-Christian in 1937 [R]. Cardinal Galen had criticised the Nazis since 1934 and revealed the killing of disabled people in 1941, and Goebbels decided against executing him for fear that the population of Munster 'could be regarded as lost to the war effort' [R]. This was a genuine threat, because it shows the regime calculating that it could not afford to punish a popular critic during a war [E].

The most dangerous opposition came from the army. Admiral Canaris tried to persuade senior officers to join a coup, and in July 1944 Claus von Stauffenberg carried a bomb into the Wolf's Lair at Rastenburg during Operation Valkyrie [R]. Hitler survived only because the briefcase had been placed behind the heavy leg of the conference table [R]. This came nearer to ending Nazi rule than anything else, since it aimed at Hitler himself and was carried out by men with the means to seize power [A].

However, the regime's response demonstrated its strength rather than its fragility. Hitler ordered the execution of 4,900 Germans after the July plot, and Canaris was arrested and executed in 1944 [R]. Timing also mattered: the plot came in 1944, after the failure of Operation Barbarossa had turned many Germans against the Party, so it reflected a regime already losing a war rather than one being overthrown from within [A]. Until then most Germans had publicly supported the war, believing Germany was right to invade Poland in 1939, and the Nazis controlled information about how it was going [R]. Even the plotters' own aim was limited: they believed killing Hitler would give Germany a better negotiating position rather than restore democracy [R].

Opposition threatened the Nazi regime only to a limited extent, though it was more substantial than the phrase 'no opposition' allows. Political, workplace and youth resistance was courageous but incapable of removing a government that controlled the police, the courts and the media [A]. Two exceptions stand out: Galen's success over the T-4 programme, which forced a public retreat in 1941, and the July 1944 bomb, which came within feet of killing Hitler. Both show what might have been possible, and both were isolated. The regime was threatened by individuals and never by a movement, and that is why it survived until it was destroyed from outside [A].

name: Was the Weimar Republic Doomed From the Start?

parts.problemMd:
The Kaiser's Germany collapsed at the end of the First World War.

What happened in Germany during the revolution of November 1918?
parts.solutionMd:
Unrest that had begun with a naval mutiny at Kiel spread across the country, and there were mass protests on the streets of Berlin [1]. In Munich the workers went on general strike on 7 November and declared Bavaria a separate communist state, while in Hanover soldiers joined the workers and rioted [1]. Councils of workers and soldiers were set up in many towns to replace the Kaiser's local authorities [1]. On 9 November the Kaiser's military advisers told him he had to abdicate, and the following day he escaped by train to the Netherlands [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point, up to a maximum of 4.
> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Explaining why the revolution happened. Food shortages, the naval blockade and war weariness are reasons, and reasons earn no credit on a recall question.
> - Running on into 1919. The Spartacist uprising, the elections and the Constitution all come after the events this question asks about.
> - Writing only that 'the Kaiser abdicated'. That is one point; three more are needed.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Max von Baden, whom the Kaiser had appointed Chancellor on 3 October, announced the abdication without the Kaiser's consent or knowledge.
> - Once Berlin was lost the Kaiser had effectively lost control of the whole country.
> - Max von Baden then resigned and handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert, leader of the SPD.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep each event in its own sentence so the examiner can count them.
> - Dates are worth having, and each one counts as a point in its own right: 7 November for Munich, 9 November for the abdication and 10 November for the flight to the Netherlands.
> - Four events is the whole task. Save the causes and the consequences for the 6-mark and 10-mark questions.

parts.problemMd:
The Weimar Republic tried to improve living standards in the 1920s.

Why did the Weimar Republic's welfare reforms benefit some Germans more than others?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that the reforms were built around regular industrial employment [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 worked by diverting three per cent of the wages of 16.4 million workers into a fund, which then paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone insured who lost their job or fell ill. A scheme funded out of wage packets can only protect people who receive wage packets. The other main gains worked the same way, since the working week was cut from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 in 1927 and real wages rose by 25 per cent between 1925 and 1928. All of this reached workers in towns and cities, and almost none of it reached a farm labourer or a smallholder [E].

A second reason is that farming was suffering from problems the reforms never touched [R]. Agricultural communities were caught between heavy debt, falling prices for what they produced and rising taxes, and no welfare measure addressed any of those three things. The result was that the gap widened rather than closed: while town workers were getting shorter hours, insurance and new housing, the income of agricultural workers fell to 44 per cent below the national average by 1929. Reforms that help one group while another group's underlying position gets worse will always look unfair to the second group [E].

**[6 marks]**

> - Explanation - [E]

> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.

> - Drifting into the hyperinflation of 1923. The reforms discussed here belong to the later 1920s, after the currency had been stabilised.

> - The Reich Pension Law paid over 1.3 million widows and ex-soldiers, which cut across town and country, but it took a very large share of government spending and so limited what could be spent elsewhere.

parts.problemMd:
The Weimar Republic tried to improve living standards in the 1920s.

How far did the lives of women improve in the Weimar Republic? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
In law and in public life the change was dramatic [R]. The Weimar Constitution gave every woman over 21 the vote on exactly the same terms as men, which few European countries had done, and Article 109 declared marriage an equal legal partnership and gave women the right to enter all professions on an equal footing. German women used these rights rather than simply holding them: turnout among women voters was usually around 90 per cent, and 111 women were elected as party representatives to the Reichstag in 1920. A country that had been ruled by a Kaiser a few years earlier now had women helping to make its laws [E].

There was also a real change in how women could live [R]. More women worked as teachers and doctors, the retail sector took on large numbers of women part-time, and the 'New Woman' of the 1920s cut her hair short, wore make-up, smoked and drank in public and put a career ahead of becoming a wife and mother. These were freedoms no earlier generation of German women had enjoyed [E].

Against this, the position at work barely moved and in one respect went backwards [R]. In 1918 around 75 per cent of women were in employment; by 1925 that had fallen to about 36 per cent, roughly where it had been before the First World War. Many employers simply ignored Article 109 and appointed men, women who did hold jobs were paid about a third less than men doing equivalent work, and a woman was still expected to give up her job when she married. At the top the door stayed shut, and Germany had only 36 female judges as late as 1933. A legal right that employers can disregard is not the same as an improved life [E].

The gains also created their own opposition [R]. The right wing blamed the 'New Woman' for destroying the traditional family, Hitler argued she was taking jobs from working-class men and campaigned to send women back to the home, and the male-dominated trade unions resented 'double earners' because they believed equality for women would damage male workers. This matters because it meant the improvements were politically fragile rather than settled [A].

I partially agree that women's lives improved [A]. As citizens they gained more in a decade than in the previous century, and the vote, Article 109 and a real presence in the Reichstag are not small things. But most women experienced their lives through work and marriage rather than through the constitution, and there the improvement was thin: fewer women in jobs than in 1918, a third less pay, and a career that ended at the altar. The lives of women improved most in the areas the state could change by law, and least in the areas that depended on employers and on what society expected of them [A].

**[10 marks]**

> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the Spartacist uprising in 1919.
parts.solutionMd:
One of the biggest challenges the newly formed Weimar Republic faced was the Spartacist uprising that took place in January 1919 in Berlin. A radical left-wing group, the Spartacist League, led the uprising [R]. Its leaders, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, were inspired by the Russian Revolution and Marxist ideology. The main aim of the uprising was to overthrow the German Republic, led by Friedrich Ebert, and set up a Soviet-style government in Germany. They envisioned a republic of workers' and soldiers' councils, or soviets, and equal sharing of wealth and power [E].

The immediate cause of the uprising was the dismissal of the left-wing police chief of Berlin, Emil Eichhorn, by Ebert on 4 January 1919. He was replaced by an MSPD minister. As a result, the Spartacists formed a Revolutionary Committee to plan the uprising and called for a general strike, staged protests and held demonstrations [R]. More than 100,000 workers took to the streets, seizing key buildings in Berlin such as newspaper offices and erecting barricades in the streets. The uprising was not a peaceful one, and there were violent clashes between government forces and the Spartacists [E].

Ebert had to seek help from the Freikorps, a right-wing group of former soldiers who strongly opposed communism, because the government did not have its own reliable army. He signed a deal with the Freikorps and used them and the army to crush the uprising [R]. The Freikorps used brutal force, not hesitating to fire on protestors with machine guns to crush the rebellion. Within a week the uprising was suppressed, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of workers [E]. On 15 January 1919 the Freikorps arrested and murdered the leaders of the Spartacist movement, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg. Their deaths were a serious setback to the communist movement in Germany. It also exposed how much the new Weimar Republic relied on right-wing military groups to maintain order [E].

The Spartacist uprising was a test for the Weimar Republic. Although it failed, it exposed the divisions in German society between communists, social democrats and right-wing forces. It also showed Ebert's dependence on the Freikorps, which would later pose its own threat to the stability of the Republic [E].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of political disorder in Weimar Germany between 1919 and 1923.
parts.solutionMd:
Between 1919 and 1923, Weimar Germany had to face political disorder, which led to severe consequences and affected the survival and stability of the new republic. Trust and confidence of ordinary people in the government were influenced by extremist uprisings, political violence, and government responses [E]. In this essay, I will discuss how these factors impacted the Weimar government.

One important impact of political disorder was the shaking of public trust in the republic. The Spartacist uprising of 1919 was the first blow. The government hired the Freikorps to crush the uprising, due to which the republic looked weak to the people. The hiring of violent paramilitary groups further aggravated the situation [E]. There were some other left-wing revolts, such as the Ruhr Uprising of 1920, due to which many Germans were convinced that democracy was nothing but instability and chaos. Due to all these uprisings, the legitimacy of the new democratic system became questionable, and it seemed unable to defend itself without using violent methods [A]. The right-wing opposition also grew due to political disorder. The Kapp Putsch of 1920 and the Munich Putsch of 1923 also tried to overthrow the government, and revealed the nationalist groups that were growing in Germany [E]. Although both uprisings failed, they not only exposed the weaknesses of the government but also made it clear that parts of the army and judiciary were leaning towards the right. Another point to observe was that the right-wing rebels were punished lightly compared to the harsh treatment of the left-wing revolutionaries. This further established the belief that the Weimar Republic was fragile [A].

Secondly, the political disorder also led to economic consequences. It was immensely difficult to stabilise the economy or attract foreign investment when political turmoil was at its peak. After a missed reparations instalment, France occupied the Ruhr, and the Weimar government encouraged workers to go on strike. The government also printed extra currency to deal with economic problems, which led to hyperinflation [E]. During this phase many people lost their savings, and this created distrust of the government, especially among the middle class. Common people held the republic responsible for their hardships, which were exploited by extremist parties. Ideas such as the 'November Criminals' and the 'stab in the back' became popular at this time [A].

Lastly, daily activities such as schooling and community life were often disrupted by constant strikes, protests, and street fighting between different groups. In cities like Berlin, Munich and the Ruhr, families were worried about their safety as riots and violence became frequent [R]. There were shortages of food and basic goods, so people had to queue for hours to buy essentials such as bread. Malnutrition grew among poorer communities. Common people felt that life was chaotic and unpredictable, which contributed to frustration and tension [E].

On the other hand, it can be argued that even after political disorder, the Weimar government survived. Under Ebert's leadership, both left-wing and right-wing rebellions were suppressed. Due to this resilience the Weimar Republic survived until 1923, when Stresemann introduced reforms to stabilise Germany and establish some political and economic stability [A].

To conclude, the political disorder of 1919 to 1923 undermined faith in the Weimar Republic and strengthened extremist opposition. While the government did survive, the instability, violence and economic turmoil caused ordinary people to lose faith in democracy, which was later exploited by the Nazis [A].
