parts.problemMd: Write an account of cultural developments in Weimar Germany during the 1920s.
parts.solutionMd:
The Weimar years saw what is often called a cultural explosion. The government gave grants to artists and to cultural organisations such as theatres and libraries, and crucially it supported rather than censored new approaches to the arts. New technologies, particularly radio and film, gave German artists mediums that had not existed a generation earlier [R].

Painting moved in an experimental direction. Expressionist artists used grotesque and exaggerated figures in violent scenes, deliberately intending to make audiences uncomfortable so that they would question the society they lived in. Otto Dix, working in the New Objectivity style, produced work drawing attention to the difficulties faced by war veterans returning to Germany, including his 1927 piece Metropolis. George Grosz painted Grey Day in 1921, using expressionist techniques to convey the monotony of ordinary life [R].

Architecture and design were transformed by the Bauhaus movement, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. The school operated in three German cities, Weimar, Berlin and Dessau, between 1919 and 1933, and its teaching staff included the painter Paul Klee and the sculptor Oskar Schlemmer. Bauhaus design used geometric shapes to produce practical buildings, found beauty in technology, and used familiar materials in unfamiliar ways, going as far as constructing entire buildings from concrete. It inspired architects such as Erich Mendelsohn, who designed the Einstein Tower, an observatory at Potsdam built to resemble a rocket [R].

Cinema grew fastest of all. By 1929 there were roughly 500 cinemas across Germany, and German studios began to compete with American production. The Cabinet of Doctor Caligari, directed by Robert Wiene in 1920, was among the first horror films and contained what is generally regarded as the first plot twist ending in cinema. F. W. Murnau's Nosferatu of 1922 was the world's first vampire film. Metropolis, directed by Fritz Lang in 1926, was funded by the government through the organisation UFA at a cost of five million Reichsmarks, and used modernist science fiction to examine the effect of technology on modern life. Germany produced its first talking picture in 1930, and by 1932 some 3800 German cinemas could show films with sound [R].

City nightlife flourished alongside this. Berlin in particular offered cabaret, theatre and nightclubs, and these encouraged a far more liberal social atmosphere than pre-war Germany had known [R].

Not everyone welcomed the change. Extreme left-wing parties such as the KPD regarded government funding of culture as money that should have gone to workers in need. Extreme right-wing parties such as the NSDAP argued that Weimar culture was destroying German traditions and was responsible for a moral decline, and movements such as the Wandervogel campaigned for a return to traditional values. Weimar culture was therefore both one of the Republic's genuine achievements and one of the grievances its enemies used against it [R].

**[15 marks]**

> - **6-10 marks:** the account describes some events and developments relevant to the question. It is mostly supported by accurate historical knowledge and is structured in its approach.
> - **1-5 marks:** limited relevance to the question. Some accurate historical knowledge. Points are generally unconnected.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.

> 
> - Covering only one art form. An account confined to cinema, or to Bauhaus, has missed most of the period's range.
> - Naming works without saying anything about them. Listing Metropolis or Nosferatu earns little; saying what each did that was new earns the marks.
> - Drifting into Nazi cultural policy. The Reich Chamber of Culture and the banning of modern art belong after 1933 and to a different question.
> - Forgetting the government's role. Public funding and the absence of censorship are what made the cultural explosion possible.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Weimar culture horrified the conservative upper classes, who had traditionally controlled Germany's cultural output and now found they no longer did.
> - Many of the leading artists held strong left-wing views, which is part of why the right treated their work as a political threat rather than simply as bad art.
> - Expressionist works were often deliberately open to several interpretations, which itself challenged the idea that the educated classes should decide what art meant.
> - Metropolis was unsuccessful on release but has influenced later film-making considerably, including Star Wars.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of the Weimar Constitution on the stability of the Republic.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is the democratic legitimacy the constitution created.** The National Assembly met at Weimar in February 1919 and took six months to write the constitution, which passed by 262 votes to 75. It gave the vote to all men and women aged 21 and over, an elected Reichstag every four years and an elected president every seven. This mattered for stability because Germany under the Kaiser had no written constitution at all and the Kaiser had made and changed laws as he pleased. The new system gave the Republic a claim on its citizens' loyalty that the old regime never had, and the first election in January 1919 drew an 82 per cent turnout, with the moderate SPD taking 40 per cent and the Centre Party 20 per cent. On this facet the constitution was a stabilising force [E].

**The second facet is proportional representation and the coalition governments it produced.** One seat was awarded for roughly every 60,000 votes, which guaranteed that smaller parties were represented in the Reichstag. The consequence was that no single party ever won a majority. There were nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923 alone, and because policy had to be agreed between partners it lacked vision and took far longer to pass. A system that was designed to be fair therefore made decisive government almost impossible, and it did so precisely in the years when Germany faced reparations, the occupation of the Ruhr and hyperinflation. Here the constitution actively worked against stability [E].

**The third facet is Article 48.** This allowed the chancellor to ask the president to pass emergency laws without the support of the Reichstag. It was included as a safeguard for genuine crises, but it quickly became a substitute for government by consent: Ebert used it 63 times between 1923 and 1924, and the abuse of the article continued into the 1930s. The significance is that the constitution contained, in writing, a lawful route around parliament. Once ministers grew used to governing that way, the Reichstag's authority was steadily hollowed out from within [E].

**The fourth facet is what the constitution could not reach.** Its checks and balances were carefully designed to stop any one person taking ultimate power, and the Reichsrat could challenge laws unless two thirds of the Reichstag overruled it. None of this subdued the extremist parties, who went on attacking the Republic violently, and the government still had to rely on force to survive, as it did against the Spartacists in 1919. Constitutional design could regulate how power was exercised, but it could not by itself create acceptance of the Republic among those who rejected democracy altogether [E].

**Judgement.** Of these, Article 48 was the most important in the long run, because it was the mechanism through which parliamentary government was ultimately set aside [A]. But it only became important because of the second facet: proportional representation fragmented the Reichstag so thoroughly that emergency rule came to look like the only way to govern at all. The deeper impact of the constitution was therefore not any single clause but the combination of the two, which together made weak coalitions normal and rule by decree routine [A].

That judgement should be qualified. The Republic did survive the crises of 1919 to 1923 and then stabilised markedly after 1924 under the same constitution, which suggests the document was not fatal in itself. Its impact was to leave the Republic with very little margin for error, so that when a crisis as severe as the Depression arrived, the constitutional weaknesses that had been survivable in the 1920s became decisive [A].

**[25 marks]**

> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**, the distinct aspects of the issue you choose to explain.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Listing the features of the constitution. Describing the president, the Reichstag and the Reichsrat is recall and will not reach the higher levels; every feature named must be turned into an argument about stability.
> - Explaining only the weaknesses. An answer that treats the constitution purely as a disaster is stuck on one facet and cannot pass 15 marks.
> - Ending with an unsupported verdict. Saying the constitution 'was the reason the Republic fell' without weighing the facets against one another is exactly the Level 3 to Level 4 boundary.
> - Jumping straight to 1933. Hitler's use of Article 48 is legitimate supporting material, but an answer that is really about the Nazi seizure of power has drifted off the question.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The Republic's association with the hated Treaty of Versailles damaged it from the start, which suggests the constitution's design mattered less than the circumstances of its birth.
> - Ebert's bargain with General Groener left the army outside civilian control, a weakness the constitution never addressed.
> - Falling turnout during the 1920s and 1930s suggests the constant elections the constitution required wore down public enthusiasm for voting rather than strengthening democratic habits.
> - After 1924 the same constitution presided over the Republic's most stable and prosperous years, which is strong evidence for the argument that economic conditions mattered more than constitutional design.

> - A qualification is worth having. Noting that the Republic stabilised after 1924 under the very same constitution shows the examiner you are testing your own conclusion.

parts.problemMd:
**Germany was in crisis by the end of 1918.**

Describe the effects of the First World War on Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Between 1914 and 1918 two million German soldiers died and four million more were wounded, among them Adolf Hitler, who was temporarily blinded by a mustard gas attack in October 1918 [1]. Germany's debt trebled, rising from 50 billion marks in 1914 to 150 billion marks in 1918 [1]. The German people were near starvation, because the British Navy had blockaded German ports so no food from overseas could enter the country [1]. The strain produced civil unrest, including the mutiny of the German navy at Kiel and Hamburg in October 1918 [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each distinct point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each distinct piece of information. Four separate points are needed for 4 marks.
> - Developing a point further does not earn an additional mark, so it is better to make a new point than to expand one you have already made.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the effects of the Treaty of Versailles instead. The treaty came after the war and is a separate cause of Germany's problems.
> - Explaining why Germany lost the war rather than describing what the war did to the country.
> - Writing about the war in general rather than about its effects on Germany.

parts.problemMd:
**The Weimar Republic faced a left-wing challenge in January 1919.**

Describe the events of the Spartacist Uprising.
parts.solutionMd:
The Weimar government sacked Emil Eichhorn, Berlin's police chief, who was popular among the workers, and Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht used this to begin the uprising on 4 January 1919 [1]. By 6 January Berlin was in chaos, with over 100,000 workers protesting on the streets after being encouraged to hold a general strike [1]. The Spartacists took control of the government's newspaper and various telegraph offices across Berlin [1]. Ebert ordered the Reichswehr to organise Freikorps units against them, the uprising ended on 13 January, and Luxemburg and Liebknecht were killed on 16 January [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Hyperinflation had destroyed the value of Germany's currency by 1923.**

What was the Rentenmark?
parts.solutionMd:
The Rentenmark was the new currency Stresemann created in November 1923, after the old mark had become worthless [1]. One Rentenmark was the equivalent of a trillion old marks, the largest old note had been for 100 trillion marks, and the government believed 400.3 billion trillion marks were in circulation [1]. Stresemann established a new state-owned bank, the Rentenbank, where the German public could bring their old marks to be exchanged for the new currency [1]. It was a gold standard currency, meaning its value matched the price of gold, which European countries trusted and which allowed German businesses to trade abroad again [1].

parts.problemMd:
**The Spartacists tried to seize control of Berlin in January 1919.**

Why did the Spartacist Uprising fail?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Ebert had allies the Spartacists could not match. The First World War had weakened the Reichswehr and there were too many protestors on the streets for it to cope alone, so Ebert ordered it to organise Freikorps units against the uprising [R]. The Freikorps were armed ex-soldiers who held extreme right-wing opinions and hated communists [R]. This was decisive because it meant the Spartacists faced experienced and heavily armed troops who were personally motivated to destroy them, while the rising itself consisted mainly of unarmed communist workers [E].

A second reason was that the uprising was poorly planned and led. Luxemburg and Liebknecht launched it on 4 January 1919 in response to the sacking of Berlin's police chief, Emil Eichhorn, rather than at a moment of their own choosing [R]. Their forces occupied the government's newspaper and telegraph offices but could not hold Berlin, and the rising was over by 13 January [R]. This mattered because a revolution begun as a reaction had no plan for what to do once the streets were taken, and killing Luxemburg and Liebknecht on 16 January then removed the leadership that might have organised another attempt [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The new German government signed the armistice in November 1918.**

Why did many Germans call their politicians the 'November Criminals'?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that most Germans did not believe they had lost the war. The Allies had not defeated the German Army in battle, and the army had retreated in November 1918 rather than being destroyed [R]. Many Germans therefore argued that the politicians had committed a 'dolchstoss', or stab in the back, and that the Weimar government had lied to them about the reality of surrendering to the Allies [R]. This explains the label, because if the army was undefeated then the only possible explanation for defeat was betrayal by politicians at home [E].

A second reason was the timing and the terms that followed. The name came from November, the month in which the government signed the armistice, and the same politicians then signed the Treaty of Versailles [R]. The treaty forced Germany to accept blame for the war under Article 231 and to pay 132 billion gold marks, and many Germans felt humiliated and weaker than the rest of Europe [R]. This mattered because the humiliation was permanently attached to the men who had signed, so the new Republic was blamed for the defeat rather than for anything it had actually done [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Stresemann became Germany's foreign minister in November 1923.**

Why was Stresemann's foreign policy important for Germany?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that his treaties ended Germany's isolation. As foreign minister from November 1923 Stresemann negotiated the Locarno Treaties in December 1925, obtained German membership of the League of Nations in September 1926 with a seat on its Council, and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in August 1928 alongside 61 other countries [R]. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 [R]. This mattered because the Treaty of Versailles had banned Germany from the League and excluded it from world politics, so being readmitted as an equal reversed the most humiliating part of the settlement without a war [E].

A second reason was the effect at home. Joining the League boosted German citizens' confidence in the Weimar Republic and gained support for moderate parties [R]. Between 1924 and 1928 the vote for the Nazi Party fell while the SPD gained steadily, there were no political assassinations between 1924 and 1929, and only six coalition governments formed in those five years [R]. This explains the importance of his foreign policy, because success abroad gave Germans a reason to believe the Republic could deliver what the Kaiser's Germany had lost, which drained support away from the extremists [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The National Assembly completed the Weimar Constitution in 1919.**

How successful was the Weimar Constitution? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Weimar Constitution gave Germany the most democratic system in Europe. Whether it worked depends on whether a democracy that cannot govern is a success [R].

Its protections were genuine. Written at Weimar in February 1919 and passed by 262 votes to 75, it gave every man and woman over 21 the vote, elected the Reichstag every four years and the president every seven, and used proportional representation so that one seat was awarded for every 60,000 votes [R]. Smaller parties were therefore represented rather than excluded, and no single group could seize the state, since the president chose the chancellor but the public chose the president [E].

It also spread power deliberately. The Reichstag and the Reichsrat worked together, the Lander kept control of schools and the police, and the Reichsrat could challenge laws unless two-thirds of the Reichstag overruled it [R]. For a country that had never had a written constitution under the Kaiser, who made and changed laws as he pleased, this was a transformation [E].

However, proportional representation made government almost impossible. No single party ever won a majority in the Reichstag, and there were nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923 alone [R]. Policies lacked vision and took far longer to pass, so the system that fairly represented every opinion could rarely act on any of them [A].

Article 48 then supplied the escape route. It allowed the chancellor to ask the president to pass emergency laws without the Reichstag, and Ebert used it 63 times between 1923 and 1924 [R]. A clause meant for genuine emergencies became the ordinary way of governing, and its abuse continued into the 1930s [A].

The constitution was therefore successful only to a limited extent. As a statement of rights it was admirable, and the freedoms it created were real [A]. But a constitution is judged by whether it lets a country be governed, and this one produced deadlock so reliably that its own presidents had to bypass it. It handed later politicians a legal method of ruling without parliament, which is the opposite of what its authors intended [A].

parts.problemMd:
**The Weimar Republic was attacked from both the left and the right.**

Which was the greater threat to the Weimar Republic: the Spartacist Uprising or the Kapp Putsch? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Spartacists wanted a different Germany; the Freikorps wanted a different government. That distinction decides which was the greater danger [R].

The Spartacist Uprising threatened the Republic's survival at its weakest moment. Beginning on 4 January 1919, before the Republic had even been elected, it put over 100,000 workers on the streets of Berlin and seized the government's newspaper and telegraph offices [R]. Ebert had no reliable army, since the First World War had weakened the Reichswehr [R]. A government that cannot control its own capital in its first month may not survive at all [E].

Its consequences also outlasted it. To defeat the rising Ebert had to use the Freikorps, armed right-wing ex-soldiers who hated communists, and the killing of Luxemburg and Liebknecht on 16 January made the left permanent enemies of the SPD [R]. The Republic therefore began by arming the very people who would attack it next, and by dividing the left against itself [A].

The Kapp Putsch, however, came from inside the state's own forces. In March 1920 Ebert planned to disband the Freikorps units in Berlin, so 5,000 of them under Wolfgang Kapp attempted to overthrow the government and invited the Kaiser to return [R]. The army would not fire on them, so the elected government had to flee its own capital [E].

Yet Kapp collapsed quickly. The lower classes would not support the Kaiser's return, having gained rights since his abdication, so the workers called a general strike which cut Berlin's gas, electricity, water and public transport, and after four days Kapp left the city [R]. Right-wing violence continued, with 376 political assassinations in the Republic's first three years [R].

The Kapp Putsch was the greater threat. The Spartacists were more visible and came first, but they were defeated by force in nine days and never had mass support beyond Berlin [A]. Kapp exposed something worse: the Republic could not rely on its own army, and was saved not by the state but by workers choosing to strike. A government whose survival depends on its opponents' unpopularity rather than on its own strength has a permanent weakness, and the right kept its weapons afterwards [A].

parts.problemMd:
**The Weimar Republic lasted from 1919 until 1933.**

'The Weimar Republic was doomed from the start.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Republic's founding problems were real, but it survived them and recovered. What destroyed it came later, and from outside Germany [R].

It was born owning a defeat it had not caused. The Weimar government's first act was to sign the armistice, and its politicians were branded 'November Criminals' who had committed a 'dolchstoss', because the Allies had never defeated the German Army in battle [R]. It then had to sign the Treaty of Versailles, accepting blame under Article 231 and reparations of 132 billion gold marks [R]. No new government could easily survive being permanently identified with national humiliation [E].

Its constitution also built in weakness. Proportional representation meant no party ever won a majority, producing nine coalition governments between 1919 and 1923, while Article 48 let the chancellor bypass the Reichstag entirely, and Ebert used it 63 times in 1923-24 [R]. Extremists attacked from both sides, and the government relied on force to hold power [E].

However, the Republic recovered strongly after 1923. Stresemann replaced the worthless mark with the Rentenmark in November 1923, negotiated the Dawes and Young Plans, brought Germany into the League of Nations in 1926 and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928 [R]. Real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928 and the working week fell from 50 hours to 46 [R]. A doomed state does not stabilise its currency and rejoin the international community within three years [A].

Politics stabilised too. There were no political assassinations between 1924 and 1929, only six coalition governments formed in that period, and support for the Nazis fell at every election between 1924 and 1928 [R]. Voters were turning towards moderate parties, not away from them [A].

The statement is therefore true only to a limited extent. The flaws were genuine and they explain how quickly the Republic fell once it was tested again [A]. But it was not doomed: it was fragile, and it depended on prosperity. Stresemann said in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' because recovery rested on American loans. It was the Wall Street Crash, not 1919, that made the collapse certain [A].

> - Ebert's alliance with General Groener left the army unreformed, so a hostile institution survived at the heart of the state.
> - Weimar culture flourished, with the Bauhaus movement founded in 1919, around 500 cinemas by 1929 and government funding for films such as Metropolis.
> - The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 covered 16.4 million workers, and building associations constructed 64,000 homes between 1925 and 1929.
> - Not everyone shared in the recovery: agricultural workers' income was 44% below the national average by 1929, and unemployment stayed at one million.
> - Stresemann died on 3 October 1929, weeks before the Wall Street Crash, so the Republic lost its most capable minister at the worst possible moment.
> - A valid judgement could be that the Republic was doomed because it never won the loyalty of the army, the judges or the civil service, provided the answer argues this rather than asserting it.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Plan four main paragraphs before you start, two on the founding weaknesses and two on the recovery. Two long paragraphs will not reach the top level.
> - The word 'doomed' is doing the work. Attack it directly by asking whether failure was inevitable or only made likely.
> - Use the years 1924 to 1929 as your evidence against the statement. An answer that stops in 1923 has only argued one side.
> - Match your conclusion to the question's wording. This asks 'how far', so answer 'to a limited extent' or 'to a large extent' and justify it.
> - Do not write 'in this answer I will'. Frame the introduction around the two sides instead.

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the German Revolution of 1918.
parts.solutionMd:
By the autumn of 1918 Germany could not continue the war. Between 1914 and 1918 two million German soldiers had died and four million more had been wounded, among them Adolf Hitler, temporarily blinded by mustard gas in October 1918 [R]. Germany's debt had trebled from 50 billion marks in 1914 to 150 billion marks in 1918 [R]. The British Navy had blockaded German ports so that no food from overseas could enter the country, and the German people were near starvation [D].

Unrest then spread from the ports across the country. In October 1918 the German navy mutinied at Kiel and Hamburg [R]. On 7 November the workers of Munich, the capital of Bavaria, held a general strike and announced that they were a separate communist state [R]. In Hanover soldiers joined workers and rioted in the streets, and in Berlin there were mass protests [R]. Many towns set up councils of workers and soldiers to replace the Kaiser's official local authorities, so the old system of government was being dismantled from below [D]. Once the capital was lost, the Kaiser had lost control of the whole country [D].

The Kaiser's position collapsed within days. On 9 November 1918 his military advisers told him he must abdicate in order to stop the civil unrest [R]. Max von Baden, whom the Kaiser had appointed as Chancellor on 3 October, announced the abdication without the Kaiser's consent or knowledge [R]. The following day the Kaiser escaped from Germany by train and arrived in the Netherlands [R].

A new government was assembled immediately. Max von Baden resigned and offered the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, who accepted [R]. On 10 November Ebert worked with General Groener and the army to suppress the communist rioters, dismissed the old Reichstag, and created a Council of People's Representatives, six politicians who would govern Germany until elections could be held [R]. The Republic's first act was to sign the armistice on 11 November, ending the First World War [R]. To hold the new state together Ebert promised the trade unions an eight-hour working day, promised big business that their property would not be nationalised, and promised General Groener that the army would not be reformed [D]. The civil servants who had served the Kaiser continued their work alongside the new workers' councils [D]. Elections for a National Assembly were held on 19 January 1919, with a turnout of 82%; the SPD won 40% of the vote and the Centre Party 20%, both moderate parties [R]. In February 1919 Ebert was elected as Germany's first president, and the Assembly met at Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin, to write a new constitution [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of Germany's economic recovery between 1923 and 1929.
parts.solutionMd:
When Gustav Stresemann became chancellor in August 1923 the German economy had crashed. The French invasion of the Ruhr had caused hyperinflation and the mark was worthless: the largest note was for 100 trillion marks, and the government believed there were 400.3 billion trillion marks in circulation [R]. Stresemann had three aims: to bring inflation under control, to regain Europe's respect, and to minimise support for extremist parties [D].

His first step was a new currency. In November 1923 he created the Rentenmark, where one Rentenmark was the equivalent of a trillion old marks, and established a new state-owned bank, the Rentenbank, at which the public exchanged their old notes [R]. The Rentenmark was a gold standard currency, meaning its value matched the price of gold, which European countries trusted [D]. In August 1924 the government created the Reichsbank to control the currency and renamed it the Reichsmark [R]. Stresemann also ended the passive resistance in the Ruhr, which increased Germany's production capability, and French and Belgian soldiers left the Ruhr in 1925 [R].

Reparations were then restructured twice. The Dawes Plan of April 1924 set reparations at 50 million pounds a year and brought American money into German industry, with US banks lending directly to German businesses [R]. It improved relations with France and improved trade and employment, but it also left Germany in debt to the USA [D]. The Young Plan of August 1929 went further, reducing total reparations to 2 billion pounds and extending the repayment period to 59 years, which allowed the government to lower taxes on its citizens [R]. Both plans angered extremist parties, who argued that Germany should not be repaying reparations produced by a corrupt treaty at all [D].

The effects were visible in ordinary life. Workers' real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928, and the working week fell from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 hours in 1927 [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 diverted 3% of the wages of 16.4 million workers into a fund which paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone unemployed or unable to work through ill health [R]. Housing improved as the Lander used foreign loans and a 15% rent tax to fund building, so that private companies built 37,000 new homes between 1925 and 1929 while building associations constructed 64,000 [R]. Over 1.3 million widows and ex-soldiers received a war pension under the Reich Pension Law [R].

The recovery was uneven. Unemployment remained at one million throughout the period, and the divide between rich and poor persisted [R]. Farmers struggled particularly badly with low prices, and by 1929 the income of agricultural workers was 44% below the national average [R]. Germany's new prosperity also rested on American loans, which is why Stresemann said in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the importance of Gustav Stresemann to the recovery of the Weimar Republic.
parts.solutionMd:
Gustav Stresemann was chancellor for only three months, from August to November 1923, and foreign minister until his death on 3 October 1929. In that time Germany went from a worthless currency and a foreign army on its soil to membership of the League of Nations. The question is how much of that recovery belonged to him [R].

The first facet is the currency, and here his importance is hard to dispute. When he took office the mark had collapsed: the largest note was for 100 trillion marks and the government believed 400.3 billion trillion marks were in circulation [R]. In November 1923 Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark, worth a trillion old marks, backed it with a new state-owned Rentenbank and tied it to the gold standard so that European countries would trust it [R]. This was decisive because a currency nobody accepts makes trade impossible; restoring one that foreign markets respected allowed German businesses to buy and sell abroad again, which is the precondition for every other recovery that followed [E]. He also ended the passive resistance in the Ruhr, restoring German production, and French and Belgian troops left the region in 1925 [R]. Stresemann had set himself three aims on taking office: to control inflation, to regain Europe's respect and to reduce support for extremist parties, and the currency reform served all three [R].

The second facet is reparations, where his importance is more qualified. Stresemann negotiated the Dawes Plan of 1924, which set payments at 50 million pounds a year and brought American investment into German industry, and the Young Plan of 1929, which cut total reparations to 2 billion pounds and extended repayment over 59 years [R]. These plans genuinely eased the burden and improved relations with France [E]. But the money was American, not German, and the arrangement left Germany dependent on the United States [A]. Stresemann understood this himself, warning in 1929 that Germany was 'dancing on a volcano' [R]. His achievement here was to buy time rather than to solve the problem, and when the Wall Street Crash came the borrowed prosperity vanished [A].

The third facet is Germany's international position, and this was arguably his greatest success. The Treaty of Versailles had banned Germany from the League of Nations and excluded it from world politics [R]. Stresemann negotiated the Locarno Treaties in December 1925, obtained German membership of the League in September 1926 with a seat on its Council, and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in August 1928 alongside 61 other countries, winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 [R]. This mattered because it reversed the most humiliating element of the settlement without firing a shot, and it made Germany a respectable state able to enter treaties as an equal [E].

The fourth facet is domestic politics, where the effects were real but not his alone. Support for extremist parties fell: the Nazi vote declined at every election between 1924 and 1928 while the SPD gained steadily, there were no political assassinations between 1924 and 1929, and only six coalition governments formed in those five years, far fewer than before [R]. Success abroad gave Germans a reason to believe the Republic could deliver [E]. Yet Hindenburg's election as president in 1925 also increased right-wing middle-class support for the Republic, and that owed nothing to Stresemann [A]. Extremist parties still held 13% of the vote, and nationalists remained angry that the government kept following the Treaty of Versailles [R].

Stresemann was the most important single figure in the Republic's recovery, but his importance lies in stabilisation rather than in cure. The Rentenmark was his, the treaties were his, and the political calm of 1924 to 1929 followed from both; no other individual contributed anything comparable [A]. A stronger reading is that a Republic kept going by foreign success needed ever more of it. That judgement is too harsh, since Germany in 1923 needed rescuing before it could be reformed. The fairest conclusion is that Stresemann was indispensable to the recovery and insufficient for its survival: he made the Republic work, but he could not make it independent of American money, and it was that dependence, not his policies, which killed it [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which life improved for the German people in the 1920s.
parts.solutionMd:
Between 1924 and 1929 the Weimar Republic gave many Germans a standard of living and a personal freedom they had never had under the Kaiser. Whether life improved depends heavily on which Germans are being discussed [R].

The clearest improvement was in living standards for workers in towns and cities. Workers' real wages rose 25% between 1925 and 1928, and the working week fell from 50 hours in 1925 to 46 in 1927 [R]. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 took 3% of the wages of 16.4 million workers and paid 60 Reichsmarks a week to anyone out of work or too ill to work [R]. Housing improved, with private companies building 37,000 homes between 1925 and 1929 and building associations a further 64,000, while over 1.3 million widows and ex-soldiers received a pension under the Reich Pension Law [R]. This was the beginning of a German welfare state, and it meant that for the first time illness or unemployment did not automatically mean destitution [E].

A second facet is the position of women, where the legal gains were genuine. The Weimar Constitution gave every woman over 21 the vote on the same terms as men, which was rare in Europe, and Article 119 declared marriage an equal legal partnership [R]. Women voted in large numbers, with turnout around 90%, and 111 women were elected to the Reichstag in 1920 [R]. More women worked as teachers and doctors, and the 'New Woman' of the 1920s could work, dress and behave with a freedom previous generations had never known [E].

A third facet is culture, which flourished as never before. The government gave grants to artists and to organisations such as theatres and libraries, and supported rather than censored new work [R]. The Bauhaus movement was founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 and taught by figures such as Paul Klee, artists including Otto Dix and George Grosz produced work that questioned German society, and by 1929 there were roughly 500 cinemas in Germany [R]. The government funded Fritz Lang's Metropolis in 1926 through UFA at a cost of 5 million Reichsmarks, and Berlin's cabarets and nightclubs made the city famous [R]. Ordinary Germans had access to art, film and nightlife that had simply not existed a decade earlier [E].

However, the countryside was left behind. There was a clear divide between the industrial and agricultural working classes, and it was town and city workers who benefited from the reforms [R]. High debt, low prices and rising taxes damaged living standards in farming communities, so that by 1929 the income of agricultural workers was 44% below the national average [R]. Unemployment also remained at one million throughout the so-called Golden Age [R]. For a substantial part of the population the 1920s were not a recovery at all [A].

Women's gains were also narrower than they appeared. The proportion of women in employment fell from 75% in 1918 to 36% by 1925, roughly the pre-war level; employers ignored Article 119 and chose men; and women in work were paid 33% less than men doing the same job [R]. Society still expected a woman to leave her job on marriage, and Germany had only 36 female judges by 1933 [R]. The right to vote had been won, but the right to a career largely had not [A].

The cultural changes also made enemies, which mattered politically. The right-wing vilified the 'New Woman' for destroying the traditional family, Hitler blamed her for working-class unemployment, and male-dominated trade unions resented 'double earners' [R]. The KPD saw funding for the arts as money taken from workers who needed it, while the NSDAP argued that Weimar culture was destroying German traditions and causing moral decline [R]. Improvements that a large minority actively resented were storing up trouble rather than building loyalty [A].

Life improved substantially, but for a narrower group than the phrase 'Golden Age' suggests. For an urban worker, and especially for a young unmarried woman in a city, the years 1924 to 1929 brought real gains in wages, security, rights and culture [A]. For a farmer, for the million who remained unemployed, and for most married women hoping to keep a job, very little changed. The improvements were also concentrated where they created most resentment, so the Republic's greatest social achievements handed its enemies their most effective arguments. Life improved to a large extent for some Germans and hardly at all for others, and that division is the most important thing about the decade [A].

parts.problemMd:
Women, children, and the family were important to the Nazis.

Describe how women helped the German war effort.
parts.solutionMd:
Women helped the German war effort by working in factories to produce weapons, ammunition and other supplies needed in the war [1]. When men were drafted into the military, women replaced them in industry and kept the German army equipped [1]. At home they supported the war effort by managing households under rationing, so that surplus could be sent to the front [1]. They also took on the role of the Landfrauen, or women on the land, which kept food production going [1].

parts.solutionMd:
Beauty of Labour was a Nazi programme set up in 1934 as part of the German Labour Front [1]. Its purpose was to improve the places where people actually worked, rather than their leisure time [1]. It provided factories and workplaces with facilities such as toilets, changing rooms, showers and canteens [1]. By 1938 around 34,000 companies had improved their facilities under the scheme [1].

parts.problemMd:
The Nazis introduced schemes aimed at German workers.

Why were the Nazis' unemployment figures misleading?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that whole groups of people were simply removed from the count [R]. Jewish Germans were forced out of their jobs but were never recorded as unemployed, and women pushed out of work and back into the home were not counted either. Political opponents held in prisons and concentration camps did not appear in the figures, and anyone working part-time was recorded as fully employed. This matters because it means the total fell partly through bookkeeping rather than through people finding work. The official drop from 4.8 million unemployed in 1933 to 300,000 by 1939 therefore overstates how much real employment the Nazis had created [E].

A second reason is that much of the work that did exist was artificial and could not have lasted [R]. Conscription was introduced in 1935 and by 1939 there were around 1.4 million men in the armed forces, which takes men off the unemployment register without giving them ordinary jobs. Armaments work only exists while a country is arming, and spending on armaments rose from 3.5 billion marks in 1933 to 26 billion by 1939. The National Labour Service was compulsory six-month work for men aged 18 to 25, badly paid and widely disliked. Employment built on conscription and rearmament describes a country preparing for war rather than a healthy economy, so the low figure of 1939 was not a sign of lasting recovery [E].

parts.problemMd:
Different groups in German society experienced Nazi rule differently.

Which gained more from Nazi rule: farmers or business owners? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Farmers gained a great deal on paper [R]. Nazi 'Blood and Soil' thinking held that true Aryans had farming ancestry, so the regime placed farmers above urban workers in its picture of German society, and after years of being looked down on they were told they mattered. This came with real protection too. The Reich Food Estate regulated the food market and gave farmers guaranteed customers at fair prices, which removed the uncertainty that had ruined so many of them in the Depression, and the Reich Entailed Farm Law stopped banks repossessing a farm if the owner fell into debt [E].

But those gains were narrower than they look [R]. The same regime that protected farmers also took control of them, telling them what they were allowed to grow, which caused real anger in farming communities. Farming stayed poor, and so many farmers' children left for the towns in search of better wages that the countryside was losing its next generation. The Entailed Farm Law even worked against them, because banks that could no longer seize land simply became unwilling to lend to farmers at all. Status and security are not the same as prosperity [E].

Business owners gained something more concrete [R]. Trade unions and strikes were banned, which handed employers a workforce that could not bargain over pay or walk out, and the communist threat that had frightened them in the early 1930s was destroyed. Rearmament then produced enormous government contracts for war goods such as steel, so firms had guaranteed customers with deep pockets. That combination of cheap, docile labour and state money is a direct route to profit [E].

Business did not get everything either [R]. The Nazis increased their control over industry, small business owners were promised that large department stores would be restricted and that promise was never kept, and the switch to rearmament meant fewer firms making consumer goods [E].

Overall business owners gained more [A]. The key difference is what each group actually received. Farmers were given respect, a guaranteed price and protection from the bailiff, but they stayed poor, lost the right to decide what to plant and found credit drying up. Business owners were given a workforce stripped of its bargaining power and a state that bought everything they could make. One group got status, the other got money. It is worth adding that this was not true of all business owners equally, since it was the large firms that took the rearmament contracts while the small shopkeepers who had been promised protection from the department stores got nothing [A].

> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.

> - Concluding that both gained equally. That is a refusal to answer; choose one and justify it.

> - Businesses seized from Jewish owners passed into the hands of other German firms, which was a further gain for some business owners and a reminder that these benefits rested on persecution.
> - Farms were inherited undivided by a single son under the Entailed Farm Law, which kept holdings intact but left other children with nothing and pushed them towards the towns.
> - Both groups lost independence, since the regime told farmers what to grow and set production targets for industry, so increased state control is common ground rather than a point of difference.

parts.problemMd: Why did Hitler attach much importance to the German family?
parts.solutionMd:
Hitler considered the German family to be central to creating a strong Nazi state. He wanted families to ensure racial purity so that the supposedly superior Aryan race could be preserved. He wanted Germany to dominate Europe and to create Lebensraum [R]. That could only be achieved by war, and for war he needed soldiers. This is why the family mattered so much. German families were expected to increase the birth rate so that Aryan children would build up the population of future soldiers and workers [E].

Families were also expected to raise children loyal to Nazi ideas, ensuring that the next generation would carry on his vision of a powerful Germany. Hitler saw the family as a way to promote traditional Nazi values [R]. Women were expected to focus on 'Kinder, Kuche, Kirche', meaning children, kitchen and church, while men fought and worked for Germany. This was intended to give women the time to raise their children in Nazi values. The family would give stability to German society and to Nazi ideology, so strong families would strengthen both the racial purity and the unity of Germany [E].

**[6 marks]**

> 
> - Describing Nazi policies towards women, such as marriage loans or barring them from jobs, instead of explaining why Hitler valued the family. The focus must be on his motives and aims for the whole family, including men and children.
> - Writing only that Hitler 'wanted more babies'. That is the starting point; the marks come from explaining what the children were for.

> 
> - The Nazis presented the 1920s as a period of moral decline, and Hitler won support by promising to reverse it. Laws and rewards such as marriage loans and the Mother's Cross encouraged women to have large families.
> - The duty of the mother was to have many children and produce more men to fight in the armed forces, since Hitler wanted to raise the birth rate.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - A simple introductory statement can be given, but it is not required.
> - Two explained reasons is the target, supported with accurate subject knowledge.
> - Keep the answer on Hitler's aims rather than on the policies themselves.

parts.problemMd: 'The Hitler Youth was popular with the young people of Germany.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Hitler Youth was founded in 1926 to train and educate the young boys of Germany in Nazi ideology, and in 1933 it absorbed or banned all rival youth groups so that it became the only youth organisation in the country. Membership was optional at first; the Hitler Youth Law of 1936 made it the official state youth organisation, and from 1939 service was compulsory [R]. In this essay, I will examine how the Hitler Youth was not as popular as Hitler expected.

In support of the statement, many German teenagers who enjoyed adventure liked activities such as sport, hiking, camping and military-style training. Parades, songs and uniforms created pride and comradeship and made members feel connected to something larger [E]. Many began to look towards careers in the military because of that training, which inspired them early and made the organisation genuinely popular.

However, not all young people liked it. Firstly, once membership became compulsory, many joined out of pressure and fear of punishment rather than enthusiasm. Strict discipline, intense marching and the constant emphasis on Nazi ideology did not suit everyone [E]. Secondly, some parents came to see it as breaking up families, because Nazi ideology took precedence over family ties and traditional values. Parents who wanted academic schooling and independent thought for their children were frustrated by the focus on loyalty to Nazi ideas, and felt school no longer taught the practical skills needed for life [A].

In addition, many religious young people disliked the way the Hitler Youth undermined religious teaching, especially when they were discouraged from attending church [E]. During the Second World War, older Hitler Youth members were sent into combat or anti-aircraft units. That was an eye-opening experience, because they found they were not treated as future leaders of Germany but as expendable troops [A].

To conclude, I agree with the statement only to an extent. The Hitler Youth was popular in its early years, but that popularity could not be sustained. It lost its appeal once membership was compulsory and the focus shifted to indoctrination and military training. Opposition groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates and the Swing Youth offered an alternative, and many young people joined them instead [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of education in Nazi Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Hitler understood that controlling what children were taught would allow him to raise a generation loyal to him, and that this mattered more than winning over adults, whose opinions were harder to change. Bernhard Rust was made Education Minister in 1934 and set about reshaping both the teaching profession and the curriculum [R].

Teachers were dealt with first. Those not loyal to the regime were dismissed, and Rust sacked over 180 teachers in Prussia alone. Those who remained had to swear an oath of loyalty to Hitler and join the Nazi Teachers' League, and membership of the Nazi Party was made compulsory. They were required to attend political education courses setting out Nazi ideas, and by 1939 around 200,000 teachers had done so. Inside the classroom, teachers had to teach the Nazi salute, begin and end every lesson with 'Heil Hitler', and display Nazi posters, flags and a picture of Hitler [R].

The curriculum was rewritten around Nazi beliefs, and boys and girls were educated separately. Existing subjects were repurposed: maths problems incorporated war and society, history blamed Jewish people for Germany's problems, and the number of PE lessons was doubled in order to produce physically strong children. New subjects were introduced, including eugenics, in which pupils classified races and were taught the supposed superiority of the Aryan race, and domestic science, in which girls learned to sew, cook and run a household [R].

Control extended to what pupils read. After 1935 the Nazis had to approve all textbooks. Every book carried pictures of Hitler, Mein Kampf became a compulsory text, and events such as the First World War were rewritten to place the blame on Jewish people and on the November Criminals who had signed the armistice [R].

A separate elite system was also created. The Napolas were schools for children judged the most gifted and racially pure. SS members replaced the traditional teaching staff, the emphasis fell on sport and physical training, and pupils were expected to go on into the SS or the police services. By 1939 there were 16 Napolas [R].

Schooling therefore worked alongside compulsory membership of the youth groups, so that a German child's day was shaped by Nazi teaching from the classroom in the morning to the Hitler Youth or the League of German Maidens afterwards [R].

**[15 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> 
> Accuracy, coverage and sequence earn the marks, not explanation.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **11-15 marks:** the account includes the main events and developments and directly addresses the question. It is consistently supported by accurate historical knowledge and is logically sequenced.
> - **6-10 marks:** the account describes some events and developments relevant to the question. It is mostly supported by accurate historical knowledge and is structured in its approach.
> - **1-5 marks:** limited relevance to the question. Some accurate historical knowledge. Points are generally unconnected.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 11-15 marks include:
> 
> - Writing about the Hitler Youth instead. The youth groups operated outside school hours and are a separate topic; they are worth a closing sentence, not the body of the answer.
> - Covering the curriculum but not the teachers. Control of who was allowed to teach was as important as control of what was taught, and a complete account needs both.
> - Explaining why the Nazis wanted control of education. That is a different question; here the marks are for what they actually did.
> - Omitting the Napolas. They are the part of the system most candidates forget and an easy way to show fuller knowledge.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Religious education was steadily reduced in schools, which fits the wider Nazi attempt to weaken church influence over the young.
> - Jewish teachers were dismissed and Jewish pupils were progressively excluded from state schools.
> - Adolf Hitler Schools operated alongside the Napolas as a second elite strand, run by the party rather than the SS.
> - Girls' education was directed towards motherhood, which connects the school curriculum to the wider Nazi policy on women.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Structure the answer around teachers, then curriculum, then textbooks, then the elite schools. That order is easy to follow and shows deliberate organisation.
> - Specific figures separate a good account from a vague one: 180 teachers sacked in Prussia, 200,000 trained by 1939, 16 Napolas.
> - Naming Bernhard Rust is worth doing, since most candidates describe the changes without knowing who introduced them.
> - Give concrete curriculum examples rather than saying lessons were 'full of Nazi ideas'. Maths questions about war, doubled PE and the introduction of eugenics all show precise knowledge.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of Nazi rule on German workers.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is the loss of independent rights.** Hitler distrusted trade unions because they supported left-wing parties and organised strikes that disrupted the economy, and he used the powers of the Enabling Act to ban them all in May 1933. In their place came the Labour Front, or DAF, which controlled workers' rights, hours and pay. The consequences were immediate: workers lost the right to negotiate over wages and conditions, the maximum working week was extended by six hours, and strikes were forbidden, with those who disrupted production punished. Whatever else happened to German workers after 1933, it happened to them without their having any means of objecting [E].

**The second facet is the compensation the regime offered in return.** The Nazis knew that abolishing the unions would cause resentment, so they created organisations within the DAF to raise living standards. Strength Through Joy, founded in 1933, provided subsidised leisure, trips and holidays and had 35 million members by 1936. Beauty of Labour, founded in 1934, improved workplace facilities such as toilets, changing rooms, showers and canteens, and around 34,000 companies had upgraded by 1938. Yet both schemes reveal the limits of the bargain. Workers were expected to build and decorate the new facilities themselves, unpaid and outside working hours. And the Volkswagen scheme, under which workers paid five marks a week towards a car costing 999 Reichsmark, ended with the factories switching to armaments after 1938 and not a single worker receiving a car [E].

**The third facet is employment itself, which is the strongest argument in the regime's favour.** Unemployment stood at 4.8 million in 1933 and had fallen to around 300,000 by 1939. The National Labour Service provided paid public work such as road repair and tree planting, becoming compulsory for unemployed men aged 18 to 25 from 1935 and reaching 422,000 members. The autobahn programme, begun by Hitler in September 1933, employed 125,000 workers by 1935 and had completed some 3500 kilometres by 1938, while spending on public works rose from 18 billion marks in 1933 to 38 billion by 1938. For a man who had been out of work in 1932, this was a transformation [E].

**The fourth facet is the gap between wages and prices, which divided workers sharply.** Most workers did earn more under the Nazis, and skilled men in the armaments industry did particularly well. But food prices rose by 20 per cent by 1939, and for the unskilled the wage increases did not keep pace. The impact of Nazi rule therefore depended a great deal on what job a worker did: the same policies that enriched a skilled engineer left an unskilled labourer worse off than before [E].

**The fifth facet is that the headline achievement was partly manufactured.** Nazi unemployment figures excluded several large groups: part-time workers were counted as fully employed, as were the armed forces and those making armaments, while prisoners, Jewish people forced out of their jobs and women pushed out of work were left out of the statistics altogether. This is invisible unemployment, and it means the fall from 4.8 million to 300,000 overstates what was achieved [E].

**Judgement.** The most important impact was the first: the removal of any independent means of representation [A]. Everything else follows from it. Wages, hours and conditions all became things the regime granted rather than things workers could win, and the Volkswagen scheme demonstrates exactly what that meant in practice, since men who had paid in for years had no way of recovering their money when the state decided the factories were needed for something else.

The employment gains were nevertheless real and should not be dismissed, even allowing for invisible unemployment [A]. The deeper problem is what they rested on. Rearmament created jobs only because Germany was preparing for war, and armaments spending rose from 3.5 billion marks in 1933 to 26 billion by 1939, with employment in aircraft construction rising from 4,000 in 1933 to 72,000 by 1935. The impact of Nazi rule on workers was therefore a trade: secure work and modest improvements in daily conditions, bought with the loss of every right to bargain, and underwritten by an economy that had to go to war to keep paying [A].

**[25 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Treating workers as one group. The evidence points both ways depending on whether a worker was skilled or unskilled, and an answer that generalises cannot reach the top level.
> - Accepting the unemployment figures at face value. Invisible unemployment is central to any serious assessment and its omission is the most common weakness in answers on this topic.
> - Describing Strength Through Joy and Beauty of Labour without judging them. Both were genuine benefits and both came with conditions attached, and the marks lie in saying so.
> - Confusing this with the New Deal or with Stalin's Five-Year Plans. Comparisons are not required and usually cost focus.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Employers benefited from the same measures that constrained workers, since banning unions and strikes made the workforce more productive, which is a useful way of showing whose interests the policies really served.
> - Farmers had a different experience again, gaining protection through the Reich Food Estate and the Reich Entailed Farm Law while remaining poor enough that their children left for the towns.
> - Dr Schacht's New Plan of 1934 cut welfare spending while investing in industry, so recovery was partly paid for by reduced support for the poorest.
> - Conscription from 1935 removed men from the labour market as well as arming the country, and by 1939 around 1.4 million men were in the armed forces.
> - Fewer consumer goods were produced as resources shifted to rearmament, so workers with higher wages had less to spend them on.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Split the workforce. Saying that skilled workers gained while unskilled workers fell behind, with the 20 per cent rise in food prices as evidence, is the single sharpest point available.
> - Use the Volkswagen scheme as your killer example. It captures the whole relationship in one story: a real benefit, promised by the state, withdrawn without recourse.
> - Deal with the unemployment figures honestly. Acknowledge the fall, then explain what the statistics leave out.
> - Ask what the gains depended on. Tying employment to rearmament turns a descriptive point into an analytical one.
> - Rank your facets in the conclusion. Deciding that the loss of bargaining rights outweighs the material gains, and explaining why, is what takes an answer from Level 4 to Level 5.

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis wanted control of Germany's young people.**

Describe the Hitler Youth.
parts.solutionMd:
The Hitler Youth was the Nazi youth group for boys aged 14 to 18, and it was led by Baldur von Schirach [1]. Younger boys joined the Pimpfe from the age of 6 and the German Young People from 10, and at 18 members became Nazi Party members and either worked or joined the armed forces [1]. Training was divided into military work such as map-reading, signalling and small-arms shooting, physical work such as camping and hiking, character training, and political training [1]. Membership of the Nazi youth groups rose from 100,000 in 1932 to nine million by 1939 [1].

> - Developing a point further does not earn an additional mark, so it is better to make a new point than to expand one you have already made.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Confusing the Hitler Youth with the League of German Maidens. The Hitler Youth was for boys; the BDM was the girls' equivalent.
> - Explaining why the Nazis wanted control of young people rather than describing the organisation.
> - Writing about the youth opposition groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates, which were formed against the Hitler Youth.
> - Developing two points at length instead of making four separate ones, which caps the mark at 2.

> - Membership grew because other youth groups were banned and membership was then made compulsory.

> - Political training included an oath of loyalty to Hitler and reporting disloyal Germans.
> - Military training included specialist routes into the naval, gliding, flying and motor branches of the armed forces.

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis wanted to increase Germany's birth rate.**

What was the Lebensborn Programme?
parts.solutionMd:
The Lebensborn Programme was started in 1935 by the SS leader Heinrich Himmler [1]. It paired SS men with single women in order to create children the Nazis regarded as 'genetically pure', as part of a wider effort to raise a birth rate that had fallen to one million births a year by 1933 [1]. Only men and women with a clear 'Aryan' ancestry were accepted onto the programme [1]. The Nazis created special Lebensborn homes where women could rest after giving birth, and one home alone helped over 540 mothers [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - 1 mark for each distinct point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each distinct piece of information. Four separate points are needed for 4 marks.
> - Developing a point further does not earn an additional mark, so it is better to make a new point than to expand one you have already made.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Confusing Lebensborn with the Law for the Encouragement of Marriage or the Mother's Cross. All three aimed to raise the birth rate, but by different means.
> - Explaining why the Nazis wanted more children rather than describing the programme.
> - Confusing Lebensborn with Lebensraum, which was Hitler's foreign-policy aim of 'living space' in Eastern Europe.
> - Developing two points at length instead of making four separate ones, which caps the mark at 2.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> Answers may include the following. This list is not exhaustive and any other valid point should be credited.
> 
> - Only around 7,000 children were born through the programme, so it had limited success.
> - The First World War had reduced the male population, which is part of why the birth rate mattered so much to the Nazis.
> - Other measures included loans of 1,000 marks under the Law for the Encouragement of Marriage in 1933, and the Mother's Cross from 1938.
> - The birth rate did rise, from 15 per 1,000 in 1933 to 20 per 1,000 in 1939, although this cannot be attributed to Lebensborn alone.
> - Gertrud Scholtz-Klink, leader of the National Socialist Women's League, oversaw all policies relating to women.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Four separate facts is the target: when it started and who ran it, what it did, who was eligible, and what facilities it provided.
> - Be careful with the spelling and the meaning. Lebensborn and Lebensraum are different things and examiners see them confused often.
> - Make four distinct points rather than developing two in detail. Extra detail on a point you have already made will not gain you a further mark.
> - No introduction or conclusion is needed, and no extra marks are available beyond four points.

parts.problemMd:
**The Nazis took control of German schools after 1933.**

Why did the Nazis change the school curriculum?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Hitler wanted a generation loyal to him. Bernhard Rust was made Education Minister in 1934, and the Nazis took control of the curriculum so that they could shape what children believed [R]. History was rewritten to blame Jewish people and the 'November Criminals', eugenics was introduced as a subject teaching Aryan superiority, and from 1935 all textbooks had to be approved and Mein Kampf became compulsory [R]. This mattered because adults in Germany held mixed opinions and were difficult to change, whereas children taught only one version of history would grow up believing it, which would guarantee support for the Nazi Party for generations [E].

A second reason was that boys and girls were being prepared for different roles in the Third Reich. Boys and girls were educated separately, PE lessons were doubled to produce physically strong children, and girls took domestic science to learn to sew, cook and run a home [R]. Maths questions incorporated war and society, and the most 'gifted' children attended Napolas, of which there were 16 by 1939, taught by SS members [R]. This explains the changes because the Nazis needed soldiers and mothers rather than independent thinkers, so the curriculum was redesigned to produce exactly those two things [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Support for the Nazi Party was high in 1941 but had collapsed by 1945.**

Why did support for the Nazi Party fall during the Second World War?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the war stopped going well. Germany had defeated France in six weeks using blitzkrieg tactics, and support for the Nazi Party remained high even in 1941 [R]. Operation Barbarossa then failed, German soldiers withdrew after the Battle of Stalingrad in 1942, and Britain began bombing German cities, causing high casualties and a falling standard of living [R]. This mattered because Nazi legitimacy rested on delivering success: a regime that had justified itself by making Germany strong could not survive the discovery that it was losing [E].

A second reason was that daily life became far harder. Rationing was extended to more products and black markets developed in many towns and cities, while shortages of fuel, coal and food spread [R]. During the 'Total War' campaign women were forced into work, children were moved to the countryside to escape the bombing, and the government stopped entertainment and luxury goods altogether [R]. This explains the fall in support because the Nazis had promised prosperity and order, and by 1943 they were delivering neither, so even Germans who had approved of the invasion of Poland in 1939 began to turn against the regime [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Nine million young Germans belonged to Nazi youth groups by 1939.**

'Young people in Nazi Germany were successfully indoctrinated.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Nine million young Germans belonged to Nazi youth groups by 1939. Yet the most determined resistance to the regime also came from the young [R].

The scale of the youth movement was overwhelming. Membership rose from 100,000 in 1932 to nine million by 1939, achieved by banning other youth groups and then making membership compulsory [R]. Children were enrolled from the age of six, moving into the German Young People or Young Maidens at ten and the Hitler Youth or League of German Maidens at fourteen [R]. A child could therefore spend twelve years inside Nazi organisations before adulthood, which left very little room for any competing influence [E].

Schools reinforced the same message. Bernhard Rust became Education Minister in 1934, disloyal teachers were sacked, and the rest swore an oath to Hitler and joined the Nazi Teachers' League [R]. From 1935 all textbooks were approved, Mein Kampf was compulsory, and eugenics was taught as a subject [R]. Children heard nothing at school that contradicted what they heard in the Hitler Youth [A].

However, membership was not the same as belief. Many young people disliked the focus on physical activities and military training, resented the regimental attitude and strict rules, and parents complained that the youth groups undermined their own authority [R]. Compulsion produced attendance rather than conviction [A].

Some young people organised against the regime outright. The Swing Youth listened to the jazz Hitler had banned, and the Edelweiss Pirates resisted the Hitler Youth directly, with over 700 arrested in 1942 and twelve publicly hanged in 1944 after members in Cologne killed the local Gestapo chief [R]. The White Rose group at Munich University published anti-Nazi leaflets in 1943, and Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed by guillotine [R].

The statement is true to a large extent, but with an important qualification. Nine million members and a school system rebuilt around Nazi ideas produced a generation that largely accepted the regime, and the Hitler Youth helped put out fires after British bombing raids [A]. Yet the opposition groups were also young, which suggests indoctrination worked on the majority and actively provoked a determined minority. It succeeded widely rather than completely [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Germany was at war from September 1939 until May 1945.**

How far did the Second World War change life for people in Germany? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
For most Germans the war changed everything after 1942. For those the Nazis persecuted, it accelerated something that had begun in 1933 [R].

Material life was transformed. Rationing was extended, black markets appeared in many towns and cities, and Germany suffered shortages of fuel, coal and food, having never achieved autarky [R]. During 'Total War' the government stopped entertainment and luxury goods, and children were moved to the countryside to escape British bombing [R]. A population that had been promised prosperity found itself worse off than before the war [E].

Work and gender roles changed just as sharply. Before 1939 Nazi policy had pushed women out of employment, but by 1937 Germany faced a shortage of workers, in 1944 the government forced women into war work, and 2.4 million returned to their jobs [R]. Over 500,000 served in the Wehrmacht as nurses or in other non-combat roles, while by 1944 one quarter of Germany's workforce was enslaved labour [R]. The regime abandoned its own central policy on women because the war left it no choice [A].

However, the first two years improved life for many. Germany defeated France in six weeks, German citizens gained access to new goods, and generous rations meant that two-fifths of workers ate better than they had before the war [R]. Support for the Nazi Party remained high even in 1941, so the early war years brought confidence rather than hardship [E].

For persecuted groups the war intensified existing policy rather than creating it. Jewish people had faced boycotts from 1933 and the Nuremberg Laws from 1935 before being forced into ghettos in 1939, and the Final Solution agreed at Wannsee in January 1942 led to the extermination camps [R]. The direction had been set long before the fighting started [A].

The war changed life to a large extent, though not evenly and not immediately. For ordinary Germans the turning point was Stalingrad rather than 1939, and from 1942 rationing, bombing and forced work reached every household [A]. For Jewish people, Roma and disabled Germans the war removed the last restraints on a persecution already twelve years old. The war did not create Nazi Germany's character; it exposed it and made everyone live with the consequences [A].
