parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the Nazi youth groups.
parts.solutionMd:
The Nazis wanted control of Germany's young people because Hitler intended a Third Reich that would last a thousand years. Adults held mixed opinions and were difficult to change, whereas control of the young would guarantee support for generations [R]. Boys were to be raised fit and healthy to support the economy and fight in wars, and girls fit and healthy so that they could be good wives and healthy mothers [D].

Membership was built up quickly and then made compulsory. Other youth groups were banned and membership of the Nazi organisations was eventually required, so numbers rose from 100,000 in 1932 to nine million by 1939 [R]. There were separate groups by age and sex: boys joined the Pimpfe at 6 and the German Young People at 10, girls joined the Young Maidens at 10, and at 14 they moved into the Hitler Youth or the League of German Maidens [R].

The Hitler Youth trained boys for war. Led by Baldur von Schirach, it took boys from 14 until 18, when they became Nazi Party members and either worked or joined the armed forces [R]. Training was divided into four areas: military training in map-reading, signalling and small-arms shooting, with specialist routes into the naval, gliding, flying and motor branches; physical training through camping, hiking and regional and national sports events; character training that taught competition, ruthlessness and a willingness to die for Hitler; and political training, including an oath of loyalty and instructions to report disloyal Germans [R].

The League of German Maidens prepared girls for motherhood. The BDM shared some activities with the Hitler Youth, but its emphasis was on the 'three Ks' of Kinder, Kirche and Kuche, so girls learned cooking and needlework alongside physical activity intended to make them capable mothers [R]. Girls also learned about racial hygiene, so that they would choose 'pure' Aryan husbands [R]. In 1938 the Nazis created a sub-group called the 'Faith and Beauty Society' for girls aged 17 to 21, because they feared BDM members would forget their training after leaving at 18 and before they were old enough to join the National Socialist Women's League [R].

Reactions to the groups were mixed. Many members were enthusiastic, enjoyed the activities, felt a sense of comradeship and believed they were building a stronger Germany [D]. Others disliked the focus on physical activities and military training and resented the regimental attitude and strict rules, while parents complained that the groups undermined their own authority [D]. During the war the indoctrinated Hitler Youth helped put out fires after British bombing raids, while youth opposition groups expanded and the Volkssturm enlisted children as young as twelve in 1945 [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of Nazi policies towards women.
parts.solutionMd:
Nazi policy towards women aimed to reverse the changes of the Weimar Republic and to raise the birth rate, which had fallen to one million births a year by 1933 [R]. Goebbels said that 'the mission of the woman is to be beautiful and bring children into the home', and the Nazis expected women to marry 'pure' Aryan men, raise large families, stay at home while the man earned, and appear blonde, athletic and without make-up [R]. A woman's life was said to revolve around the 'three Ks' of Kinder, Kirche and Kuche [D]. Gertrud Scholtz-Klink was appointed leader of the National Socialist Women's League and oversaw all policies relating to women [R].

Organisations were unified and then used to train women. All women-related organisations had to join the German Women's Enterprise, and any that refused were banned [R]. The DFW enrolled members on courses in childcare, cooking and sewing, and by the late 1930s it had six million members, of whom 1.7 million had attended its courses [R]. Around 360,000 women had left their jobs by 1934, embracing the domestic role the Nazis wanted [R].

A series of laws encouraged marriage and childbirth. The Law for the Encouragement of Marriage of 1933 offered loans of 1,000 marks, about eight months' wages, to women who married and either quit their jobs or stayed unemployed, with a quarter of the loan cancelled for each child, so a mother of four repaid nothing [R]. Himmler began the Lebensborn Programme in 1935, pairing SS men with single women of clear Aryan ancestry to produce children the Nazis regarded as genetically pure [R]. New divorce laws in 1938 let husbands divorce wives who failed or refused to have children or who had abortions, and the Mother's Cross, awarded on Mother's Day from 1938, honoured women with four or more children, with gold medallists receiving a public salute from the Hitler Youth [R]. Families with ten children had to name Hitler as godfather to the tenth child, and by 1939 three million women were eligible for a Mother's Cross [R].

Employment was restricted at the same time. In 1933 women were banned from being teachers, doctors and other professionals, and around 19,000 female civil servants were sacked [R]. In 1936 they were banned from becoming judges or lawyers or from serving on juries, and in 1937 schools preparing girls for university were banned, so around 11,000 fewer women were starting university by 1939 [R]. This changed once the war approached: by 1937 Germany faced a national shortage of workers, women with marriage loans were allowed to work, and in 1944 the government forced women into war work, with 2.4 million returning to their jobs and over 500,000 serving in the Wehrmacht as nurses or in other non-combat roles [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of how the Nazis reduced unemployment.
parts.solutionMd:
Reducing unemployment was one of the Nazis' first priorities. Around six million Germans were unemployed by 1932 because of the Great Depression, and five million were still out of work when Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 [R]. The Nazis regarded the unemployed as a political danger, because they might support parties such as the KPD, and as a group contributing nothing to the economy [D].

Public works came first. The National Labour Service was set up in 1933 to provide paid work repairing roads and planting trees, and from 1935 it was compulsory for unemployed young men aged 18 to 25 to serve six months; it had 422,000 members in 1935, although pay was poor and workers complained about the food, the uniforms and the conditions [R]. Hitler personally started the autobahn project in September 1933, intending a network of around 11,000 kilometres; it employed 125,000 workers by 1935 and around 3,500 kilometres had been built by 1938 [R]. Spending on public works, including roads, bridges and the Berlin Olympic Stadium, more than doubled from 18 billion marks in 1933 to 38 billion by 1938 [R].

The economy was then reorganised. Hitler appointed Dr Schacht, a respected banker who had helped resolve the hyperinflation crisis of 1923, as Minister of the Economy [R]. Schacht's New Plan of 1934 cut welfare spending, invested in industry and created trade deals with countries such as Hungary, and by 1936 the economy had recovered [R].

Rearmament provided the largest number of jobs. Hitler announced conscription in 1935 in breach of the Treaty of Versailles, and by 1939 there were around 1.4 million men in the German armed forces [R]. Spending on armaments rose from 3.5 billion marks in 1933 to 26 billion by 1939, and employment in aircraft construction rose from 4,000 people in 1933 to 72,000 by 1935 [R]. Official unemployment fell year by year, from 4,800,000 in 1933 to 2,700,000 in 1934, 2,100,000 in 1935, 1,500,000 in 1936, 900,000 in 1937, 500,000 in 1938 and 300,000 by 1939 [R]. From 1936 Goering's Four Year Plan took the process further, setting production targets for industry and creating the Hermann Goering Works as centres for heavy industry [R].

The figures were not what they appeared. The Nazis excluded whole groups from the statistics, a practice known as invisible unemployment: part-time workers were counted as fully employed, and the armed forces, prisoners, Jewish people forced out of their jobs and women who had left work were all left out of the count [R]. The schemes were also expensive and hard to sustain as long-term policies, and rearmament only created jobs so long as Germany was preparing for war [D]. Wages rose for most workers through the 1930s, but so did working hours, and by 1939 food prices had risen by 20%, so unskilled workers were worse off despite being counted as employed [R].

> - Hitler needed workers for armaments production and for improving German infrastructure, so reducing unemployment and rearming were the same project.
> - Many people had voted Nazi because the party promised to make Germany great again, so unemployment was a political promise as well as an economic problem.
> - The Treaty of Versailles had limited the army to 100,000 soldiers, so conscription in 1935 was a deliberate breach.
> - The Nazis also needed to produce more weapons and equipment to supply a larger army, which created further industrial employment.
> - Jewish people were forced to give up their jobs but were not counted as unemployed.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - No introduction or conclusion is needed. Begin with the scale of the problem in 1933 and end with the state of the figures by 1939.
> - Aim for three or four paragraphs in a clear, logical sequence: public works, then the New Plan, then rearmament.
> - Learn the unemployment table. Quoting the fall from 4.8 million to 300,000 is the single most creditable thing in this answer.
> - Invisible unemployment is worth including as description, because it is part of how the figures were achieved.
> - Do not spend time evaluating. Marks here are for accurate, well-organised knowledge of what happened.

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which Nazi policies towards women were successful.
parts.solutionMd:
Nazi policy towards women had two clear aims: to remove women from work and to raise the birth rate. By 1939 the regime had partly achieved both, and by 1944 it had abandoned the first entirely [R].

The first facet is marriage and the birth rate, where the results were genuinely positive for the Nazis. The Law for the Encouragement of Marriage of 1933 offered loans of 1,000 marks, roughly eight months' wages, to women who married and left work, with a quarter cancelled for each child [R]. Around 700,000 couples took out marriage loans within four years, marriages rose from 500,000 in 1932 to 750,000 by 1934, and the birth rate rose from 15 per 1,000 in 1933 to 20 per 1,000 in 1939 [R]. This was a real success because the birth rate had been the Nazis' central demographic worry, and the policy reversed a decline rather than merely slowing it [E].

The second facet is the removal of women from employment, which worked at first. Women were banned from being teachers, doctors and other professionals in 1933, and around 19,000 female civil servants were sacked; in 1936 they were barred from becoming judges or lawyers; and in 1937 schools preparing girls for university were closed, so 11,000 fewer women were starting university by 1939 [R]. Around 360,000 women had left their jobs by 1934 [R]. The Nazis were explicit that this was the point: women were to stay at home and care for the family while the man earned the money [R]. Measured against the aim, this was effective: the Nazis wanted women at home and large numbers of women went home [E].

The third facet is the organisations, which reached enormous numbers but were resented. The German Women's Enterprise had six million members and 1.7 million women attended its courses in childcare, cooking and sewing, and three million women were eligible for the Mother's Cross in 1939 [R]. Yet many women disliked Scholtz-Klink and found the DFW demeaning [A]. Reach is not the same as enthusiasm, and a policy that produces compliance while generating resentment has only half succeeded [A]. The regime also prescribed how women should look, expecting blonde plaited hair, athleticism, no make-up, flat heels and no smoking, and Goebbels declared that 'the mission of the woman is to be beautiful and bring children into the home' [R]. Judged as an attempt to remake women's lives around the 'three Ks' of Kinder, Kirche and Kuche, the policy went far beyond employment law and reached into appearance and behaviour, which is why resentment matters as evidence [E].

Several policies also failed outright. Only around 7,000 children were born through the Lebensborn Programme, despite it running from 1935 [R]. Few mothers had more than two children, so the Mother's Cross rewarded a minority rather than changing behaviour [R]. The divorce laws of 1938, which let husbands divorce wives who would not have children, increased the divorce rate and so contradicted the Nazis' own rhetoric about family unity [A]. A regime that claimed to be restoring the family had written a law that broke families up [E].

Most damagingly, the central policy was reversed. By 1937 Germany faced a national shortage of workers, and women holding marriage loans were allowed to work after all [R]. In 1944 the government forced women into war work, 2.4 million returned to their jobs, and over 500,000 served in the Wehrmacht as nurses or in other non-combat roles [R]. Some resented the loss of the professional roles they had been pushed out of a decade earlier [E]. Even before the war women's employment rates never returned to their 1930 levels, so the reversal did not restore what the bans had removed [R].

Nazi policies towards women succeeded only to a limited extent, and the limits were self-inflicted. On the birth rate and on marriage the Nazis achieved measurable change, and in the peacetime years they largely got the domestic role they wanted [A]. But the employment policy was never sustainable, because a regime committed to rearmament and then to total war could not also spare half its workforce. The Nazis were forced to choose between their ideology about women and their ambitions abroad, and they chose the ambitions. That reversal is the clearest evidence that the policy failed on its own terms [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the importance of the Second World War to the collapse of Nazi Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Nazi Germany surrendered in May 1945, twelve years after Hitler became Chancellor, having lost a war it started. Whether the war caused the collapse or merely delivered it is one of the genuine disagreements among historians [R].

The first facet is military defeat, which is the most obvious cause. Germany defeated France in six weeks and forced the British army out of Europe, and support for the Nazi Party remained high even in 1941 [R]. Operation Barbarossa then failed through poor tactics and planning, and the defeat at Stalingrad in 1942 showed that this would not be the quick war Germans had been promised [R]. By 1944 Germany faced a war on two fronts it could not win, and in April 1945 Hitler and Goebbels killed themselves [R]. This matters because Nazi legitimacy rested on success: a regime that had justified dictatorship by restoring German strength could not survive visible defeat [E].

The second facet is the collapse of support at home. Rationing was extended and black markets appeared, Britain's bombing caused high casualties and falling living standards, and during 'Total War' women were forced to work, children were evacuated and entertainment and luxury goods were stopped [R]. Goebbels ran a propaganda campaign in 1943 and it failed to halt the decline, and an increasing number of Germans began to oppose the regime [R]. The July 1944 plot came from inside the army itself [A]. In the final stage Hitler created the Volkssturm, a Home Guard of conscripted young and elderly men which failed in battle, and the bombing of Dresden in February 1945 caused very heavy civilian casualties [R]. A regime reduced to conscripting twelve-year-olds had already lost the consent it began with [E].

The third facet is that the German economy was never built for the war it fought. Germany had not achieved autarky and still imported one-third of its raw materials in 1939, and Albert Speer only converted the country to a war economy in 1942, by which point it was too late [R]. There were shortages of fuel, coal and food, Germany relied on plundering occupied countries, and by 1944 a quarter of the workforce was enslaved labour [R]. During Operation Barbarossa there were not even enough supplies to use blitzkrieg tactics properly against the USSR, and battles steadily consumed what war supplies remained [E].

However, some historians argue the regime was already failing before 1939. On this view Germany's economy was in trouble by 1939, causing discontent, and Hitler brought forward his plans to invade Poland precisely in order to win back public support [R]. Rearmament had produced a 'guns, not butter' economy that lowered living standards, business leaders had not supported the Four Year Plan, and by 1939 food prices had risen 20% so unskilled workers were worse off, while the Volkswagen scheme took five marks a week from workers who never received a car [R]. If that is right, the war was a symptom of the regime's weakness rather than its cause [A].

Against this, the evidence of pre-war strength is substantial. Four million people joined the Nazi Party between 1933 and 1939, unemployment fell from 4.8 million in 1933 to 300,000 by 1939, and 90% voted for Hitler to become Fuhrer in 1934 [R]. Other historians therefore argue that support was strong before the war and that only the experience of total war weakened the regime [A]. There was also no organised opposition capable of removing the Nazis in 1939: parties and unions had been banned in 1933 and the Night of the Long Knives had destroyed internal rivals [R].

The Second World War was decisive, but the two explanations are less far apart than they look. The regime was not on the point of collapse in 1939: it had popular support, low official unemployment and no organised opposition capable of removing it [A]. Yet its economy was already distorted by rearmament and dependent on aggression to sustain itself, which meant the war it needed was also the war it could not survive. The Nazi state was built in a way that made war necessary and defeat fatal, so the war did not simply end the regime, it completed a contradiction that had been there from the beginning [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which farmers and businesses benefited from Nazi rule.
parts.solutionMd:
The Nazis promised to protect German farmers and small businesses, two groups that had voted for them in large numbers. Both got something, and both discovered what Nazi protection cost [R].

The first facet is what farmers gained, which was real. The Nazis believed in 'Blood and Soil', and Hitler spoke of true Aryans having farming ancestry, so farmers were valued far more highly than urban workers [R]. The Reich Food Estate regulated the food market and offered farmers guaranteed customers at fair prices, while the Reich Entailed Farm Law protected them by preventing banks from repossessing property if they fell into debt [R]. This mattered because farming had been the worst-hit sector of the Weimar economy, with agricultural incomes 44% below the national average by 1929, so guaranteed prices and protection from repossession addressed the two things that had ruined farmers [E]. Autarky gave the countryside a further political importance, since a Germany that fed itself could not be starved by a naval blockade as it had been in the First World War [R].

The second facet is that the same measures took away farmers' independence. The Nazis increased their control and told farmers what produce to grow, which caused anger in farming communities [R]. The protection from repossession also made banks reluctant to lend to farmers at all, so a law meant to help them cut off their access to credit [A]. Farming communities remained poor, and many farmers' children moved to towns and cities for better wages [R]. From 1936 the Four Year Plan added a further layer of direction, with Goering re-establishing the Reich Food Estate to guarantee prices while pressing for higher farming output in pursuit of autarky [R]. A farmer by 1939 had a guaranteed price and almost no say in what he grew [A].

The third facet is what businesses gained. The banning of trade unions and strikes removed the threat of workers turning to communism and made the workforce more productive [R]. Rearmament then created enormous opportunities, with the government offering large contracts for war goods such as steel, and armaments spending rising from 3.5 billion marks in 1933 to 26 billion by 1939 [R]. For any business connected to rearmament this was transformative, which is why corporations such as Thyssen, Krupp and Bosch had funded the party in the first place [E].

Businesses also lost their independence. The Nazis increased their control over what businesses produced, setting production targets and taking charge of iron ore, coal mining, steel and armaments under the Four Year Plan from 1936 [R]. Goering, who had no experience in economics, replaced Schacht as Minister of the Economy, and many Nazis and business leaders did not support the plan [R]. Firms outside rearmament suffered, because fewer businesses were producing consumer goods [A]. The pursuit of autarky pushed industry towards ersatz substitutes, using coal to make rubber and acorns to make coffee, and business leaders objected that excessive rearmament was lowering Germany's standard of living in what became known as a 'guns, not butter' economy [R]. By 1944 a quarter of the workforce was enslaved labour drawn from concentration camps and occupied territory, so even the firms that prospered did so on terms set entirely by the state [E].

Small businesses were also straightforwardly deceived. The Nazis had promised small business owners that they would restrict the larger department stores, and the government simply did not do it, so large businesses continued to dominate the market [R]. The group that had been most attracted by Nazi promises was the group whose promise was broken [A]. Small shopkeepers had no organisation left to complain through either, since the banning of unions and parties in 1933 removed every channel of protest [E].

Farmers and businesses benefited to a limited extent, and the pattern is the same for both. Each received genuine material help, guaranteed prices for farmers and government contracts for industry, and each paid for it with the loss of the right to make its own decisions [A]. The difference lies in who was inside the rearmament economy: heavy industry did extremely well, while farmers, small shopkeepers and consumer-goods manufacturers did not. Nazi rule benefited whoever was useful to rearmament and left everyone else with control instead of prosperity [A].

name: Why was Hitler Able to Dominate Germany by 1934?

parts.problemMd:
After a long wait, Hitler was firmly in power by the end of 1934.

Describe the events in 1932 and 1933 that led to Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933.
parts.solutionMd:
In the November 1932 elections the Nazi Party again emerged as the largest party [1]. Von Schleicher was appointed Chancellor but did not have enough support in the Reichstag [1]. Von Papen convinced Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor with himself as Vice Chancellor, so that he could control Hitler [1]. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 [1].

> - Talking only about Nazi popularity without stressing the crucial role of von Papen, von Schleicher and Hindenburg's decisions.

parts.problemMd:
Hitler rebuilt the Nazi Party after the failure of the Munich Putsch.

What happened at the Bamberg Conference of 1926?
parts.solutionMd:
Hitler called a conference of the Nazi Party at Bamberg in Bavaria in 1926, because the party was splitting into a nationalist wing in the south and a socialist wing in the north [1]. Because the meeting was held in the south, most of those who travelled to it were southern gauleiters who already agreed with Hitler [1]. At the conference Hitler attacked the socialist wing of his own party, calling them Communists and enemies of the Nazi Party [1]. He also won over Goebbels, who abandoned the socialist wing and was rewarded with promotion to gauleiter of Berlin [1].

> - Confusing the two wings. The socialist wing was in the north under Strasser and Goebbels; Hitler and the nationalist wing were based in the south.

> - Strasser believed Goebbels had betrayed him, and from this point Strasser lost Hitler's trust. He was murdered in 1934.
> - The conference brought the party's policies into line with the ideas Hitler had set out in Mein Kampf.
> - It confirmed Hitler's personal authority over the whole party rather than just its southern branches.

parts.problemMd:
Hitler rebuilt the Nazi Party after the failure of the Munich Putsch.

Why did Brüning's government fail?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that his policies made life harder for ordinary Germans at the worst possible moment [R]. Brüning became Chancellor in 1930 as leader of the Centre Party, and his response to the Depression was to raise taxes on workers and cut the money paid to the unemployed. He did this while unemployment was climbing from 4.3 million in September 1931 towards 6.1 million by January 1933. Asking people to pay more and receive less while they were losing their jobs destroyed his popular support and drove voters towards parties promising something radical. The Nazi share of the vote rose from 18.3 per cent in 1930 to 38 per cent by July 1932 [E].

A second reason is that he lost the backing his government actually depended on [R]. Brüning had no majority in the Reichstag, so he governed using President Hindenburg's emergency powers under Article 48, which meant he survived only for as long as Hindenburg was willing to sign. He then managed to offend the people he could least afford to lose. Banning the SA and SS angered Hitler and alarmed other parties who feared their own paramilitaries would be next, and his plan to break up the large land estates to house the unemployed turned the landowning class against him, including Hindenburg, who was a wealthy landowner himself. Once Hindenburg withdrew his support Brüning had nothing left to govern with, and he resigned on 30 May 1932 [E].

parts.problemMd:
Hitler rebuilt the Nazi Party after the failure of the Munich Putsch.

Which did more to make Hitler Chancellor in January 1933: von Papen or von Schleicher? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Von Schleicher has a strong claim [R]. He was the ambitious soldier and politician who designed the coalition that made von Papen Chancellor in May 1932, and he did so believing that letting Hitler have a small share of influence would keep the Nazis under control. That judgement was catastrophic, because the price of Nazi support was unbanning the SA, and it gave the Nazi Party its first foothold in government [E]. He then dismantled his own creation, going to Hindenburg in November 1932 to argue that if von Papen stayed there would be unrest on the streets that the army could not contain, which forced von Papen out [E].

His final act mattered most of all [R]. As Chancellor from 2 December 1932 he had no Reichstag majority and no popular mandate, and when he could not govern he asked Hindenburg to suspend the Weimar Constitution so that he could rule as a military dictator. Hindenburg refused. That refusal is important, because it removed the last alternative to Hitler that Hindenburg was willing to consider [E].

Von Papen, though, was the one who actually did it [R]. He was Hindenburg's personal friend, which gave him access no other politician had, and after being pushed out he used it. On 30 January 1933 he warned Hindenburg that von Schleicher was preparing to seize power by military coup, and then offered the solution: appoint Hitler Chancellor with von Papen himself as co-chancellor to keep him in check. Hindenburg accepted, and Hitler was appointed the same day [E].

On balance von Papen did more [A]. The distinction worth drawing is between creating a situation and taking a decision. Von Schleicher made Hitler possible: his coalition scheme first brought the Nazis into government, and his demand for a military dictatorship exhausted Hindenburg's alternatives. But those were miscalculations that opened a door rather than steps through it. Von Papen made the specific proposal, used a friendship to sell it to a president who disliked Hitler, and supplied the co-chancellor arrangement that let Hindenburg believe Hitler could be controlled. Von Schleicher made Hitler unavoidable; von Papen made him Chancellor [A].

parts.problemMd: Why did the Nazis have little success before 1930?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason why the Nazis had little success was the stability of the Weimar Republic under Gustav Stresemann. Germany's relations with other countries started improving, as was seen in the Locarno Pact of 1925. Due to the efforts of Stresemann, Germany was admitted to the League of Nations in 1926 [R]. This improved the image of the Weimar Republic, so many German citizens no longer wanted radical change [E]. The Dawes Plan of 1924 and US loans also helped economic recovery, and unemployment started falling. Wages improved and ordinary people began to see the Weimar Republic in a positive light. Many wanted to give it a chance to continue [E].

During the 1920s the Nazi Party was still disorganised and small. It had no strong nationwide support, and won only 2.6 per cent of the votes in the 1928 election [R]. Many ordinary Germans saw the Nazis as a violent group that had failed in the Munich Putsch in 1923. The violent street fighting of the SA, the Brownshirts, made them look dangerous, which had little appeal to people who wanted peace in Germany. Hitler's Mein Kampf, written in 1925 and popular later, was too radical and racist for many Germans during a period of stability. The Nazi Party was therefore not offering an attractive alternative to the Weimar Republic [E].

parts.problemMd: 'The Night of the Long Knives was the most important factor in Hitler's consolidation of power in 1933 and 1934.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Night of the Long Knives happened on 30 June 1934, when Hitler ordered the SS to kill high-ranking leaders of the SA, including Ernst Röhm. This incident was a very significant event in the consolidation of Hitler's power. However, it was not the most important factor. In this essay, I will examine how other political and ideological factors were equally, if not more important than the Night of the Long Knives in consolidating Hitler's power [R].

The Night of the Long Knives helped Hitler eliminate a potential rival within the Nazi movement. Röhm had become extremely powerful and ambitious, and there were rumours that he was planning a coup to replace Hitler as supreme leader of the party [E]. Röhm controlled the SA, whose size and strength made him a real threat. The army distrusted the SA for the same reason and feared that Röhm intended to absorb it, so by destroying the SA leadership Hitler removed a rival and won the support of the generals at the same time [E]. Hitler's decision to get rid of opposition within his own party was therefore a crucial moment in the early years of his leadership [A]. It established him as supreme leader of the Nazi Party and set an example for any future opposition inside it.

At the same time, other factors played a vital role between 1933 and 1934. Firstly, in February 1933 the Reichstag Fire allowed Hitler to blame the communists for setting the parliament building alight and to ban them. Civil rights were suspended through the Emergency Decree [E]. One of the Nazis' strongest rivals was removed, and Hitler gained the power to arrest and censor [A]. That power later helped him crush opposition before it could grow. The press glorified him as a great leader and silenced criticism of him and of the party.

Secondly, the Enabling Act gave him the power to make laws without the approval of the Reichstag. Using it, he banned political parties and created a one-party state [E]. After the death of Hindenburg in August 1934, the army swore a personal oath of allegiance to Hitler. Hitler could not have consolidated his dictatorship so quickly if these events had not happened [A].

To conclude, I agree that the Night of the Long Knives was important in consolidating Hitler's power, but not that it was the most important factor. It eliminated opposition inside the Nazi Party and secured the loyalty of the army. However, it was one event among several. The Reichstag Fire allowed him to crush communist opposition, and the Enabling Act gave him the legal framework to establish a dictatorship [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the Nazi Party during the lean years, 1924-28.
parts.solutionMd:
The period began with Hitler in Landsberg Prison after the failure of the Munich Putsch. There he dictated Mein Kampf to Rudolf Hess, setting out what he believed the core values of the party should be, and published it in July 1925. Its central ideas were the superiority of the Aryan race, Social Darwinism, Lebensraum or living space to be taken from Eastern Europe, the Führerprinzip of rule by a single all-powerful leader, and a return to traditional values [R].

Hitler served only nine months of a five-year sentence, because judges were markedly more lenient towards right-wing offenders. The government lifted the ban on the NSDAP in February 1925 and Hitler relaunched the party on 27 February 1925 [R].

The failure of the putsch had convinced Hitler that power would have to be won by election rather than by force, and this drove a thorough reorganisation. A party headquarters was established, with Franz Schwarz as treasurer handling funding and Philipp Bouhler as secretary running the office, and departments were created for finance, agriculture, foreign affairs, industry and education. Germany was divided into 35 regions called gaue, each under a local party leader or gauleiter. Hitler deliberately left rival members to fight over who became gauleiter, believing in the survival of the fittest. Strasser emerged as a powerful gauleiter in northern Germany and Goebbels established himself in the Rhineland [R].

Funding came from business owners who shared Hitler's nationalist vision, including the corporations Thyssen, Krupp and Bosch. They calculated that Hitler's influence over the workers would limit the power of the trade unions, which they feared both for their wage demands and for their links to communism [R].

Hitler also restructured his paramilitary forces. By 1925 he was losing trust in the SA, which had 400,000 members and had fallen further under Ernst Röhm's control while Hitler was in prison. Middle- and upper-class Germans regarded the SA as violent thugs, which was an obstacle to making the party electable. Hitler therefore sent Röhm abroad, and created a smaller private army, the Schutzstaffel or SS, which wore black uniforms from 1932 and conducted itself far less violently. Heinrich Himmler became its head, and by 1930 it had 3,000 members [R].

The most important internal moment was the Bamberg Conference of 1926. The party had been splitting between a nationalist wing in the south, around Hitler, and a socialist wing in the north, where Strasser and Goebbels were winning workers by attacking local businessmen. Because the conference met in Bavaria, most delegates were southern gauleiters. Hitler denounced the socialist wing as communists and enemies of the party, and persuaded Goebbels to change sides. Strasser lost Hitler's trust permanently, while Goebbels was promoted to gauleiter of Berlin [R].

Despite all this, the years are called lean for good reason. Membership reached 100,000 by 1929, but in the May 1928 election the Nazis won only 12 seats, roughly three per cent of the vote, leaving them the seventh largest party in the Reichstag. Hindenburg's election as President in 1925 had drawn nationalists towards the Republic, Stresemann's policies had improved living standards, the SPD took 30 per cent of the vote in 1928, and agreements such as Locarno and Kellogg-Briand had restored Germany's international standing. In prosperous times the Nazi message had little to offer [R].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of the death of Hindenburg in August 1934.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is that Hindenburg's death removed the last constitutional check on Hitler.** Paul von Hindenburg had been President since 1925, and under the Weimar Constitution the President appointed the chancellor, could dismiss him, and controlled the emergency powers of Article 48. This was not a theoretical restraint. As late as 1934 Hindenburg had threatened to impose martial law if Hitler could not bring the SA under control, and Hitler took that threat seriously enough to act on it. While Hindenburg lived there was one man in Germany with the legal authority to remove Hitler from office. His death on 2 August 1934, from lung cancer at the age of 86, ended that [E].

**The second facet is that it allowed Hitler to merge the two offices.** Rather than allow a new presidential election, Hitler combined the posts of president and chancellor in himself and took the title Führer. This was then put to the public, and 90 per cent voted in favour. The importance here is as much presentational as legal: Hitler could claim that absolute personal rule had been granted by the German people rather than seized, which mattered to a regime that had always been careful to take power through apparently lawful means [E].

**The third facet, and the genuinely new one, is the army oath.** Every soldier was required to swear an oath of loyalty to Hitler personally rather than to the state or the constitution. The Reichswehr was the only institution left in Germany with the physical capacity to overthrow the regime, and this bound it to Hitler as an individual. It also completed a bargain begun five weeks earlier: in the Night of the Long Knives on 30 June 1934 Hitler had had Röhm and around 400 SA members arrested and shot, along with von Schleicher, Gregor Strasser and von Kahr. By destroying the SA leadership, which had wanted to absorb the army, Hitler had bought the generals' goodwill; the oath was what he took in return [E].

**The fourth facet works against the question, because much of the dictatorship was already built.** The Enabling Act had become law on 24 March 1933 by 444 votes to 94, allowing Hitler's cabinet to pass laws without the Reichstag and to overrule the constitution itself. Using those powers, trade unions were abolished in May 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front, every party except the NSDAP was banned in July 1933, and the regional Länder parliaments were dissolved and replaced by loyal Nazi governors. By August 1934 Germany was already a one-party state with no independent parliament, unions or local government. On this reading Hindenburg's death confirmed Hitler's power rather than created it [E].

**Judgement.** Weighing these against one another, the death was less important as a cause of the dictatorship than as its completion, because the decisive legal break had come with the Enabling Act seventeen months earlier [A]. But of the four facets the army oath is the one that added something genuinely new, and it is therefore the most important. Every other source of opposition had already been dismantled; the armed forces had not, and the oath closed the last door through which Hitler could have been removed [A].

The speed of events supports that judgement. The merger of offices and the oath followed within hours of an 86-year-old man's death from a known illness, which indicates the response had been prepared in advance. Hindenburg's death is best understood not as a turning point that changed Hitler's position but as the final scheduled step in a takeover that had been under way since March 1933 [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Hitler joined a small political party in Munich in 1919.**

Describe how Hitler took control of the Nazi Party by 1922.
parts.solutionMd:
The government hired Hitler to spy on political parties in Munich, and he attended his first DAP meeting on 12 September 1919 before signing up as a member a week later [1]. In January 1920 he became the party's head of propaganda, and the following month he and Drexler wrote the Twenty-Five Point Programme and renamed the party the NSDAP [1]. In July 1921 Hitler triggered a leadership contest and defeated Drexler to take control of the party [1]. At a party conference in January 1922 he persuaded members to surrender their right to elect the leader, which made the NSDAP a dictatorship [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Political parties in Weimar Germany often had their own paramilitary forces.**

What was the SA?
parts.solutionMd:
The Sturmabteilung, or SA, was the Nazi Party's private army, formed in August 1921 [1]. Its members were nicknamed 'Brownshirts' because of the colour of their uniform, and Hitler recruited the unemployed, students and ex-soldiers by offering them money and a daily structure [1]. Hitler used the SA to control crowds at meetings, start fights in the streets and disrupt the meetings of opposition groups such as the KPD [1]. There were 800 Brownshirts by 1922, and Ernst Rohm became their leader in 1923, which meant the SA was not under Hitler's direct control [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Hitler attempted to seize power in Bavaria in November 1923.**

Why did the Munich Putsch fail?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the putsch lost the official backing it depended on. Hitler knew from the failures of the Freikorps and the Spartacists that a putsch needed the support of the army and the police, which is why he involved General Ludendorff, a respected war veteran [R]. But when Hitler left the beer hall he put Ludendorff in charge of the Bavarian officials, and Ludendorff was persuaded to let Kahr, Seisser and Lossow go [R]. This was decisive because those three controlled the Bavarian government, the police and the army: without them the rising had no official authority, and the army suppressed the SA with ease [E].

A second reason was that Hitler acted too soon and with too little. He rushed the putsch in November 1923 in order to take advantage of the hyperinflation crisis, when a delay would have allowed better preparation [R]. He and the SA had only 2,000 guns, and most citizens of Munich neither stopped the uprising nor actively supported it [R]. This mattered because a putsch without popular backing has to win by force, and 2,000 rifles were never going to defeat an army that had stayed loyal to the government [E].

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 6 marks will be awarded for two fully explained reasons.
> - Explaining only one reason will be awarded a maximum of 5 marks, where 5 marks requires the explanation to be supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them will be awarded 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification or description.
> - 1 mark will be awarded for writing about the topic without addressing the question.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the consequences of the putsch, such as Hitler's trial and Mein Kampf, rather than explaining why it failed.
> - Narrating the events in the beer hall without ever explaining what went wrong.
> - Confusing the Bavarian officials. Kahr led the state government, Seisser the police and Lossow the army in Bavaria.
> - Explaining only one reason and then restating it in different words.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> Answers may include the following. This list is not exhaustive and any other valid material should be credited.
> 
> - Hitler had studied the Kapp Putsch and the Spartacist Uprising and knew that military and police support was essential, which makes losing it the central failure.
> - Involving Ludendorff was meant to rally the army behind the rising, but the army remained loyal to the government regardless.
> - Rohm was responsible for securing the local army and police headquarters in Munich, and could not hold them.
> - Support for the Nazis in 1923 rested on the hyperinflation crisis rather than on settled loyalty, so it evaporated quickly.
> - Hitler himself concluded from the failure that violent putsches did not work, and afterwards sought power through the Weimar legal system.

> - Finish each paragraph by saying why that factor meant defeat, rather than stopping at the narrative.

parts.problemMd:
**The Reichstag building burned down on 27 February 1933.**

Why was the Reichstag Fire important to Hitler?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that it gave Hitler a legal weapon against his strongest opponents. Hitler had become Chancellor on 30 January 1933 but the Nazi Party controlled only one third of the Reichstag [R]. When the Reichstag building burned on 27 February 1933 the police arrested a Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, at the scene, and Hitler persuaded Hindenburg to pass the Reichstag Fire Decree [R]. This mattered because it let Hitler treat the KPD as a criminal conspiracy rather than a rival party: around 4,000 communists were arrested and communist newspapers were shut down, removing his main opposition without breaking the law [E].

A second reason was that it shaped the election that followed. The elections of 5 March 1933 were held only a week later, and the decree allowed Hitler to control the radio while the SA and SS intimidated opponents [R]. The Nazis took nearly 44% of the vote, and Hitler then forced a coalition with the Nationalists and the Centre Party [R]. This was important because the Enabling Act needed a two-thirds majority to change the constitution, and without the fire Hitler would not have had the seats or the absent communist deputies that made it possible [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.**

'The Depression was the main reason Hitler became Chancellor.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Depression made Germans willing to vote for Hitler. It did not put him in office: politicians did that [R].

The economic collapse was severe and it changed how people voted. The USA recalled its loans after the Wall Street Crash, German banks called in loans of their own, and businesses cut production or closed [R]. Unemployment reached 4.3 million by September 1931 and 6.1 million by January 1933 [R]. Having suffered two economic crises in a decade, Germans lost faith in moderate parties and looked for an alternative [E].

The Nazi vote tracks that collapse exactly. The NSDAP won just 3% in May 1928, rose to 18.3% and 107 seats in 1930, and reached 38% and 230 seats in July 1932 to become the largest party in the Reichstag [R]. Goebbels organised the campaigns of 1930 and 1932, funding posters, radio broadcasts and pamphlets [R]. Prosperity had kept the Nazis at 3%; hardship took them to 38% [A].

However, votes alone never made Hitler Chancellor. Even at his peak he was short of the 50% needed for a majority, and in November 1932 the Nazi share actually fell to 33% [R]. Hindenburg twice refused to appoint him, keeping von Papen in July 1932 and choosing von Schleicher in December, precisely because he disliked Hitler and expected Nazi support to decline [R]. Hitler was appointed when his popularity was falling, not rising [A].

The decisive factor was the conduct of the politicians. Von Papen and von Schleicher ignored election results to govern for the wealthy, and von Schleicher then asked Hindenburg to suspend the constitution and create a military dictatorship [R]. On 30 January 1933 von Papen warned Hindenburg a coup was coming, and proposed making Hitler Chancellor with himself as co-chancellor, believing they had Hitler 'in their hand' [R].

The statement is therefore true only to a limited extent. The Depression was the necessary condition, and without 6 million unemployed the Nazis would have stayed the seventh largest party [A]. But it created a large minority, not a majority, and Hitler could not win power by election. What put him in the Chancellery was von Schleicher's threat of a coup and von Papen's confidence that he could control a man he had badly misjudged [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Hitler moved against the SA leadership in June 1934.**

How important was the Night of the Long Knives to Hitler's control of Germany? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Enabling Act removed Hitler's opponents outside the Nazi Party. The Night of the Long Knives removed the ones inside it, and that was the harder problem [R].

It eliminated the only rival with the strength to challenge him. Ernst Rohm led around three million SA members, roughly 60% of whom were unemployed by 1933, and had distanced himself from Hitler [R]. He wanted a 'second revolution' focused on the working class, which conflicted with Hitler's aim of winning the support of the rich [R]. At Bad Wiessee on 30 June 1934 Rohm and around 400 SA members were arrested and shot [E].

It also secured the army, which was the decisive institution. Rohm wanted to merge the SA with the army, the SA had a poor reputation, and Hindenburg had threatened to impose martial law if Hitler could not bring it under control [R]. By destroying the SA leadership Hitler removed the army's greatest fear and bought its loyalty, which mattered five weeks later when Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 and every soldier swore an oath of loyalty to Hitler personally [E].

However, the legal foundations had already been laid. The Reichstag Fire Decree of February 1933 allowed the arrest of around 4,000 communists, and the Enabling Act of 24 March 1933 let Hitler's cabinet pass laws without the Reichstag and overrule the constitution [R]. By July 1933 all parties except the NSDAP were banned and Germany was already a one-party state [A].

Other opposition had also gone. Trade unions were abolished in May 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front, and in January 1934 the regional Lander parliaments were dissolved and replaced with Nazi governors [R]. Hitler entered June 1934 facing no organised opposition anywhere in Germany except within his own movement [A].

The Night of the Long Knives was important to a limited extent: it was the last step, not the greatest one. The Enabling Act gave Hitler the power to rule; the purge made sure nobody could take it from him [A]. Its real significance is what it bought: the army's consent. Without that, combining the offices of chancellor and president in August 1934 would have been impossible [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the Munich Putsch.
parts.solutionMd:
By November 1923 Hitler had decided the Nazi Party was ready to take control of Germany. Support had risen because the Weimar government had failed to deal with the hyperinflation crisis, and many Germans were looking to extremist parties for solutions [R]. Mussolini's successful 'March on Rome' in 1922 had shown that a paramilitary force could seize a state, and the French invasion of the Ruhr had caused shortages across Germany [R].

Hitler planned the putsch around the support of the authorities. He had studied the failed risings of the Freikorps and the Spartacists and concluded that a putsch needed the backing of the army and the police [R]. He therefore brought in General Ludendorff, a respected First World War veteran, to rally the army, while Ernst Rohm was made responsible for securing the local army and police headquarters in Munich [R]. Hermann Goering and Julius Streicher also took part [D]. Hitler judged that if he could seize control of Bavaria it would be far easier to take Berlin afterwards [D]. Everything depended on three Bavarian officials: Gustav von Kahr, who led the state government, Colonel von Seisser, who headed the police, and General von Lossow, who commanded the army in Bavaria [R].

The rising began in a Munich beer hall, where Hitler interrupted a meeting and forced Kahr, Seisser and Lossow at gunpoint to support the coup [R]. Hitler then left, placing Ludendorff in charge of the three officials, and Ludendorff allowed them to go [R]. Without their backing the putsch had no official authority, and the Bavarian leaders immediately withdrew their support [D]. Hitler continued regardless, marching into Munich the following day, but he and the SA had only 2,000 guns, the army remained loyal to the government, and the rising was crushed [R].

The consequences were mixed for Hitler. He was arrested and tried for high treason, and in February 1924 he represented himself in court rather than hiring a lawyer, so that he could use his skills as a speaker [R]. He was found guilty and sentenced to five years at Landsberg Prison, and the Munich authorities banned the NSDAP, which briefly changed its name and won 32 seats at the May 1924 Reichstag election [R]. As an Austrian citizen he could have been deported, but he impressed the right-wing judges and avoided this [D]. Newspapers across Germany reported the trial and Hitler became a national celebrity, and in prison he wrote Mein Kampf, which formalised his ideas [R]. He served only nine months of his sentence, because judges were far more lenient towards right-wing offenders, and the ban on the party was lifted in February 1925 [R]. Hitler had also learnt that violent putsches did not work, and afterwards sought power through the Weimar legal system instead [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of the origins of the Nazi Party between 1919 and 1922.
parts.solutionMd:
Anton Drexler, a railway mechanic from Munich, founded the German Workers' Party, or DAP, in February 1919 [R]. It was a right-wing party that targeted the working classes, and in September 1919 it had just 23 members [R]. Hitler came to it by accident: the Weimar government, worried about the threat new parties posed to public safety, employed him to spy on political parties in Munich, work he needed because the Treaty of Versailles had cut the army to 100,000 men and left most of Germany's soldiers unemployed [R]. He attended his first DAP meeting on 12 September 1919, found that its ideas matched his own, and joined as a member on 19 September, against his government assignment [R].

Hitler rose quickly because of his skill as a speaker. His speeches impressed Drexler, who put him on the party's organising committee and then made him head of propaganda in January 1920 [R]. Hitler practised a distinctive style of oration, increasing his tempo to a frantic and aggressive crescendo, rehearsed his hand gestures and photographed himself doing so [D]. He delivered 31 speeches in his first year as a member, and membership rose from 1,000 in June 1920 to 3,000 by the end of that year [R].

The party was then rebuilt around him. In January 1920 Hitler and Drexler wrote the Twenty-Five Point Programme, which mixed nationalist demands such as Anschluss and the exclusion of Jewish people from citizenship with socialist ones such as jobs for German citizens and a ban on private land ownership [R]. The party was renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party to appeal to several groups at once, adopted the swastika and the straight-armed salute to distinguish itself from other nationalist parties, opened a headquarters in Munich, and from December 1920 published a newspaper, the Volkischer Beobachter, distributing 17,000 copies within a year [R].

Hitler completed his takeover in two steps. In July 1921 he triggered a leadership contest and his popularity allowed him to defeat Drexler and take control of the NSDAP [R]. He then appointed his own inner circle, with Rudolf Hess as his deputy, Hermann Goering commanding the SA, Julius Streicher producing the newspaper Der Sturmer and Ernst Rohm linking the SA to the army [R]. The SA itself was created in August 1921 as the party's private army, nicknamed the 'Brownshirts', and numbered 800 men by 1922 [R]. Because the SA was not fully under his control, Hitler also formed the Stosstrupp, or 'Shock Troop', from Brownshirts he selected personally as bodyguards [D]. At a party conference in January 1922 Hitler spoke for two and a half hours and persuaded members to surrender their right to elect the leader, which effectively made the NSDAP a dictatorship [R]. By November 1923 it had 50,000 members [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Write an account of how Hitler became Chancellor of Germany.
parts.solutionMd:
Hitler's route to the chancellorship began with the collapse of the German economy. After the Wall Street Crash the USA recalled its loans, German banks lost heavily and called in loans of their own, and businesses cut production or closed [R]. Unemployment reached 4.3 million by September 1931 and 6.1 million by January 1933 [R]. Chancellor Heinrich Bruning, leader of the Centre Party, raised taxes and cut benefits to the unemployed, and by April 1932 had lost the support of the Reichstag; he resigned on 30 May 1932 [R].

The Nazi vote rose alongside the crisis. The NSDAP won 18.3% and 107 seats in 1930, and in the presidential elections of 1932 Hitler took 30% in March and 36% in April, though Hindenburg was re-elected [R]. Goebbels organised the campaigns, funding posters, radio broadcasts and pamphlets and hiring aeroplanes so that Hitler could speak across the country [R]. In the Reichstag election of July 1932 the NSDAP won 38% of the vote and 230 seats to become the largest party, after street fighting between the SA and the KPD's Red Front Fighters left over 100 dead and 7,000 injured [R].

Hindenburg refused to appoint Hitler. He disliked him, regarding a former corporal as unsuitable, so he kept von Papen as chancellor and called another election in November 1932, gambling that Nazi support would fall [R]. Von Papen's government was nicknamed 'the Cabinet of Barons', because the upper classes controlled its inner circle and its policies did not benefit the lower classes; it had no majority and passed policy mainly through Hindenburg's presidential powers, and Hitler had agreed to support it only if the ban on the SA was lifted [R]. Nazi support did fall: the NSDAP's share dropped to 33%, while the KPD rose to 17%, which alarmed moderate and right-wing politicians [R]. Von Schleicher then abandoned the coalition and persuaded Hindenburg that von Papen could not continue, and von Papen resigned [R].

The final stage was a struggle between the men who thought they could manage Hitler. Hindenburg appointed von Schleicher chancellor on 2 December 1932, out of desperation to avoid a Nazi government [R]. Von Schleicher had no majority in the Reichstag and had not been elected, and the Nazis opposed him at every opportunity [D]. He asked Hindenburg to suspend the Weimar Constitution so that he could form a military dictatorship, and Hindenburg refused [R]. Von Papen learned of the plan and contacted Hindenburg on 30 January 1933, warning that von Schleicher would otherwise seize power in a military coup [R]. Von Papen proposed instead that Hitler be made chancellor with himself as co-chancellor, and Hindenburg agreed [R]. Hindenburg and von Papen believed they had Hitler 'in their hand' and would make the real decisions [D]. Hitler became Chancellor of Germany on 30 January 1933 [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the importance of propaganda to the rise of the Nazi Party.
parts.solutionMd:
The Nazi Party was one of dozens of extremist groups in Weimar Germany, and in May 1928 it held just 12 of the Reichstag's seats. Five years later Hitler was Chancellor. Propaganda is one explanation for that transformation, but it is not the only one [R].

The first facet is that propaganda was built into the party from the start. Hitler became the DAP's head of propaganda in January 1920, and it was in that role that he pushed for the Twenty-Five Point Programme so the party had a clear statement of its aims [R]. He gave 31 speeches in his first year, practised a distinctive style of oration that built to a frantic crescendo, rehearsed and photographed his hand gestures, and produced images of himself speaking [R]. Membership rose from 1,000 in June 1920 to 3,000 by the end of the year [R]. This mattered because a party of 23 members had no money, no seats and no reputation: publicity was the only asset it could generate for itself, and Hitler's speaking was what turned a Munich discussion group into a movement [E].

The second facet is Goebbels and the mass campaigns after 1929. Goebbels organised Hitler's campaigns in 1930 and 1932, using funding from big businesses to hire aeroplanes so Hitler could tour the country, to stage marches and rallies, and to produce posters, radio broadcasts and pamphlets attacking the government's handling of the Depression [R]. The party had also been publishing the Volkischer Beobachter since December 1920, distributing 17,000 copies within a year [R]. The results were dramatic: 18.3% in 1930, 30% for Hitler in the March 1932 presidential election, 36% in April, and 38% in July 1932 [E]. Hitler became a national celebrity, and his oratory converted many who had been sceptical of Nazi policies [R]. The money came from big corporations such as Thyssen, Krupp and Bosch, who believed Hitler's influence over workers would limit the power of trade unions, so the scale of the campaigns depended on backers the party had cultivated rather than on propaganda alone [A].

However, propaganda only worked because conditions had changed. In the prosperous years the same techniques achieved almost nothing: the Nazis won roughly 3% of the vote in May 1928 and were the seventh largest party in the Reichstag [R]. What changed between 1928 and 1930 was not Nazi communication but German unemployment, which reached 6.1 million by January 1933 [R]. Propaganda amplified a message that hardship had made people willing to hear; it did not create the willingness [A].

There is also a limit visible in the numbers themselves. Even at their peak the Nazis never won a majority, and in November 1932 their share fell to 33% [R]. Hindenburg twice refused to appoint Hitler, and he was appointed in January 1933 at a moment when Nazi support was declining rather than rising [R]. Propaganda could not deliver the 50% that would have made the chancellorship unavoidable [A]. It had also failed once before at the decisive moment: the Munich Putsch of 1923 collapsed despite Hitler's reputation as a speaker, because publicity is no substitute for the support of the army and the police [R].

The decisive factor was the conduct of other politicians. Von Papen and von Schleicher ignored election results in order to govern for the wealthy, von Schleicher asked Hindenburg to suspend the constitution so he could create a military dictatorship, and von Papen then warned Hindenburg on 30 January 1933 that a coup was coming [R]. Von Papen's solution was to make Hitler chancellor with himself as co-chancellor, believing they had Hitler 'in their hand' [R]. No amount of propaganda produced that decision [A].

Propaganda was essential but not sufficient, and the distinction matters. Without it the Nazi Party would have remained a Munich fringe group, because it had no other way of reaching a national audience, and Hitler's personal appeal is the single most important reason the party grew at all [A]. But propaganda's effect depended entirely on circumstances it did not control: it failed in 1928 and succeeded in 1932 with the same methods and the same speaker. Propaganda made the Nazis the largest party, the Depression made that possible, and the miscalculations of Hindenburg, von Papen and von Schleicher turned the largest party into a government [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the extent to which Hitler's rise to power was the result of his own actions.
parts.solutionMd:
Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933, fourteen years after he joined a party with 23 members. How much of that was his own doing, and how much was done for him by circumstances and by other men, is the central question about his rise [R].

The first facet is that Hitler built the party himself. He joined the DAP on 19 September 1919, became head of propaganda in January 1920, co-wrote the Twenty-Five Point Programme, forced a leadership contest in July 1921 which he won against Drexler, and at the conference of January 1922 persuaded members to surrender their right to elect a leader [R]. He also created the SA in August 1921 and appointed his own inner circle of Hess, Goering, Streicher and Rohm [R]. This matters because none of it was inevitable: the DAP was one of many small right-wing parties, and it was Hitler's oratory and organising that made it different [E].

The second facet is that he learned from failure. The Munich Putsch of November 1923 collapsed because Ludendorff released the Bavarian officials and the army stayed loyal, and Hitler was sentenced to five years for high treason [R]. He turned the trial into publicity by representing himself, became a national celebrity, wrote Mein Kampf in prison, and concluded that violent putsches did not work [R]. He then rebuilt the party during the Lean Years, dividing Germany into 35 regions each under a gauleiter, creating the SS under Himmler, and settling the party's direction at the Bamberg Conference of 1926, where he defeated the socialist wing by branding it communist and promoted Goebbels to gauleiter of Berlin [R]. He also secured funding from corporations such as Thyssen, Krupp and Bosch [R]. That preparation is why the NSDAP was ready to exploit the Depression when it came, and it was entirely his own work [A].

However, the conditions that made him electable were not of his making. The Nazis won roughly 3% in May 1928 and were the seventh largest party, using the same leader and the same methods that later won 38% [R]. What changed was the Wall Street Crash, the recall of American loans and unemployment reaching 6.1 million by January 1933 [R]. Hitler did not cause the Depression, and without it the reorganised party would have remained a well-run fringe movement [A].

The weaknesses of the Weimar system also helped him. Proportional representation made majorities almost impossible, chancellors repeatedly abused Article 48, and Hindenburg's willingness to govern by decree had already turned many Germans away from democracy [R]. Bruning's harsh policies from 1930 to 1932 failed to control unemployment and cost him the support of the Reichstag [R]. Hitler inherited a discredited democracy rather than discrediting it himself [E]. Nor did he win the presidency when he contested it: Hindenburg beat him in April 1932 despite Hitler raising his share to 36% [R].

Most decisively, other politicians handed him office. Hindenburg disliked Hitler and twice refused to appoint him, keeping von Papen in July 1932 and choosing von Schleicher in December [R]. Hitler's vote had actually fallen to 33% by November 1932 [R]. What changed Hindenburg's mind was von Schleicher's request to suspend the constitution and rule as a military dictator, and von Papen's warning on 30 January 1933 that a coup was coming, together with his offer to serve as co-chancellor and keep Hitler 'in their hand' [R]. Hitler was given power at his weakest electoral moment by men who thought they were using him [A]. Hindenburg's own conduct mattered too: he had never fully supported the Republic, and his readiness to allow the abuse of Article 48 weakened the Reichstag long before Hitler could [R].

Hitler's own actions were the most important single factor, but they were necessary rather than sufficient. He created the party, survived its greatest failure, and rebuilt it into the only organisation capable of profiting from a crisis, and no one else could have done that [A]. Yet he never won an election outright, and the last and most important step was taken by other people for their own reasons. Hitler made himself the obvious beneficiary of a collapse he did not cause, and his real achievement was to be ready when Germany's politicians decided they needed him [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study B: Germany, 1918–45**

Discuss the importance of the SA to the Nazi Party.
parts.solutionMd:
The SA was created in August 1921 with a few hundred men and destroyed in June 1934 with three million. In between it was the Nazi Party's most visible asset and its most persistent problem [R].

The first facet is what the SA did for the party in its early years. Formed as the NSDAP's private army and nicknamed the 'Brownshirts', it recruited the unemployed, students and ex-soldiers by offering them money and a daily structure [R]. Hitler used it to control crowds at meetings, start fights in the streets, disrupt the meetings of opponents such as the KPD, and strengthen the party's image [R]. This mattered in the conditions of Weimar Germany, where political violence was normal and most parties had a paramilitary force: a party without one could not hold a meeting safely, so the SA was the price of existing at all [E]. It grew from 800 men in 1922 to 400,000 by 1925 [R].

The second facet is its role in the Nazi seizure of power. During June and July 1932 fighting between the SA and the KPD's Red Front Fighters left over 100 people dead and 7,000 injured, which created exactly the disorder that made Germans want a strong government [R]. After the Reichstag Fire the SA used the emergency decree to justify violence and intimidation against opponents, helping deliver nearly 44% of the vote on 5 March 1933, and it then intimidated Reichstag members before the Enabling Act vote on 24 March [R]. The SA was therefore directly involved in producing both the election result and the majority that ended German democracy [E]. It had been given the same role a decade earlier, when Rohm was made responsible for securing the army and police headquarters in Munich during the putsch of November 1923, though on that occasion it failed [R].

However, the SA repeatedly damaged the party it served. Many middle- and upper-class Germans regarded the Brownshirts as violent thugs, which was a serious obstacle once Hitler decided to seek power by election rather than by force [R]. By 1925 Hitler was losing trust in an organisation of 400,000 men that Rohm had strengthened while Hitler was in prison, so he sent Rohm abroad and created the much smaller and better-disciplined SS under Himmler, which had 3,000 members by 1930 [R]. A party trying to look respectable was being held back by its own army [A]. The SS wore black uniforms from 1932, conducted itself far less violently than the SA, and was made up of men Hitler had selected and trusted personally, which shows exactly what he thought the SA lacked [R].

The SA was also a political threat in its own right. Rohm led around three million men, roughly 60% of them unemployed by 1933, wanted the SA merged with the army, and demanded a 'second revolution' focused on the working class, which conflicted directly with Hitler's need for the support of the rich [R]. Hindenburg threatened martial law if Hitler could not control it [R]. At Bad Wiessee on 30 June 1934 Rohm and around 400 SA members were arrested and shot [E].

Its destruction was as useful as its existence. Killing the SA leadership removed the army's greatest fear and secured its loyalty, which was decisive when Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 and every soldier swore an oath of loyalty to Hitler personally [R]. Other rivals were killed alongside the SA leadership, including von Schleicher, Gregor Strasser and von Kahr, and the party told the public that Rohm had been planning to replace Hitler [R]. The SA's final service to Hitler was to be sacrificed [A].

The SA was extremely important, but its importance changed completely over time. In the 1920s it was indispensable, because without it the NSDAP could not have operated in the street politics of Weimar Germany, and in 1932 and 1933 its violence and intimidation shaped both the March election and the Enabling Act [A]. Once Hitler was in office, however, the same organisation became the main obstacle to the army's support, which he needed more. The SA was essential to getting Hitler into power and an obstacle to keeping him there, and Hitler's willingness to destroy his own three-million-strong movement in a single night is the clearest evidence of how much the army mattered more [A].

name: How Did Stalin Gain & Hold on to Power?

parts.problemMd:
Stalin used many different methods to hold on to power.

How complete was Stalin's control of the Soviet Union by 1941? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
In politics his control was as close to total as a ruler can get [R]. The purges had torn through the Communist Party and the officer corps, so those who remained in post owed their survival to Stalin and had every reason to stay loyal. Behind them stood the NKVD, which needed neither evidence nor witnesses to make an arrest and which from 1935 could prosecute children as young as twelve as adults, and behind the NKVD stood the labour camps. Organised political opposition simply could not form under those conditions, because anyone who began to build it disappeared [E].

Control over what people were allowed to think was almost as tight [R]. Pravda was the only legal newspaper, western radio was banned, and the arts were censored and monitored. On top of this sat the cult of personality, with portraits, photographs and statues presenting Stalin as a god-like father of the nation, so that opposing him felt not merely dangerous but wrong. The regime even edited photographs to remove purged figures and rewrote the textbooks so that Stalin, not Trotsky, stood beside Lenin in 1917 [E].

Against this, control of the economy and of daily behaviour was much weaker than the propaganda suggested [R]. Workers and peasants moved around the country constantly and the government struggled to keep track of them. Many failed to meet their production targets and simply bribed officials to cover it up, or turned out substandard goods so the figures would look right. That is not a population doing what it is told; it is a population working around instructions it cannot meet [E].

There is also the problem of reach [R]. Stalin directly governed only central Russia and depended on party officials to run everywhere else, which meant his authority passed through exactly the kind of local officials who had an interest in reporting good news. The purges made this worse rather than better, because they stripped out skilled people from every sector and left the country short of the experts it needed [E]. Underground opposition groups, particularly among the young, also went on existing [R].

I partially agree that Stalin's control was complete [A]. Where control rested on terror it really was total, and by 1941 no one in the Soviet Union could organise against him and expect to live. But where control depended on people cooperating rather than fearing, it leaked badly, and the bribery, the shoddy output and the reliance on unsupervised local officials all show it. Stalin could make the Soviet people obey him; he could not make them work well for him, and the difference between those two things is what stops his control being complete [A].

**[10 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 10 marks require you to explain both sides and then support a valid judgement on 'how far'.
> - Explaining both sides without a supported judgement is worth 7-9 marks. Seven marks are given for one explanation on each side, with one further mark for each additional explanation on either side.
> - Explaining only one side is worth 4-6 marks, with one mark for each explanation.
> - Identifying or describing valid points without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 10 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the purges, the NKVD and the cult of personality one after another without ever asking how complete the resulting control was. Methods are evidence; the question is about the result.
> - Arguing only that control was total. An answer that never considers the limits is capped at 6 marks however detailed it is.
> - Drifting past 1941 into the Second World War. The date in the question sets the boundary.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Collectivisation and the Five-Year Plans gave the state direct control over where peasants and workers lived and what they produced, which extended Stalin's reach into the countryside.
> - The scale of the machinery is itself evidence: the GULAG population passed two million by 1938.
> - A useful distinction is between public and private life. Open opposition was almost impossible, but what people did and said among themselves was far harder for the regime to reach.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Aim for at least three explanations, two on one side and one on the other, then judge.
> - The strongest structure here is to separate the areas of life. Control over politics, over information, over the economy and over private behaviour were not equally complete, and saying so is exactly the kind of analysis Level 5 rewards.
> - Use 'fully' or 'partially' in your conclusion. A qualified judgement scores better than a flat yes or no.
> - Avoid listing methods. Every method you name should be followed by what it did or failed to do to Stalin's grip on the country.

parts.problemMd:
Stalin used many different methods to hold on to power.

What happened in the Soviet show trials of 1936 to 1938?
parts.solutionMd:
Leading Bolsheviks were put on public trial accused of crimes such as disrupting the Five-Year Plans, murdering Kirov and plotting to overthrow the government [1]. The accused confessed, having been tortured by the NKVD beforehand, and the judge already knew the sentence before the trial began [1]. In the Trial of 16 in 1936, sixteen people including Zinoviev and Kamenev were found guilty and executed [1]. The Trial of 21 in 1938 included Bukharin and Yagoda, the head of the NKVD, and all twenty-one were executed [1].

> - Saying only that people were 'put on trial and killed'. Naming who, when, or what they were accused of is what turns a vague statement into a creditable point.

> - Bukharin used his trial in 1938 to speak out about how corrupt the proceedings were.
