parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–41**

Write an account of the Provisional Government's failure to retain power in 1917.
parts.solutionMd:
After Tsar Nicholas abdicated in March 1917, the Provisional Government was created by the duma with twelve representatives, intended as a temporary solution while Russia moved towards democracy. [R] From its first weeks it had to share authority with the Petrograd Soviet in a system called Dual Power, and the Soviet's Order No.1 told the army to obey the Soviet rather than the government. [R] Extremist parties, including the Bolsheviks, steadily increased their representation within the Soviet as 1917 went on, making it a more hostile rival with every month that passed. [D]

The government continued Russia's involvement in the First World War, needing British and French investment and hoping a victory would boost its standing. [D] In March the Petrograd Soviet declared it could no longer support the war, creating a growing divide within Dual Power. [R] In June, Kerensky, as Minister of War, launched the June Offensive against Austrian troops. [R] It failed badly, casualties and desertions rose sharply, and soldiers increasingly listened to Bolshevik propaganda rather than their own government, which they blamed for prolonging a war that most Russians had already come to hate. [D]

The government also failed to tackle land reform. Peasants wanted landowners to give up their estates, and the government promised change but would not set a date for elections that could give it a mandate to act. [D] By mid-1917 peasants stopped waiting and began seizing land illegally across the countryside, convinced that a government which could not even set an election date would never act on their behalf. [R]

Food shortages, the failed June Offensive and ministers resigning combined to spark the July Days. [D] Between 3 and 6 July, mass protests broke out in Petrograd, joined by the Kronstadt sailors, chanting Bolshevik slogans such as 'Peace, Bread, Land' and 'All Power to the Soviets'. [R] Lenin refused to support the unrest, unsure the moment was right, and the government responded with force, arresting many Bolsheviks and driving Lenin to flee to Finland. [R]

By September the government was collapsing further. [D] Prince Lvov resigned and Kerensky became Prime Minister, the only person who sat on both the government and the Petrograd Soviet. [R] To restore order, Kerensky appointed General Kornilov as commander of the army, but when Kornilov marched towards Petrograd, Kerensky panicked. [R] He freed the Bolsheviks his own government had arrested in July and armed the Red Guard to defend the capital. [D]

The Bolsheviks infiltrated Kornilov's troops, encouraged mass desertion and disrupted his supplies by persuading railway workers to strike. [D] By the end of September the government had arrested Kornilov, but the Red Guard, now armed, never gave back its weapons. **Depth study C: Russia 1905–41**

Write an account of the events of the October Revolution.
parts.solutionMd:
Lenin had been exiled by the Tsarist government and was not in Russia during the March Revolution. [R] In April 1917 he returned, funded by Germany and travelling on the sealed train through countries without passport checks, since Germany hoped his presence would push Russia out of the war. [R] On his arrival in Petrograd he delivered the April Theses, demanding peace, an end to food rationing, the redistribution of land and 'All power to the Soviets'. [R] These slogans won growing support among workers, who chanted them during the July Days, though Bolshevik support fell afterwards when Lenin refused to back that protest, key Bolsheviks including Trotsky were arrested, and Lenin himself fled to Finland to avoid the same fate. [D]

By September the Bolsheviks held a majority in the Petrograd Soviet, and Trotsky became its chairman. [R] On 7 October Lenin returned to Petrograd in disguise, and on 10 October he persuaded the Bolshevik Central Committee to back an armed seizure of power, against the objections of Zinoviev and Kamenev, who voted against the plan and later made their disagreement public. [R] Soldiers at the Peter and Paul Fortress agreed to arm the Bolsheviks, and Trotsky reported that fifteen of eighteen army units stationed in the city supported the planned uprising rather than the Provisional Government. [D]

On 23 and 24 October, Kerensky tried to close down the Bolshevik newspapers that had been calling openly for an uprising, but soldiers loyal to the Petrograd Soviet simply blocked his efforts to enforce the order. [R] On 24 October Bolshevik-controlled ships, led by the cruiser Aurora, arrived on the Neva and aimed their guns at the city, while during the night of 24 to 25 October Bolshevik forces seized the bridges, the telephone exchange, the railway stations and the main post office, meeting almost no resistance from government troops loyal to Kerensky. [D]

At ten o'clock on the morning of 25 October, Lenin declared that the Provisional Government had been overthrown. [R] Around an hour later Kerensky fled the Winter Palace to try to rally loyal troops elsewhere, leaving the remaining ministers undefended inside the building. [R] Late that night the Aurora fired on the Winter Palace and Bolshevik forces stormed the building, arresting the government at around two in the morning. [R] Only around six deaths were reported across the entire operation, a striking contrast with the mass casualties of the March Revolution earlier that year. [D]

The Bolsheviks now controlled Petrograd, a key city of the former Russian Empire, but not the whole of Russia. [D] Many enemies, within Russia and abroad, opposed their seizure of power, and the Bolsheviks would spend the following years fighting a bitter civil war against the Whites and foreign powers to hold on to what they had won in a single night in Petrograd. [D]

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the reasons why the Provisional Government was unable to maintain its authority in 1917.
parts.solutionMd:
The Provisional Government came to power in March 1917 as a temporary solution while Russia moved towards democracy, but by October it had lost all authority. Several linked problems combined to destroy it [R].

The first facet is Dual Power. From the start the government had to share authority with the Petrograd Soviet, which issued Soviet Order No.1 telling the army to obey the Soviet rather than the government. As extremist parties like the Bolsheviks gained representation within the Soviet, it became an increasingly hostile rival, encouraging strikes and undermining every decision the government tried to take. This mattered because it meant the government could never govern with full authority, since real power in the capital was split between two competing bodies from the very beginning, and every reform depended on a rival institution's cooperation rather than the government's own decisions [E].

The second facet is the government's failure to act on land and elections. Peasants wanted landowners' estates redistributed, but the government feared taking such a major decision before it had a democratic mandate, and it never set a date for the elections that would give it one. By mid-1917 peasants stopped waiting and began seizing land illegally across the countryside. This was damaging because the peasantry made up the great majority of Russia's population, and their patience with a government that promised elections and reform but delivered neither eventually ran out entirely, undermining any claim it had to represent ordinary Russians [E].

The third facet is the government's decision to continue the First World War. It needed British and French investment and hoped a victory would strengthen its position, but this put it directly at odds with the Petrograd Soviet, which declared in March that it could no longer support the war. Kerensky's June Offensive against Austrian troops failed badly, producing heavy casualties and rising desertion, and soldiers turned increasingly to Bolshevik propaganda rather than their own government. A government that kept an unpopular war going while failing to win it lost the loyalty of the very army it depended on for its survival [E].

The fourth facet is the July Days. Food shortages, the failure of the June Offensive and the resignation of ministers combined to spark mass protests in Petrograd between 3 and 6 July, joined by the Kronstadt sailors and chanting Bolshevik slogans. Although Lenin refused to support the unrest and fled to Finland once the government cracked down and arrested key Bolsheviks, including Trotsky, the protests showed how fragile the government's support had already become only four months after the Tsar's abdication, and its violent response alienated many workers still further [E].

The fifth facet is the Kornilov Affair. By September, with the government failing on every front, Kerensky appointed General Kornilov to command the army, but when Kornilov marched towards Petrograd, Kerensky panicked, freed the Bolsheviks his own government had imprisoned in July, and armed the Red Guard to defend the city. The Bolsheviks helped stop Kornilov by persuading his troops to desert, and although Kornilov was arrested, the Red Guard never returned its weapons. This was the most damaging single episode because Kerensky's own decision handed his most determined enemies both freedom and firearms in the space of a few days, a mistake none of the government's other failures came close to matching in its consequences [E].

These facets connect closely. The government's failures on land and the war had already convinced peasants and soldiers, many of whom were peasants in uniform, that it could not be trusted, which is part of why so many were willing to accept Bolshevik rifles once Kornilov threatened Petrograd, and why the Red Guard felt no obligation to disarm itself afterwards [A].

On balance, the Kornilov Affair was the most important reason for the collapse of the government's authority [A]. Dual Power, the war and the land question had all steadily eroded its support over many months, but none of them put weapons directly into Bolshevik hands. It was Kerensky's own panic in September that armed the Red Guard and destroyed what remained of his authority over the army, converting a slow, months-long decline into the specific military weakness that let the Bolsheviks seize power only seven weeks later [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the importance of Lenin's leadership to the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917.
parts.solutionMd:
Lenin is often credited as the single figure most responsible for the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917, but several other factors also mattered a great deal in explaining exactly why the Bolsheviks succeeded when they did [R].

The first facet is Lenin's ideological leadership. Although he had been exiled and missed the March Revolution, he returned to Russia in April 1917, funded by Germany and travelling on the sealed train, and immediately delivered the April Theses, demanding peace, the end of rationing, land redistribution and 'All power to the Soviets'. These slogans gave the Bolsheviks a clear and popular message at a time when other parties still supported continuing the war, and they were chanted by workers during the July Days. This mattered because it gave the party a distinct identity that set it apart from its rivals months before October arrived, at a time when the Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries still shared power with the Provisional Government and offered no such clear alternative [E].

The second facet is Lenin's personal insistence on timing. Even after the Bolsheviks won a majority in the Petrograd Soviet by September, other leading Bolsheviks, including Zinoviev and Kamenev, argued against an armed uprising, fearing it was too risky and premature. Lenin returned to Petrograd in disguise on 7 October and personally persuaded the Central Committee to commit to a seizure of power on 10 October. Zinoviev and Kamenev were so opposed to the plan that they later criticised it openly once it succeeded, showing genuine division within the leadership that only Lenin's insistence overcame. Without his pressure, the Bolsheviks might have delayed and let the opportunity created by the Kornilov Affair slip away entirely [E].

The third facet is Trotsky's organisational role, which was arguably just as important. As chairman of the Petrograd Soviet from September, Trotsky reported that fifteen of eighteen army units in the city supported the Bolsheviks, and it was his Military Revolutionary Committee that coordinated the actual seizure of the bridges, the post office and the telephone exchange on the night of 24 to 25 October. Lenin provided the ideology and the decision to act, but Trotsky provided the machinery that carried the plan out, coordinating the Military Revolutionary Committee that actually directed soldiers and Red Guards to their targets across the city that night [E].

The fourth facet is the weakness of the Provisional Government itself. Kerensky's decision to arm the Bolshevik Red Guard during the Kornilov Affair in September gave the party weapons it never returned, and his government's failures over land, the war and Dual Power had already destroyed its support among workers, soldiers and peasants long before October. When Kerensky tried to shut down Bolshevik newspapers on 23 October, loyal soldiers simply ignored his order, showing how little authority the government retained by that point, only a month after Kerensky had himself armed the very Red Guard now defying him [E].

These facets are closely connected. Lenin's April Theses had built the popular support that made soldiers willing to defect to the Bolsheviks, but that support only became real power because Trotsky turned it into an organised force and because Kerensky's own mistakes had left the government almost undefended by October. Lenin's leadership was necessary to create the conditions for October, but it was not sufficient on its own to explain the eventual outcome, since a popular message and a determined leader could still have failed against a government capable of defending itself [A].

On balance, Lenin's leadership was important but not the most important single factor [A]. His insistence on acting on 10 October was decisive in ensuring the Bolsheviks moved when they did rather than hesitating further, but the government's own collapse after the Kornilov Affair meant that Petrograd was left almost undefended regardless of exactly who led the Bolsheviks that autumn. Lenin decided that the moment should be seized, and his refusal to let the party hesitate after Zinoviev and Kamenev's objections was genuinely decisive. Yet it was the Provisional Government's accumulated weakness, exploited skilfully by Trotsky's organisation on the ground, that made seizing power in Petrograd so easy to achieve with so little bloodshed [A].

parts.problemMd:
The Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd in October 1917.

'The October Revolution was more a coup than a popular revolution.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Historians widely agree that the October Revolution looked nothing like the popular uprising the Bolsheviks later claimed it to be [R]. In 1928 the Bolsheviks commissioned Sergei Eisenstein to make a film showing crowds storming the gates of the Winter Palace under heavy gunfire. In reality the gates were unguarded and open, and the remaining ministers of the Provisional Government offered almost no resistance at all to the Bolshevik takeover of the capital [E].

The events themselves support the idea of a coup rather than a revolution [R]. By September the Bolsheviks already held a majority in the Petrograd Soviet, with Trotsky as chairman, and small, organised groups seized the bridges, the post office and other key buildings overnight on 24 and 25 October. Only around six people died taking the Winter Palace. This was a carefully planned seizure by a committed and well-organised minority, not thousands of ordinary Russians spontaneously rising up together in the streets, as they had during the popular revolution of March 1917 [A].

There is also a case for calling the October Revolution more popular, however [R]. Lenin's April Theses, delivered in April 1917, demanded peace, bread, land and 'All power to the Soviets', and these slogans won genuine mass support among workers and soldiers exhausted by the war and food shortages. They were chanted by protesters during the July Days, showing that Bolshevik ideas already commanded a real popular following months before October arrived [E].

That popularity continued to grow through the autumn [R]. The Kornilov Affair in September forced Kerensky to arm the Bolshevik Red Guard to defend Petrograd, and the party's role in helping stop Kornilov's advance won it further credibility with workers and soldiers who feared a right-wing takeover. The Bolsheviks could not have acted so confidently in October without knowing that resistance to their takeover would be minimal, and Tsereteli, the Menshevik leader, publicly predicted that Bolshevik power would not last three weeks, which shows that even the government's own opponents saw it at the time as a small, temporary putsch rather than a genuine mass movement [E].

On balance, the statement is true to a large extent [A]. The Bolsheviks did not have control of the whole of Russia in October 1917 and relied on genuine wider support to survive the months that followed, but the seizure of Petrograd itself was the disciplined, planned action of a minority party rather than a spontaneous popular rising, which is exactly why most historians today choose to describe October 1917 as a coup [A].

parts.problemMd:
Bolshevik support grew significantly in the months before October 1917.

Which was more important in explaining the growth of Bolshevik support by October 1917: the Kornilov Affair or the Provisional Government's failure to act on land? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
By September the Provisional Government was already failing badly [R]. Kerensky had become Prime Minister as Russia performed poorly in the war and strikes and food shortages spread. When General Kornilov marched on Petrograd, a panicked Kerensky freed key Bolsheviks from prison and armed the Red Guard to defend the city [E].

The Bolsheviks made the most of this opportunity [R]. They infiltrated Kornilov's troops, persuaded many soldiers to desert, and disrupted his supply lines through a railway strike. By the end of September the government had arrested Kornilov, but the Red Guard never returned its weapons, giving the Bolsheviks military strength and huge credibility as the party that had saved Petrograd, while Kerensky's own authority never recovered [E].

The government's failure over land was equally important, but in a slower and steadier way [R]. Peasants had demanded that landowners give up their land, and the government promised reform, yet it never set a date for the elections that would give it a mandate to act, choosing instead to keep delaying the decision [E].

By mid-1917 peasants stopped waiting for that mandate and began seizing land illegally across the countryside [R]. This mattered because it showed millions of ordinary Russians, not just the politically committed revolutionaries in the cities, that a government which kept delaying its most basic promises would never actually deliver what they wanted [E].

The two problems reinforced each other [R]. The government's failure on land had already convinced peasants and soldiers, many of whom were peasants in uniform, that it could not be trusted, which is part of why so many soldiers were willing to accept Bolshevik-issued rifles once Kornilov threatened the city [A].

On balance, the Kornilov Affair was more important [A]. The land question had been damaging the government's reputation for months, but reputation alone did not put weapons in Bolshevik hands. It was Kornilov's march that armed the Red Guard and gave the Bolsheviks the physical means to seize power in October, turning months of long-term unpopularity over land into the specific, immediate opportunity that Lenin then used just seven weeks later [A].

name: What was the Impact of Stalin's Economic Policies?

parts.problemMd:
Stalin made huge changes to Soviet agriculture and industry.

Describe how villages were collectivised.
parts.solutionMd:
Large collective farms, known as kolkhozes, were formed, and farmers were compelled to join them, bringing their land, animals and tools [1]. The kulaks were eliminated as a class, and private ownership of land was removed [1]. These collectivised farms were run as a single unit, with shared machinery and tools [1]. The process was often violent, because when peasants resisted, the Red Army and the secret police were allowed to use force [1].

parts.problemMd:
Collectivisation reorganised farming across the Soviet Union.

What was the difference between a kolkhoz and a sovkhoz?
parts.solutionMd:
A kolkhoz was owned collectively by its members, while a sovkhoz was owned outright by the state [1]. On a kolkhoz the peasants received a share of the farm's output and profit, calculated according to the number of days they had worked, whereas on a sovkhoz they were simply salaried employees paid a wage [1]. Decisions on a kolkhoz were taken jointly by the peasants working there, but on a sovkhoz they were made by government officials [1]. Sovkhozes were also much larger, averaging around 15,300 hectares against roughly 5,900 hectares for a kolkhoz [1].

>

>

> - Four separate differences are needed for four marks. Developing a difference you have already made does not earn a second mark.

>

> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Describing collectivisation in general without ever separating the two types of farm. The question asks for the difference between them.
> - Getting the two the wrong way round. The sovkhoz was the state farm with wages; the kolkhoz was the collective with profit shares.
> - Explaining why Stalin introduced collectivisation. Reasons earn no credit here.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Peasants on either type were allowed to keep a small personal plot, usually about one acre, compared with an average of 13.5 acres before collectivisation.
> - The state supplied shared machinery and tools to both, later through the machine tractor stations.
> - Both were part of the same policy introduced from 1928, so the similarities are worth knowing as well as the differences.

> - Four differences is the whole task. There are no marks for explaining the effects of either.

parts.problemMd:
Collectivisation reorganised farming across the Soviet Union.

Why did Stalin's government target Ukraine during collectivisation?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is what Ukraine produced [R]. It was the most profitable agricultural region of the whole Soviet Union and grew a vast amount of grain, and grain was exactly what Stalin needed. Selling surplus grain abroad was how he intended to pay for the machinery and foreign expertise required by the Five-Year Plans, and in 1928 the USSR had been reduced to importing two million tons of food. A region that could supply the surplus was therefore essential to the whole industrialisation programme, which meant Stalin could not allow Ukrainian peasants to farm as they wished [E].

A second reason is that Ukraine resisted [R]. Ukrainians had a strong national and cultural identity of their own and fought back against collectivisation harder than most, destroying crops and livestock rather than surrender them. Stalin treated this as a political challenge as much as an economic one, because a region that could defy him on farming might defy him on anything. The government responded with violent repression, and in 1932, despite a poor harvest, it raised the grain quota rather than lowering it. Food was taken even from peasants who could not meet the quota, producing the famine Ukrainians call the Holodomor, meaning death by hunger. Historians estimate that famine in this period killed as many as 13 million people across the Soviet Union, with Ukraine worst affected [E].

parts.problemMd:
Stalin's economic policies transformed the Soviet Union.

Which suffered more under Stalin's economic policies: the peasants or the industrial workers? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The peasants have the stronger claim [R]. Collectivisation was compulsory, and those who resisted by burning crops or killing livestock were treated as enemies of the state: nearly ten million kulaks were executed or driven off their land, and dekulakisation had eliminated them as a class by 1934. The disruption to farming, combined with grain requisitioning, produced famines that historians estimate killed close to thirteen million people, with Ukraine worst affected. These are deaths on a scale that nothing in the industrial programme matches [E].

What survivors were left with was also worse [R]. Peasants became dependent on a state that paid them badly for their crops, and they were reduced to a single acre of land for their own use where before collectivisation they had farmed an average of 13.5 acres. A family could lose almost everything it owned and still be expected to meet the state's quotas [E].

Industrial workers suffered too, and it would be wrong to present the Five-Year Plans as painless [R]. The plans prized speed over safety, and workers were killed or maimed on state projects: around 10,000 people died in the first five years of building Magnitogorsk alone. Around ten million people were deported as political opponents, and prisoners in the GULAG system did forced labour under production targets like any other workforce. Discipline was severe and consumer goods were scarce, so living standards for many stayed low even as output soared [E].

On balance the peasants suffered more [A]. The fairest way to compare is to ask what each group risked. An industrial worker faced hard discipline, poor housing, and a real danger of injury or of being swept up in the purges. A peasant faced the loss of land, livestock and livelihood, and then a famine that killed millions of people who had done nothing except live in the countryside. Both groups paid for Stalin's modernisation, but the industrial workers paid with their conditions and the peasants paid with their lives.

One qualification is worth adding [A]. The two groups overlapped, because many of the peasants driven off the land became the industrial workforce in the new cities, so a single family could experience both. That does not change the judgement, but it shows the policies were two halves of one process rather than separate burdens [A].

parts.problemMd: Why did industrial production increase under Stalin?
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin used several policies and methods to increase industrial production in the USSR. He introduced centrally planned economic programmes, called Five-Year Plans, with targets for industries such as coal, steel, oil and electricity [R]. Huge amounts of money were used to build large industrial complexes such as Magnitogorsk. Workers were motivated and also threatened to meet production targets, and those who failed could be severely punished or imprisoned in the GULAG system [E]. The Stakhanovite movement was used as a propaganda tool that promoted model workers who exceeded their targets, which pushed other workers to work harder [E].

Industrial production also increased because of centralised planning and the command economy, under which the state took complete control of economic activity. Private enterprise was eliminated and all resources were directed towards industrialisation [R]. Millions of prisoners from the GULAG system were forced to work in dangerous conditions building railways, canals and factories. This provided a massive, cheap workforce and contributed to the rapid expansion of heavy industry [E].

parts.problemMd: How far had the lives of Russians improved by the mid-1930s? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin adopted several policies in the 1930s to improve social, economic and political conditions in the USSR. He was successful in some of them; however, the impact of others was not as widespread as expected. In this essay, I will examine how Stalin's policies were not beneficial for all groups in society, and were not long-lasting.

On the positive side, Stalin's industrialisation drive, especially in heavy industries such as coal, oil and steel, created more jobs and opportunities for advancement [R]. Higher wages, better education and training schemes helped workers turn the USSR into a modern industrial power. Women benefited particularly from Stalin's economic plans [E]. They gained more freedom to work, and because creches were provided at workplaces even mothers could take jobs. Free health care and paid holidays made employment more attractive still [E].

However, not all Russians shared these benefits. Firstly, collectivisation caused famine in Ukraine in the early 1930s, leading to millions of deaths. Animals and land were seized, so living standards in the countryside did not improve [A]. The kulaks were treated brutally and sent to labour camps. Although jobs were available in the cities, conditions there did not improve much either, because housing was overcrowded, consumer goods were expensive and scarce, and food shortages were common [A]. Between 1928 and 1937 wages fell sharply: heavy industrial production rose, but consumer goods such as clothing and rations were neglected [A].

Secondly, political repression made life dangerous and uncertain. The secret police, the purges and the show trials created an atmosphere of fear [E]. Millions of people were arrested without warning, many were sent to the GULAG system and some were executed. Even loyal communists could suddenly be accused of disloyalty, and most people did not know whether they were safe [A].

To conclude, the lives of Russians had not improved very far by the mid-1930s. There were real improvements in education, employment opportunities and industrial growth. However, the living standards of ordinary Russians remained poor, and what improvement there was in some areas was overshadowed by famine, food shortages and fear [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the Stakhanovite movement.
parts.solutionMd:
The Stakhanovite movement began in 1935, during the second Five-Year Plan. By this stage Soviet industry was working to targets set by Gosplan for every region, factory, manager and worker, and those targets were ambitious and usually unachievable. The movement was the regime's attempt to solve that problem through example rather than through planning [R].

It took its name from Aleksei Stakhanov, a coal miner. On 31 August 1935 he reportedly mined 102 tons of coal in under six hours, which was fourteen times his quota. The communist government seized on the achievement immediately [R].

Stakhanov was turned into a national celebrity. He travelled the country, and the government rewarded him with a home, extra pay and additional holiday, making it plain that exceptional output would be exceptionally rewarded. Contests were then organised across the country to find the best worker in every industry, and the publicity encouraged others to follow his example [R].

Imitators duly appeared. On 1 February 1936 Nikita Izotov reportedly mined 640 tons of coal in a single shift, a figure far beyond even Stakhanov's. Stakhanovites were soon identified in many different industries, in the countryside as well as in the towns, and the movement became a central feature of Soviet propaganda about labour [R].

The reality was different from the publicity. Stakhanov and those who followed him almost certainly did not achieve the output figures claimed for them, since such records depended on teams of assistants and carefully prepared conditions that were never mentioned. The published totals were propaganda rather than measurement [R].

The consequences for ordinary workers were serious. Because the state treated these figures as proof of what was possible, expectations and pressure on both workers and managers increased. Norms could be raised on the strength of a record that had not really been set alone, so a movement presented as a celebration of Soviet labour in practice made everyday work harder and targets less attainable [R].

**[15 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> 
> Accuracy, coverage and sequence earn the marks, not explanation.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **11-15 marks:** the account includes the main events and developments and directly addresses the question. It is consistently supported by accurate historical knowledge and is logically sequenced.
> - **6-10 marks:** the account describes some events and developments relevant to the question. It is mostly supported by accurate historical knowledge and is structured in its approach.
> - **1-5 marks:** limited relevance to the question. Some accurate historical knowledge. Points are generally unconnected.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 11-15 marks include:
> 
> - Writing a general account of the Five-Year Plans. The plans are the setting, but the question is about one movement within them.
> - Accepting the output figures uncritically. The best accounts report the claims and note that they were almost certainly not achieved as presented.
> - Stopping at Stakhanov himself. The spread of the movement to other workers and industries, and its effect on norms, is what makes it a movement rather than an anecdote.
> - Confusing it with collectivisation. Stakhanovism was an industrial campaign, not an agricultural one.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The movement served the wider purpose of the second Five-Year Plan, which aimed to develop heavy industry further while also expanding chemicals, railways and communications.
> - Rewarding Stakhanovites with housing and higher pay created a favoured group of workers, which sat awkwardly with official claims about equality.
> - Workers who failed to meet targets faced fines, dismissal or in serious cases arrest, so the movement operated alongside real penalties for failure.
> - Some workers resented Stakhanovites for driving up the norms everyone else had to meet.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Set the scene in one short paragraph, then get to Stakhanov quickly. The marks are in the movement, not in the background.
> - The dates and figures are the backbone: 1935, 31 August 1935, 102 tons in under six hours, fourteen times his quota, and Izotov's 640 tons on 1 February 1936.
> - Distinguish claim from fact. Saying the records were 'reportedly' achieved shows the examiner you understand you are handling propaganda.
> - End with the effect on other workers. Showing that the movement raised expectations across Soviet industry demonstrates you understand why it mattered.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of the Five-Year Plans in preparing the Soviet Union for war.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is that military security was a purpose of the plans from the beginning.** Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans in 1928, and one of the stated motivations was that heavy industry was needed to protect the USSR from invasion from the west. New industrial centres were deliberately developed in the east, far from any likely European front, and a modern industrial base was understood to be the precondition for modern armaments. This was not industrialisation that happened to prove useful in wartime; it was industrialisation undertaken partly with war in mind [E].

**The second facet is that the plans delivered the industrial base a modern war required.** The first plan, from 1928 to 1932, concentrated on coal, iron, steel and electricity, and coal and iron output doubled, with vast new works such as Magnitogorsk built from nothing. The second, from 1933 to 1937, more than doubled heavy industrial production again and completed the Moscow Railway. By 1940 the USSR was the second largest producer of steel in the world. A country that could not produce steel in quantity could not have produced tanks, artillery or aircraft in quantity either [E].

**The third facet is that the plans could be redirected to rearmament when the danger became clear.** The third Five-Year Plan, begun in 1938, had been intended to mechanise agriculture and produce some consumer goods, but Stalin abandoned it in order to concentrate on rearmament. The centralised planning system, which had been built to move resources by command rather than by market, allowed that switch to be made quickly [E].

**The fourth facet works against the question, because the plans were built for speed rather than quality.** They prioritised meeting targets over efficiency, which produced a great deal of waste and goods that were often of poor quality compared with Western products. Targets were routinely unrealistic and unmet, and there was a persistent shortage of skilled workers. Output figures therefore overstate real military capability, since weapons that are produced quickly but badly do not win battles [E].

**The fifth facet is that the regime damaged its own preparations.** The third plan suffered from a shortage of competent managers and specialists because Stalin's purges had removed them. The same state that was building the industrial base was simultaneously destroying the people needed to run it, and it did so in the years immediately before the invasion. The human cost was enormous in its own right: 10,000 people died in the first five years of building Magnitogorsk alone, around ten million were deported as political opponents and set to labour on state projects, and wages fell between 1928 and 1937 [E].

**Judgement.** The plans were necessary to Soviet survival but not sufficient for it [A]. The strongest evidence is the location decision. Building industry in the east was a choice made for military reasons years in advance, and it is the single most important way in which the plans prepared the country for invasion, because it put production beyond the reach of the advancing enemy.

Set against that, the preparation was far less complete than the output totals suggest [A]. Quality was poor, targets were missed, and the purges had stripped out the managerial expertise the system depended on at precisely the wrong moment. The fairest conclusion is that the Five-Year Plans made survival possible without making it likely: they gave the USSR the capacity to fight a long industrial war, while the regime's own political violence ensured it entered that war far less ready than it should have been [A].

**[25 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating the Second World War. The depth study ends in 1941 and the question is about preparation, not about campaigns.
> - Listing the targets and outcomes of each plan in turn. That is recall; every figure used has to be connected to military capability.
> - Writing about collectivisation at length. Agriculture mattered for feeding the country but the question is about the plans and war readiness.
> - Concluding only that the plans 'helped'. A judgement needs to say how much and to weigh the successes against the failures of quality and management.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The plans also served Stalin politically, since abandoning the NEP for state-owned industry undermined Bukharin and the right of the party, so military preparedness was never the only motive.
> - Foreign help and investment from Britain and the USA contributed to early industrialisation, which complicates the claim that the plans made the USSR self-sufficient.
> - Political prisoners provided labour on state projects, so part of the industrial base was built by the same repression that later weakened it.
> - Grain exports of 1.69 million tons in 1933 funded foreign experts and machinery, linking agricultural policy to industrial capacity.
> - Living standards did improve in some industrial towns, and by the third plan some consumer goods were available, so the plans were not solely about armaments.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep the focus on 1941 and before. Everything after the invasion is outside the depth study and outside the question.
> - The eastern location of new industry is your strongest single argument, because it shows deliberate military planning rather than lucky accident.
> - Use the purges as your counter-argument. Showing that the regime undermined its own preparation is a sophisticated point that few candidates make.
> - Distinguish quantity from quality. Being the second largest steel producer in 1940 is impressive; producing goods of poor quality at speed is not, and holding both ideas at once is what the top level rewards.
> - Aim for a judgement with two halves, such as necessary but not sufficient. That structure lets you rank the facets without pretending the evidence all points one way.

parts.problemMd:
Stalin transformed the Soviet economy from 1928.

What were Stalin's reasons for introducing the Five-Year Plans?
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin wanted heavy industry to protect the USSR from invasion from the west, so new industrial centres were deliberately developed in the east, further from any likely European front [1]. The plans also aimed to establish 'Socialism in One Country', since becoming self-sufficient would remove the USSR's need for foreign goods and let it catch up with the West [1]. Stalin had moved from supporting the New Economic Policy to state-owned industry during the power struggle, which undermined Bukharin and the right wing of the party [1]. Stalin also wanted to be seen as a great leader, and industrialisation helped earn him the nickname 'Man of Steel' [1].

parts.problemMd:

What were Stalin's reasons for introducing collectivisation?

Stalin wanted greater state control over rural areas, since many parts of the USSR were remote and dissent in the countryside had been common under both the Tsars and Lenin [1]. One reason for the Five-Year Plans is security. Stalin believed that heavy industry was needed to protect the USSR from invasion from the west, and new industrial centres were deliberately developed far to the east, well beyond the reach of any likely European front, so that a modern industrial base could go on producing modern armaments even in wartime [R]. parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
One clear reason is that collectivisation extended Stalin's political reach deep into remote rural areas of the USSR. parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of the reasons why Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans in 1928, aiming to rapidly transform the USSR from a largely agricultural society into a modern industrial power within a series of five-year targets [D]. There were several distinct motivations behind such a radical and demanding policy.

The first, and most immediate, motivation was security. Stalin believed that heavy industry was needed to protect the USSR from invasion from the west, and more industrial centres were deliberately developed in the east, away from any likely European front [D]. A modern industrial base was seen as the necessary foundation for developing modern armaments, since tanks, artillery and aircraft could not be produced by a country that still relied on imported machinery and foreign expertise for almost everything [D].

The second motivation was ideology. The plans helped establish 'Socialism in One Country', the policy Stalin had used against the left wing of the party during the power struggle [R]. Becoming self-sufficient would remove the USSR's need for foreign goods, and a stronger economy would allow the country to catch up with the capitalist West, proving to sceptics both inside and outside the party that communism could succeed on its own terms without external support [D].

The third was power and control within the party. Stalin had moved from supporting the New Economic Policy to backing state-owned industry during the leadership contest, and this shift undermined Bukharin and the right wing of the party, who had favoured the NEP's more gradual approach [R]. Political prisoners from the GULAG system could also be used for forced labour on major state industrial projects, linking the economic plans directly to Stalin's wider methods of political control and repression [D].

The fourth was personal reputation. Stalin wanted to be seen as a great and successful leader, and rapid industrialisation earned him the nickname 'Man of Steel', a title that reinforced the carefully constructed image he wanted both the Soviet people and the wider world to have of him as a decisive, transformative leader [D].

To carry out the plans, Stalin created Gosplan, the State Committee for Planning, which set targets for every region, factory, manager and worker [R]. These targets were consistently ambitious and usually unachievable in the timeframe set, and Stalin also relied heavily on foreign help and investment from countries such as Britain and the USA to support the earliest and most difficult stages of Soviet industrialisation [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of the reasons why Stalin introduced collectivisation.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin introduced collectivisation in 1928, aiming to combine individual peasant farms into large collective units [D]. Several distinct motivations lay behind the policy.

The first, and most fundamental, motivation was power and control. Stalin wanted greater state control over rural areas, since many parts of the USSR were remote and difficult for the central government to reach, and dissent in the countryside had been common under both the Tsars and Lenin [R]. Collectivisation offered a way to bring millions of previously independent peasants under direct, permanent government supervision for the first time in Russian history, extending Stalin's authority into areas the Tsars themselves had never fully controlled [D].

The second was ideology. Collectivisation was seen as a way to implement socialism in the countryside, since Marxist theory held that agriculture, like industry, should eventually be organised collectively rather than through private ownership [R]. The policy also reduced the influence of kulaks, wealthier peasants who were viewed as class enemies standing in the way of a genuinely communist society, and the process known as dekulakisation aimed to eliminate this group entirely from Soviet rural life [D].

The third was food supply. Stalin aimed to fix Russia's long-standing agricultural problems, since parts of the USSR suffered from famine or unsuitable growing conditions, and by 1928 the country had been reduced to importing two million tons of food [R]. Exporting Soviet grain abroad, once collectivisation had supposedly modernised farming through mechanisation and larger units, could also generate the funds needed to pay for the machinery and foreign expertise required by the Five-Year Plans running alongside it [D].

The fourth was personal reputation. Stalin wanted to be seen as a strong and successful leader, and developing Soviet agriculture through a bold new policy generated positive propaganda that reinforced his image as the man solving problems the Tsars and even Lenin had failed to fix [D].

In practice, peasants were told to form collective farms, known as kolkhozes, or in some cases state-owned sovkhozes, bringing their land, animals and tools with them, while being allowed to keep only a small personal plot [R]. Many peasants resented being forced from their homes and destroyed crops and slaughtered animals rather than hand them over to the state, and this resistance was most severe of all in Ukraine, where the government responded with violent repression and, in 1932, an increased grain quota despite an already poor harvest, producing the devastating famine that Ukrainians call the Holodomor [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Write an account of the First and Second Five-Year Plans.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin created Gosplan, the State Committee for Planning, to organise the entire programme of the Five-Year Plans, and it set detailed, specific targets for every region, every factory, every manager and even every individual worker across the whole USSR [R]. These targets were consistently ambitious and usually unachievable in practice, and Stalin also relied heavily on foreign help and investment from countries such as Britain and the USA to support the programme in its early stages [D].

The first plan ran from 1928 to 1932, aiming to develop heavy industry such as coal, iron, steel and electricity, with an overall target of increasing production by 300% [R]. Vast new complexes such as the Magnitogorsk steelworks were built almost entirely from nothing on the open steppe, and coal and iron output doubled during this five-year period alone [R]. However, the wider targets, including the overall goal of a 300% increase in production, were unrealistic and could not be met in full, and the plan suffered throughout from a severe and persistent shortage of skilled workers [D].

The second plan, from 1933 to 1937, aimed to develop heavy industry further while also expanding lighter industries such as chemicals, railways and communication [R]. Heavy industrial production more than doubled again during this second period, and the Moscow Railway was completed as a major symbol of Soviet engineering, but targets remained far too unrealistic and much of the output that was produced continued to be of noticeably poor quality [D].

It was during the second plan, in 1935, that the Stakhanovite movement began [R]. Named after the coal miner Aleksei Stakhanov, who reportedly mined 102 tons of coal in under six hours on 31 August 1935, fourteen times his quota, the movement encouraged workers across many industries to try to match or beat his example, with the government organising contests across the country to find the single best worker in each industrial sector, and Nikita Izotov reportedly mining an even more extraordinary 640 tons of coal in one shift on 1 February 1936 [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the reasons why Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin formally introduced the Five-Year Plans in 1928, launching a programme of rapid, state-directed industrialisation that would transform the USSR at enormous human cost within little more than a decade [R]. Historians have long and genuinely debated exactly what combination of motives drove such a demanding and disruptive policy.

The first, and perhaps most fundamental, facet is security. Stalin believed that heavy industry was essential to protect the USSR from invasion from the west, and new industrial centres were deliberately developed in the east, beyond the reach of any likely European attack [R]. A modern industrial base was understood as the necessary foundation for producing modern armaments, so an agricultural, backward USSR could never have defended itself against a more industrialised enemy [E]. This mattered because it shaped concrete decisions about where factories were actually built, showing the motive was not merely rhetorical propaganda designed to justify hardship after the fact [A]. Stalin genuinely believed that a country still relying on imported machinery could never fight a modern war on equal terms [E].

The second facet, closely related to the first, is ideology. The plans helped firmly establish 'Socialism in One Country', the policy Stalin had used to defeat the left wing of the party, led by Trotsky, during the power struggle after Lenin's death [R]. Becoming self-sufficient would remove the USSR's need for foreign goods, and a stronger economy would let the country catch up with the capitalist West, offering proof both at home and abroad that communism could succeed on its own terms without waiting for the worldwide revolution that Trotsky's rival policy of 'permanent revolution' had demanded [E].

The third facet, more directly political than the first two, is power and control within the Communist Party itself. Stalin had moved from supporting the New Economic Policy to backing state-owned industry during the leadership contest of the 1920s, and this shift directly undermined Bukharin and the right wing of the party, who had favoured the NEP's more gradual, market-based approach to economic development [R]. Adopting rapid, state-directed industrialisation therefore let Stalin defeat his very last remaining political rivals using economic policy itself as a weapon, since Bukharin could offer no equally dramatic alternative once the plans were announced [A]. Political prisoners from the growing GULAG system could also be used as forced labour on the resulting state projects, tying the economic programme directly to Stalin's methods of political repression [E].

The fourth and final facet is Stalin's own personal reputation. He wanted to be seen as a great and successful leader, and rapid industrialisation earned him the nickname 'Man of Steel', an image that reinforced his authority at home and abroad and his standing as the singular leader who had transformed a backward, largely agricultural country into a modern industrial power within barely a single generation of Soviet rule [R]. This mattered politically as well as personally, since a leader associated with visible national achievement was far harder for any remaining critics within the party to challenge [E].

These facets connect closely to one another rather than operating as separate, independent motives. Defeating Bukharin required a genuine alternative economic policy to offer the wider party, and that alternative only worked as effective propaganda for Stalin's reputation because it was also grounded in a real, widely shared fear about Soviet security that ordinary party members and citizens alike could readily understand and support [A].

On balance, having weighed all four facets against one another, security concerns were the single most important reason for the Five-Year Plans [A]. Ideology gave Stalin a theoretical justification, defeating Bukharin gave him a political opportunity, and personal reputation gave him a motive to publicise the plans loudly, but it was the underlying fear of invasion from a more industrialised West that explains why Stalin was willing to accept such enormous human suffering to achieve rapid results [A]. A leader concerned only with ideology, party politics or reputation might have pursued a slower, less costly programme; it was genuine strategic fear about the USSR's vulnerability to a more industrialised enemy that pushed the plans forward at such reckless, uncompromising speed, whatever the cost to the people who had to build the factories, mines and railways the country now demanded [A].

**[25 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss the reasons why Stalin introduced collectivisation.
parts.solutionMd:
Stalin formally introduced full collectivisation in 1928 alongside the Five-Year Plans, forcing millions of peasants onto collective farms at enormous human cost and producing famines that killed millions of people [R]. Historians have debated for decades what combination of motives could possibly justify a policy that produced such devastating and lasting consequences for the Soviet countryside.

The first, and arguably the most fundamental, facet is power and control over the countryside. Stalin wanted greater state control over rural areas, since many parts of the USSR were remote and difficult for the central government to reach, and dissent in the countryside had been common under both the Tsars and Lenin [R]. Collectivisation therefore offered the state direct, permanent supervision over millions of peasants who had previously farmed largely outside government reach, extending Stalin's personal authority into parts of Soviet society that neither the Tsars nor even Lenin's own government had ever managed to fully control before him [A].

The second facet, closely related to the first, is ideology and the demands of Marxist theory. Collectivisation was consistently presented by the government as a way of implementing genuine socialism in the countryside, since orthodox communist theory held that agriculture, exactly like industry, needed to be organised collectively rather than left in private hands indefinitely [R]. The policy also targeted kulaks, wealthier peasants viewed as class enemies, and the deliberate process known as dekulakisation aimed to eliminate their influence entirely and permanently from Soviet rural life, treating an entire social class as a political enemy to be destroyed rather than persuaded [E].

The third facet is food supply, and it was arguably the single most urgent of all the pressures Stalin faced in 1928. Stalin aimed to fix Russia's long-standing agricultural problems, since some regions of the vast USSR suffered from recurring famine or genuinely unsuitable growing conditions, and by 1928 the country had once again been embarrassingly reduced to importing roughly two million tons of food from abroad despite covering roughly a sixth of the world's land surface [R]. Exporting Soviet grain, once farming had supposedly been modernised through collective methods and larger, mechanised units, could generate the hard currency and funds needed to pay for the foreign machinery, engineers and technical expertise that the Five-Year Plans urgently required, especially during their difficult earliest years [E].

The fourth and final facet is Stalin's own personal reputation as a national leader. He wanted to be seen as a strong and successful leader who could achieve what previous Russian governments had never managed, and a bold new agricultural policy generated genuinely positive propaganda across the country, presenting Stalin as the one man finally solving deep-rooted agricultural problems that had defeated the Tsars for centuries and had even defeated Lenin's own government during its early, uncertain years in power [R].

These facets connect closely to one another rather than operating as separate, unrelated aims. The drive for food and export revenue only made sense as such an urgent policy because Stalin already wanted greater political control over the peasantry for its own sake, and framing that control in ideological terms, as a war against kulak class enemies, made forced collectivisation far easier to justify to the wider party as principled communism rather than as simple repression of the countryside [A].

On balance, having weighed all four facets against one another, the need for food supplies and export revenue was the single most important reason for collectivisation [A]. Ideology explained why kulaks specifically were targeted, and political control explained why the state wanted permanent authority over the countryside, but it was the urgent economic crisis of 1928, symbolised by having to import food into a country as vast as the USSR, that explains the speed and brutality with which collectivisation was carried out [A]. Without that pressing economic need, Stalin's ideological and political goals in the countryside might well have been pursued far more gradually, through education and persuasion rather than force, and with far less catastrophic human cost than the millions of deaths that collectivisation actually produced [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia 1905–1941**

Discuss how successful Stalin's economic policies were in transforming the Soviet Union by 1941.
parts.solutionMd:
By 1941 Stalin's economic policies, the Five-Year Plans and collectivisation together, had transformed the USSR from a largely backward, agricultural society into a major industrial power in scarcely more than a decade, but at a cost historians still argue about today [R].

The first facet is genuine industrial success [R]. The first Five-Year Plan, from 1928 to 1932, concentrated on coal, iron, steel and electricity, and output in these areas doubled, with vast new industrial complexes such as Magnitogorsk built almost entirely from nothing on the open steppe [R]. The second plan, from 1933 to 1937, more than doubled heavy industrial production again and completed the Moscow Railway, a major symbol of Soviet engineering achievement [R]. By 1940 the USSR was the second largest steel producer in the world, behind only the United States, transforming its economic and military standing within little more than a single decade of state-directed effort [E]. Gosplan, the state planning committee, coordinated targets across every region, factory and worker, and although those targets were routinely unrealistic, the sheer scale of investment produced results that no previous Russian government had ever come close to achieving [E].

The second facet is agricultural failure, which stands in sharp contrast to industrial success [R]. Collectivisation caused widespread resistance, as peasants destroyed crops and slaughtered livestock rather than hand them over to the state, and the resulting collective farms, or kolkhozes, were frequently poorly run and genuinely inefficient compared with the individual farms they replaced [E]. The disruption, combined with harsh grain requisitioning, produced famines that historians estimate killed between five and eight million people across the Soviet Union, with Ukraine, where the government actually raised quotas despite an already poor 1932 harvest, worst affected by what Ukrainians call the Holodomor, meaning death by hunger [R]. Grain production did not recover to its pre-collectivisation levels for several years afterwards, meaning the policy failed even by its own stated economic goals [E].

The third facet is the quality and reliability of what was actually produced, which qualifies the impressive headline figures considerably [R]. The Five-Year Plans consistently prioritised speed over quality, and targets set by Gosplan were routinely unrealistic and usually unmet in full, producing goods that were frequently of poor quality compared with those made in Britain, Germany or the USA [R]. There was a persistent, serious shortage of skilled workers and experienced managers throughout the period, which limited how efficiently the new industrial capacity could actually be used even once it had been built [E]. The third Five-Year Plan, begun in 1938, was undermined further still by a shortage of competent specialists after Stalin's purges had removed so many of them from their posts [E].

The fourth facet is the enormous human cost, which touched both industry and agriculture alike and cannot be separated from any honest assessment of success [R]. Around 10,000 people died in the first five years of building Magnitogorsk alone, around ten million people were deported as political opponents and set to forced labour on state projects across the country, and real wages actually fell between 1928 and 1937 even as heavy industrial output rose sharply in the official statistics [R]. Nearly ten million kulaks were executed or driven from their land during dekulakisation, a deliberate policy that eliminated an entire social class in the name of economic and ideological reorganisation, while millions more peasants died in the resulting famines [R]. Any measure of success that ignores this scale of suffering is, at best, dangerously incomplete [A].

These facets connect very closely to one another rather than existing as separate, unrelated outcomes of policy. The industrial success depended directly on the human cost described above, since forced labour, deported political prisoners and a workforce kept disciplined by genuine fear all contributed to the sheer speed at which factories like Magnitogorsk could be built [A]. Equally, the agricultural failure fed directly into the industrial statistics, since peasants driven off collectivised land, often against their will, became part of the urban industrial workforce the Five-Year Plans required [A].

On balance, having weighed all four facets against one another, Stalin's economic policies were genuinely successful in transforming Soviet industry but were a profound failure in agriculture and, more importantly, an enormous and largely avoidable human tragedy [A]. Judged purely by industrial output and by the USSR's later ability to withstand a major war, the Five-Year Plans achieved a great deal of what they set out to do, turning the country into a major industrial power within little more than a decade of sustained, brutal effort [A]. Judged instead by their effect on ordinary Soviet citizens, and particularly on the peasantry, the policies were a genuine catastrophe, and no measure of steel output, however impressive, can ever be fairly weighed against an estimated five to eight million famine deaths [A].

parts.problemMd:
Stalin made huge changes to Soviet agriculture and industry.

Which was more important in Stalin's decision to launch the Five-Year Plans: military security or his personal reputation? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
New industrial centres were deliberately built in the east of the USSR, far beyond the reach of any likely attack from a European power [R]. Locating major factories so far from the western border reduced the risk that an invading army could quickly seize or destroy the USSR's new industrial base, so this geographical choice shaped exactly where factories were actually built, not merely the general direction of stated policy [E].

A modern industrial base was also the essential precondition for producing modern armaments [R]. Stalin judged that a backward, largely agricultural USSR could never have defended itself against a more industrialised power such as Germany, so heavy industry mattered because it directly determined whether the Red Army could ever be properly equipped for a future war [E].

Stalin's personal reputation also mattered a great deal [R]. He wanted to be seen as a great and successful leader, and rapid industrialisation earned him the nickname 'Man of Steel', reinforcing his image as the man who was transforming a backward country into a modern power [E].

This reputation was also a matter of political legitimacy, not just image [R]. Stalin had only recently secured his position after the long power struggle of the 1920s, so a triumphant economic programme helped present his leadership as strong and genuinely deserved, rather than merely won through political manoeuvring against former colleagues [E].

The two motives reinforced one another closely rather than pulling Stalin's policy in different directions [R]. A leader who could point to steel output and new industrial cities had solid evidence for his reputation, while genuine fears about security gave the whole propaganda campaign real substance rather than empty boasting [A].

On balance, military security was the more important motive [A]. Personal reputation explains why Stalin wanted the plans to be seen as a triumph, but security explains why he was willing to accept such enormous human cost to achieve them. A leader concerned only with reputation might have settled for a smaller, safer programme; it was the genuine, underlying fear of invasion that drove Stalin to demand rapid, complete industrialisation across the whole country regardless of the price paid by ordinary Soviet citizens along the way [A].

parts.problemMd:
Stalin's government introduced the policy of collectivisation across Soviet agriculture from 1928 onwards.

'Ideological reasons were more important than economic reasons in explaining why Stalin introduced collectivisation.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Ideological reasons shaped Stalin's decision to introduce collectivisation from 1928 [R]. It was seen as a way to implement socialism in the countryside, replacing private peasant landholding with collective and state farms that fitted Marxist theory. This shows ideology was central to the decision, since ending private land ownership was a goal in itself for a government building a communist society [E].

A further ideological strand was dekulakisation, the drive to eliminate kulaks, wealthier peasants viewed as class enemies blocking a communist countryside [R]. Collectivisation let Stalin remove their influence while seizing their land and livestock, showing the policy was not simply economic but also meant to eliminate a group ideology identified as an obstacle to socialism [E].

Economic reasons were equally significant, and one strand was the urgent need to fix Russia's agricultural problems [R]. By 1928 the USSR had been reduced to importing two million tons of food, and some regions still suffered from famine or unsuitable growing conditions, showing peasant farming was failing to feed the country. This gave Stalin a genuine, pressing crisis to solve, not simply a theory to apply [E].

A second economic strand was the need to fund rapid industrialisation [R]. Exporting surplus grain from the new collective farms could generate the funds needed for the Five-Year Plans, so Stalin needed agriculture to produce a reliable surplus rather than just enough for peasants to survive on. This meant collectivisation was also meant to solve a food-supply problem threatening industrialisation [E].

The two motives were closely connected in practice, rather than operating as separate aims [R]. Removing the kulaks on ideological grounds also removed the peasants most likely to resist state control of grain, so eliminating a class enemy and securing an economic resource were often achieved by the same action [A].

On balance, this is true only to a limited extent, since economic reasons were more important than ideological ones [A]. Stalin's need for grain to fund the Five-Year Plans and feed the growing industrial workforce explains the urgency and timing of collectivisation far better than ideology alone, which could in principle have waited. Ideology gave Stalin a justification he could present to the party, but it was the pressing economic crisis of 1928, shown by having to import food into so vast a country, that gave him a genuine reason to act immediately [A].

name: Why Did the Tsarist Regime Collapse in 1917?

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the revolution of March 1917
parts.solutionMd:
The March Revolution of 1917 was a result of several economic, political, social, and ideological factors. During the war, the Tsar decided to take personal command of the army, and Tsarina Alexandra was in charge, with Rasputin as advisor. Due to the war, Russia had to face enormous social and economic issues [E]. Inflation and the shortage of food made it difficult for people to survive. Soldiers were demoralised and poorly equipped. Many Russians could no longer stand these conditions, causing them to revolt [E].

The revolution started on 8 March 1917 in Petrograd. Since it was also International Women's Day, thousands of women joined strikes and peaceful protests to demonstrate against food shortages. All sections of society, including workers and students, joined the strikes [R]. The size of the crowd kept increasing as more and more people joined, demanding bread. They also wanted an end to the Tsar's rule and Russia's involvement in the First World War. When the Tsar ordered the soldiers to fire on the protesters in Petrograd, the army mutinied and instead joined the protesters. This was a big boost to the revolution as they provided weapons and discipline to the movement. Workers and soldiers created the Petrograd Soviet, and the Tsar found it impossible to restore order [E].

The Duma, the Russian parliament that the Tsar tried to dissolve, formed a Provisional Committee. Tsar Nicholas II set out to return to Petrograd from the frontlines. However, he realised it was too late. 300 years of rule of the Romanov dynasty came to an end on 15 March 1917, when the Tsar abdicated the throne [R]. The Provisional Government took control until elections could be held, but it chose to carry on fighting the First World War, so the hardships that had driven people onto the streets continued [E].

To conclude, the March 1917 Revolution took place due to food shortages, war hardships, and political discontent, but the most crucial turning point was the mutiny of the army in Petrograd. This not only eroded the Tsar's authority but also made his abdication inevitable [E].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance to Russia of military defeats in the First World War.
parts.solutionMd:
The Tsar decided to involve Russia in the First World War even when it was not fully ready for it. The Russian army suffered multiple military defeats, which led to catastrophic consequences [E]. Apart from the loss of people and property, the Russian economy began to decline, political destabilisation led to unrest, and eventually all this resulted in the fall of the Tsarist regime.

The weaknesses of the Russian military were exposed as early as 1914, and it became clear that the army was not fully trained or equipped [E]. It also lacked strong leadership, and the early defeats demoralised both soldiers and civilians. This was not the soldiers' fault: they were demotivated, poorly disciplined and short of rifles, food, boots and ammunition. They could see defeat coming. Russia faced huge casualties and an enormous human cost, with over 1.7 million soldiers killed and many more wounded or captured by 1917 [R]. Many soldiers deserted, and some rose in rebellion against their superiors. During the March 1917 revolution, soldiers refused to fire on revolutionaries and instead joined them. Military loyalty was therefore under threat, and the Tsar found it impossible to assert his authority. Ordinary people were angry at the incompetence of the government. All of this added economic strain from the cost of the war and eroded confidence in the Tsar's regime [A].

Military defeats also had a serious economic impact. When millions of workers and farmers were conscripted into the army, the workforce available on farms and in factories was reduced. The army needed supplies, which created shortages of food [E]. Transport was diverted to the war fronts, so food could not be moved reliably from villages to the towns and cities. Bread queues could be seen in every part of the cities, and starvation became common. The government printed more money to fund the war, which caused inflation, and workers' wages did not keep pace with rising prices. The defeats aggravated this situation further. Socialists, Mensheviks, Bolsheviks and other groups spread revolutionary ideas. Workers, peasants, soldiers and other working-class groups were dissatisfied and became attracted to the idea of overthrowing the Tsar [A].

Politically, these defeats put a large question mark over Tsar Nicholas II's leadership and undermined confidence in him. In 1915, when he decided to take personal command of the army, he became directly responsible for its performance [E]. His reputation was at stake, which meant the army's defeats would erode his own authority. In his absence, Tsarina Alexandra was in charge of administrative affairs with Rasputin as adviser [R]. This fuelled resentment and ridicule, as people already disliked both of them. Alexandra was also a German princess, and Germany was Russia's opponent in the First World War, so there were rumours that she was a German spy. Military defeats added fuel to the fire and accelerated the downfall of the monarchy [A].

However, the Tsarist system was facing serious problems before the military defeats. The absence of political reform, the dissatisfaction of peasants and opposition from workers all existed before the war began in 1914 [E]. Inflation and food shortages, especially in the cities, were common and could have caused unrest even if the Russian army had not been defeated. The Bolsheviks, a revolutionary party, offered an alternative idea of government when the Tsar failed [A].

In conclusion, military defeats in the First World War were crucial to Russia because they destroyed the authority of the Tsar, caused mass casualties, eroded army loyalty and aggravated economic hardship. They were the short-term factor that transformed discontent into revolution. However, defeats alone did not cause the revolution. They exposed and sharpened problems that already existed in Tsarist Russia, alongside food shortages, poor government decisions and political discontent [A].
