parts.problemMd:
Tsar Nicholas II made limited political concessions after 1905.

What was the Duma?
parts.solutionMd:
The Duma was an elected parliament, promised by Tsar Nicholas II in the October Manifesto of 1905 [1]. All men were allowed to vote for a representative to sit in it [1]. It met in order to pass laws, although the Tsar remained head of the government and was advised by his own Council of Ministers [1]. Four Dumas met between 1906 and 1914 [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following code has been used:
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point, up to a maximum of 4.
> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Explaining why the Duma failed to make Russia democratic. That is a separate question and earns no credit here.
> - Confusing the Duma with the Soviets. The Soviets were councils elected by workers in 1905; the Duma was the national parliament created by the Tsar.
> - Writing only that it was 'a parliament'. Adding who could vote, what it did or how many met is what turns that into further marks.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The Fundamental Laws of 1906 allowed the Tsar to veto its legislation and dissolve it whenever he chose.
> - The first two Dumas were radical and demanded further reform, so the Tsar closed them down quickly.
> - The government then changed the voting laws to reduce the influence of peasant voters, so the third and fourth Dumas were dominated by right-wing parties and were far more compliant.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep each point in its own sentence so the examiner can count them.
> - The date range 1906 to 1914 and the fact that there were four Dumas each count as a point in their own right, so they are useful if you are struggling to reach four.
> - Resist the temptation to explain. This question asks what the Duma was, and analysis of its weakness belongs in the 6-mark and 10-mark questions.

parts.problemMd:
Tsar Nicholas II made limited political concessions after 1905.

Why did so many Russian soldiers desert during the First World War?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that men were sent to fight without the means of fighting [R]. It is estimated that 800,000 men in the Russian army had no rifle, and Russian factories could produce only 13,000 rounds of ammunition a day. The results were visible from the start: at Tannenberg in August 1914 over 30,000 Russians were killed or wounded, and at the Masurian Lakes a month later Russia lost 125,000 men and 150 artillery guns. Soldiers who are ordered forward unarmed against a better-equipped enemy have no reason to believe they can win, and by 1916 over 1.7 million Russians had died. Desertion becomes a rational choice when staying offers no prospect of victory, only of death [E].

A second reason is that most of these soldiers were conscripted peasants with families in trouble at home [R]. Because millions of peasants had been taken off the land, farming production fell, inflation reached 200 per cent and food prices climbed. Russia's railways could not cope, so supplies rotted at stations while the towns went hungry. A peasant in uniform knew his family was suffering and that his labour was needed on the farm, which gave him a powerful reason to walk away. The Brusilov Offensive of June 1916 sharpened this further, because although it destroyed much of the Austro-Hungarian army it cost 500,000 Russian lives for gains that could not be held, and by 1917 over a million men had deserted [E].

>

> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Describing Russia's defeats without connecting them to the decision to desert. The battles are evidence; the question is about why men left.
> - Writing about the March 1917 revolution. Desertion contributed to it, but the question is about the soldiers' own reasons during the war.
> - Blaming the Tsar's leadership alone. His decision to take personal command in 1915 is worth a mention, but it explains who was blamed rather than why individual soldiers walked away.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Many conscripts were untrained and completely unprepared for modern warfare, which made the losses feel futile as well as heavy.
> - The war fell more heavily on peasants than on any other class, so the burden was unevenly shared and resented.
> - Once desertion became common it fed on itself, because a man was far more likely to leave if he could see others doing so without consequence.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two explained reasons is the target. A good pairing is conditions at the front and conditions at home.
> - Keep asking what the war looked like from an individual soldier's point of view. That keeps the answer on the question rather than drifting into general causes of the revolution.
> - Precise figures earn the fifth mark. The 800,000 men without rifles, 13,000 rounds a day and over a million deserters by 1917 are all worth learning.

parts.problemMd:
Tsar Nicholas II made limited political concessions after 1905.

Which did more to destroy support for the Tsar: the Russo-Japanese War or the First World War? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Russo-Japanese War did serious damage [R]. Russia went to war with Japan in 1904 over Manchuria expecting an easy victory, because the Tsar regarded the Japanese as an inferior people. Instead the war exposed an army that was poorly organised and under-equipped, and the great fortress of Port Arthur fell in January 1905. The humiliation of losing to a power Russians had been taught to look down on was itself a blow to the Tsar's prestige, and the war disrupted food supplies at home. Within weeks came Bloody Sunday and the 1905 Revolution [E].

The First World War, though, did damage of a different order [R]. Over 1.7 million Russians had died by 1916 and more than a million men had deserted by 1917. Crucially, Nicholas took personal command of the army in 1915 despite having no military experience, which meant every subsequent defeat was personally his. It also left the government in the hands of the Tsarina and Rasputin, whose dismissal of capable ministers discredited the monarchy among the very aristocrats who were meant to support it [E].

The damage at home was worse still [R]. Inflation reached 200 per cent, the railways failed so that food rotted at stations while cities starved, and by 1917 there were over 1300 strikes. This time the discontent reached the one group the Tsar could not afford to lose, and soldiers began refusing to fire on demonstrators [E].

The decisive comparison is what each war ended in [A]. The Russo-Japanese War produced a revolution that Nicholas survived, because he still had an army willing to obey him and could combine the concession of the October Manifesto with repression. The First World War produced a revolution he did not survive, because by 1917 he had neither. The 1905 crisis cost him prestige; the 1917 crisis cost him the instruments of power.

So the First World War did more [A]. The qualification worth making is that the two are connected rather than separate. The Russo-Japanese War revealed the weaknesses of the regime and raised expectations of reform that Nicholas then disappointed by gutting the Duma, so it prepared the ground. The First World War then destroyed a monarchy that the first war had already shown to be hollow [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the role of Rasputin at the Russian court.
parts.solutionMd:
Rasputin's importance to the Romanovs began with the health of the heir to the throne. Nicholas II and Alexandra had five children but only one son, Alexei, who suffered from haemophilia. The condition was kept secret from the Russian people, because Nicholas did not want the heir to appear weak, and this secrecy meant the family could not seek help openly [R].

Rasputin was born in Tyumen in Siberia in 1869. He married and had four children, and from 1898 he lived as a wandering holy man, preaching the unusual doctrine that the more a person sinned, the holier they became. He arrived in St Petersburg in 1903, where a reputation for mystic powers made him popular among the aristocracy, and in 1905 he was introduced to the Romanov family [R].

His position was secured in 1908, when he was summoned to treat one of Alexei's bleeding episodes. It was reported that his hypnotic influence eased the boy's pain, and from that point Alexandra regarded him as indispensable. By 1911 his behaviour had turned the aristocracy against him, and Nicholas dismissed him, but Alexandra continued to call on him to treat Alexei [R].

Rasputin's role changed decisively in 1915. When Nicholas took personal command of the Russian Army, he left Alexandra in charge of the government at home, and she used Rasputin as her adviser. Ministers were dismissed in large numbers and the government made poor decisions at exactly the moment when the war demanded competence [R].

The damage to the monarchy's reputation was severe. It was widely believed that Rasputin was Alexandra's lover, a rumour historians consider untrue but which opponents such as the Bolsheviks used in propaganda against Tsarism. The Tsarina was herself German, which already made her suspect in wartime, so much so that Nicholas had renamed St Petersburg as Petrograd in 1914 to remove its Germanic sound. The Orthodox Church also gave the Tsar less support, because Rasputin's religious practices conflicted with Orthodox teaching [R].

In December 1916 a group of Russian aristocrats murdered Rasputin, hoping to save the monarchy from further disgrace. It came too late: within three months the Tsar had abdicated. Rasputin's role at court had begun as a private matter of a sick child and ended as a public scandal that helped strip the Romanovs of the respect of the Church, the nobility and the ordinary people alike [R].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of the Duma to Tsarist rule, 1906-1914.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is that the promise of a Duma saved the regime in 1905.** Witte persuaded Nicholas to issue the October Manifesto, which promised an elected duma with the power to pass laws, looser censorship, freedom of speech and assembly, and the vote for all men. Its importance was immediate and political: it split the opposition. Liberals declared themselves satisfied, the Kadets under Milyukov held out for a written constitution, and the socialist parties continued to demand the overthrow of the Tsar altogether. A united opposition became a divided one, and Nicholas was able to use the army to suppress the strikes while the moderates stood aside [E].

**The second facet is that the Fundamental Laws of 1906 removed most of what had been promised.** They confirmed the reforms of the Manifesto but simultaneously asserted the Tsar's rights: to direct foreign relations and declare war, to veto legislation, to dissolve the Duma, to command the army and navy, to rule by decree whenever the Duma was not sitting, to control the Orthodox Church and to overturn verdicts given in court. A parliament that can be dissolved at will, whose laws can be vetoed, and which can be bypassed by decree, is not a limitation on autocracy. The Duma's importance here is as evidence of how little Nicholas intended to concede [E].

**The third facet is what happened to the four Dumas in practice.** The first two, in 1906 and 1907, were genuinely radical and pressed for further reform, and Nicholas closed them down quickly. The government then changed the voting laws to limit the influence of peasant voters and increase right-wing representation, and the effect is visible in the results: the Kadets fell from 182 seats in the first Duma to 91, then 54, then 53, while right-wing parties rose from 8 seats to 10, then 147, then 154. The third and fourth Dumas ran their full terms because they had been engineered into compliance [E].

**The fourth facet is the opportunity that was refused.** The Duma system gave Nicholas a route towards constitutional monarchy of the kind that had allowed other European dynasties to survive. Many historians argue that had he worked with it, Tsarist Russia would have developed a system comparable to Britain's and might have endured. Instead he made the Duma powerless, and in doing so angered a great many people who had been prepared to work within the system [E].

**The fifth facet argues that the Duma was not the regime's central problem.** Alongside it ran Stolypin's combination of reform and repression: land reform and loans through the Peasant Land Bank on one side, and on the other more than a thousand executions and 20,000 exiles, so many that the hangman's noose became known as Stolypin's necktie. Both approaches failed in the long term, since few peasants became kulaks and poorer peasants grew poorer, while workers' pay after 1905 was lower than it had been in 1903. The strikes at the Lena Goldfields in 1912 were brutally repressed. These social and economic failures would have threatened the regime whatever the Duma did [E].

**Judgement.** The Duma mattered less for the power it exercised, which was very little, than for what its treatment revealed [A]. Its most important consequence was the destruction of the credibility of reform itself. By granting a parliament under pressure in 1905 and then stripping it of meaning within a year, Nicholas taught the moderate opposition that concessions extracted from him would be withdrawn as soon as he felt safe.

That is why the fourth facet outweighs the others [A]. The Duma's real significance is as a missed opportunity rather than as an institution. Its existence proved that constitutional government was possible in Russia, and its emptiness proved that the Tsar would not permit it, which left those who wanted change with no argument against the revolutionaries who had said all along that the regime could not be reformed. Judged by influence over policy the Duma was unimportant; judged by its effect on what Russians believed possible, it was central to the collapse that followed [A].

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating the 1905 Revolution. Bloody Sunday and the Potemkin mutiny are the background; the question begins with the Duma that resulted.
> - Describing what the Duma was. Explaining its structure is recall, and the marks here are for assessing how much it mattered.
> - Treating it as a real parliament. Any answer that does not deal with the Fundamental Laws has missed the central point.
> - Running forward to 1917. The question closes in 1914, and the war belongs elsewhere.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The State Council sat above the Duma and was chosen partly by the Tsar, giving the crown a further check on anything the Duma passed.
> - The Bolsheviks did not contest the first two Duma elections at all, which shows that some of the opposition never regarded it as worth engaging with.
> - The Duma did achieve real work in areas such as education and military reform, which is a fair argument that it was not entirely powerless.
> - Nicholas's willingness to reverse the reforms of 1905 fits a wider pattern of behaviour that also explains his conduct during the war.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Distinguish the promise from the reality. Setting the October Manifesto against the Fundamental Laws is the sharpest structure available for this question.
> - The election figures are the strongest evidence you have. The collapse of the Kadets from 182 seats to 53, alongside the rise of the right from 8 to 154, shows manipulation far better than any assertion could.
> - Argue about significance, not power. The Duma was weak, and saying so is the beginning of the argument rather than the end of it.
> - Bring in Stolypin as the counter-facet. It stops the answer becoming a single-issue essay and gives you something genuine to weigh the Duma against.
> - Consider the counterfactual. Asking what might have happened if Nicholas had worked with the Duma is exactly the kind of analysis the top band rewards.

parts.problemMd:
**Local government in Tsarist Russia took several forms.**

What were the zemstva?
parts.solutionMd:
The zemstva were rural councils elected by the people to manage local affairs such as education, medical services, public welfare, food supplies and the maintenance of roads [1]. They were not truly democratic, because a landowner's vote counted for more than a peasant's [1]. Government officials initially welcomed the zemstva because they helped control the rural population in the mirs and helped collect taxes [1]. By 1905 the zemstva, whose members were mostly middle and upper class, had begun to demand constitutional reform and the right to vote, a shift the government had not expected when it created them [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Peter Stolypin became Prime Minister of Russia in 1906.**

Describe Stolypin's 'carrot and stick' approach to ruling Russia.
parts.solutionMd:
Tsar Nicholas chose Peter Stolypin as Prime Minister in 1906, and his policies followed a 'carrot and stick' approach [1]. As a 'carrot', Stolypin introduced land reforms and gave loans through the Peasant Land Bank so that more peasants could become kulaks, and reduced the power of the mirs [1]. As a 'stick', he harshly punished opponents of the tsar, using the noose so often that people called it 'Stolypin's Necktie', with over 1,000 people hanged and 20,000 exiled [1]. Historians argue both methods failed in the long term, since there were very few kulaks and poorer peasants only became poorer [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Tsar Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917.**

Describe the events of the March 1917 Revolution.
parts.solutionMd:
Strikes spread across the Russian Empire in January and February 1917 because of unemployment and shortages [1]. From 7 to 10 March, 40,000 Putilov steel workers went on strike alongside women marking International Women's Day, and the number of strikers rose to 250,000 [1]. On 12 March the army was ordered to stop the protests but many soldiers joined the strikers instead, and the Petrograd Soviet took control of supplies in the city [1]. Tsar Nicholas II tried to return to Petrograd but was blocked by railway workers, and he abdicated, with his brother Michael refusing the throne [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Tsar Nicholas II remained in power despite the crisis of 1905.**

Why did Nicholas II survive the 1905 Revolution?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason Nicholas survived was that he offered reform. Advised by his prime minister Witte, he issued the October Manifesto on 30 October 1905, promising an elected Duma, freedom of speech and assembly, and looser censorship [R]. This won back the support of much of the middle class, since moderate liberals such as the Octobrists were satisfied by the promise of an elected Duma and greater civil liberties, whereas the more radical Kadets, led by Milyukov, wanted a full written constitution, which the Manifesto did not give them [E].

A second reason was that he combined this with repression. Nicholas used the army, which had returned from the war with Japan by December 1905, to suppress the general strikes and put down disorder in the countryside [R]. This was possible because working-class opposition was not united behind a single organisation: the St Petersburg Soviet and the general strike of 800,000 workers in September had no equivalent nationwide leadership, so the government could crush protests piecemeal rather than facing one coordinated uprising [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Russia experienced widespread unrest in 1905.**

Why did the 1905 Revolution break out?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was Russia's economic and social backwardness. From 1902 there were widespread disturbances over poor wages and famine, and 1903 and 1904 were known as the Years of the Red Cockerel because peasants set fire to landowners' properties [R]. Non-Russian nationalities were treated unfairly under Russification and wanted independence, while illegal strikes became more frequent in the towns and cities [R]. This mattered because it meant opposition to the tsar came from several directions at once: peasants, workers and national minorities all had separate grievances that came together in 1905 [E].

A second reason was the shock of military defeat and Bloody Sunday. Russia's poorly organised and under-equipped army lost the key base of Port Arthur to Japan in January 1905, humiliating a country that regarded Japan as an inferior power [R]. On 22 January 1905 Father Gapon led 200,000 protesters to the Winter Palace to petition the tsar for reform, and the army opened fire on them, killing and wounding many [R]. This was decisive because Bloody Sunday destroyed the image of the tsar as a father figure who protected his people, turning peaceful petitioners into a nationwide revolutionary movement [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Nicholas II allowed four Dumas to sit between 1906 and 1917.**

How far did the Duma give Russia genuine democratic reform? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Duma could have turned Russia into a constitutional monarchy. Instead it became proof that Nicholas had never intended to share power [R].

The October Manifesto promised something real. Issued on 30 October 1905 on the advice of Witte, it offered an elected Duma to pass laws, freedom of speech and assembly, and looser censorship, and all men were allowed to vote for their representatives [R]. This mattered because it went further than any previous concession: for the first time ordinary Russians had a formal, legal route to influence government [E].

Nicholas reversed the promise almost immediately. The Fundamental Laws of 1906 confirmed the reforms on paper but also asserted the tsar's own powers to veto legislation, dissolve the Duma, rule by decree, and command the army and the Orthodox Church [R]. A parliament that could be dissolved by the man it was meant to check could never actually check him [A].

The first two Dumas of 1906 and 1907 tested this immediately. Both were radical, demanded further reform, and Nicholas closed them down quickly rather than negotiate [R]. The Kadets alone held 182 seats in the first Duma, showing how much appetite there was for change, and Nicholas simply refused to work with it [E].

The third and fourth Dumas of 1907 to 1917 were made harmless instead. The government changed the voting laws to limit the power of peasant voters and increase the representation of right-wing parties, so that right-wing seats rose from 8 in 1906 to 154 by the Fourth Duma of 1912-17 [R]. This converted the Duma from an opponent into an ornament [A].

The Duma therefore gave Russia genuine democratic reform to only a very limited extent, and its failure mattered enormously. Nicholas could have used it to build a genuine constitutional monarchy and share the blame for difficult decisions, but instead he treated every version of it as a threat to be either dissolved or rigged [A]. This meant that when the crisis of 1917 arrived, there was no functioning institution through which discontent could be channelled peacefully, so opposition had nowhere to go but the streets. The Duma's failure did not cause the collapse of tsarism directly, but it removed the one mechanism that might have prevented it [A].

parts.problemMd:
**The tsar faced very similar unrest in 1905 and in 1917.**

Which was more important in explaining why the tsar survived in 1905 but not in 1917: the loyalty of the army or the unity of the opposition? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
In 1905 the tsar survived a revolution. In 1917 an almost identical situation destroyed him. What changed was what was left to meet it with [R].

Both crises began the same way. In 1905 economic hardship and military humiliation in the war with Japan combined with Bloody Sunday to trigger mass strikes and a general strike of 800,000 workers by September [R]. In 1917 fuel and food shortages caused by the war, alongside enormous casualties, produced strikes by 250,000 workers by March [R]. Both times the trigger was a mixture of economic collapse and a discredited government [E].

In 1905 Nicholas still had the tools to respond. He offered the October Manifesto as genuine reform, since no comparable concession had been tried before, and used the army, freshly returned from Japan, to suppress the strikes; opposition was also not united, letting the government crush protests piecemeal [E].

By 1917 both tools had gone. Nicholas had discredited reform himself: the Fundamental Laws of 1906 reasserted his powers, and the third and fourth Dumas were rigged, so nobody believed a fresh promise in 1917 [R]. He had lost the army too, since he personally commanded it from 1915; in March 1917 soldiers ordered to suppress the protests joined them instead [A].

The Petrograd Soviet gave 1917 an organised alternative that 1905 never had. Soviets had existed in 1905 but were suppressed; in 1917 the Petrograd Soviet took control of supplies on 12 March with the loyalty of workers and soldiers together [R]. Opposition in 1917 was therefore both wider and organised, exactly where it had been narrow and scattered twelve years before [A].

The army mattered more. In 1905 it was the single tool that let Nicholas crush the general strike regardless of how united his opponents were; in 1917 its defection on 12 March was the moment the revolution actually succeeded, since the government could no longer be protected by force once soldiers were on the crowd's side [A]. The unity of the opposition explains why 1917 was harder to suppress, but the loyalty of the army explains why suppression stopped being possible at all. His own decisions had already spent both: rigging the Duma spent his credibility, and commanding the army from 1915 spent its loyalty [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia, 1905–41**

Write an account of the social structure of Tsarist Russia before 1905.
parts.solutionMd:
Russian society under the tsar was rigidly hierarchical. Power ran from the tsar, through the Orthodox Church and army officers, down to the bourgeoisie and finally the proletariat, who had the least power of all [R].

Peasants made up around 80% of the population and were poorly educated [R]. The Emancipation Edict of 1861 had freed them from serfdom and allowed some to buy land through the Peasant Land Bank, but only a small number, known as kulaks, could afford to do so, and many poorer peasants resented them [R]. Land passed down through generations by inheritance, so by 1905 family plots were often too small or scattered around the mir, and peasants lacked the equipment or techniques to farm efficiently [D]. More than 60% of Russians were illiterate, compared with only 3% in Britain, and the empire relied on peasants as soldiers for the army [R].

Industrial workers were far fewer, at less than 5% of the population, but lived in some of the worst conditions in the empire [R]. Russian cities offered substandard housing and poor sanitation, so diseases such as cholera spread rapidly [D]. There were no laws governing working hours, pay or conditions, and trade unions were illegal, so workers had almost no way to improve their situation through legal means [R].

Russia's industry itself was underdeveloped: unlike Britain and Germany, which had industrialised in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and by 1905 produced railways, motorised tractors and alloy steel, Russia mostly produced pig iron and its workers lacked the skills to match Western production [R]. The bourgeoisie, industrialists and business owners, made up less than 2% of the population but were a growing class [R]. They had a great deal of money but very little political power, since the tsar's government gave no formal role to businessmen [D]. This mismatch between their economic importance and political powerlessness pushed many towards liberal ideas and, eventually, towards demanding constitutional reform through the zemstva [R].

The empire's geography deepened these divisions further. It stretched nearly 5,000 kilometres and only 40% of the population was ethnic Russian, with large Ukrainian, Polish, Jewish and other minority populations, many of whom wanted independence or resented policies such as Russification [R]. The Ural Mountains divided the industrialised west, where Nicholas lived in St Petersburg, from Siberia in the east, which had limited transport links to the rest of the empire [R]. Communication and legal enforcement were difficult across such distances, so the Orthodox Church, which taught that the tsar was God's representative on Earth, became essential for enforcing the tsar's laws among a largely illiterate population, with priests reading new laws aloud to their congregations [R]. In theory a government of an Imperial Council, a Cabinet of Ministers and a Senate sat beneath the tsar, but none of these bodies held real power: their members were appointed by the tsar himself and existed only to advise or administer, since there was no elected parliament until 1906 [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia, 1905–41**

Write an account of the impact of the First World War on Russia between 1914 and 1916.
parts.solutionMd:
Russia entered the First World War in a position that looked secure. In 1913 Nicholas had celebrated the tercentenary of the Romanov dynasty, the economy had improved, and he believed his people loved him [R]. Russia mobilised an army of 5.3 million people within ten days, and patriotism was initially high [R].

The war exposed how backward Russia's economy remained. It is estimated that 800,000 men in the Russian Army lacked rifles, and factories could only produce 13,000 rounds of bullets a day [R]. Early battles were disastrous: at Tannenberg in August 1914 over 30,000 Russian soldiers were killed or injured, and at Masurian Lakes that September Russia lost 125,000 men and 150 artillery guns, forcing a withdrawal from East Prussia [R]. By 1915 the German army held territory in Poland, Lithuania and Latvia, all parts of the Russian Empire, and the Russian army was forced into a general retreat [D]. The Brusilov Offensive of June to September 1916 destroyed 1.5 million Austro-Hungarian soldiers and gained 25,000 square kilometres, but cost Russia 500,000 of its own men, and its human cost turned many Russians against the war [R]. By 1916 over 1.7 million Russians had died, and over one million soldiers had deserted by 1917 [R].

Nicholas made his own position worse by taking personal command of the army in 1915. He had no military experience, which meant every subsequent defeat could be blamed on him directly, and it created a power vacuum in the capital that allowed unrest to grow unchecked [R].

The economy collapsed under the strain of war. Russia had entered the war with the largest gold reserve in Europe and the fourth-largest economy, but industry was diverted to the war effort while imports were disrupted, so the army still faced shortages of ammunition and raw materials [R]. Millions of peasants were conscripted, cutting farming production, and inflation rose to 200%, so real wages fell and workers could not afford food [R]. Russia's railway system could not cope, so food supplies rotted at stations while towns and cities went hungry, and by 1917 there had been over 1,300 strikes [R].

The government in Petrograd meanwhile lost control of decision-making. With Nicholas commanding the army, Tsarina Alexandra took charge in the capital and relied on the advice of Rasputin, whose reputation and religious practices scandalised the aristocracy and the Orthodox Church [R]. Ministers were dismissed and replaced erratically, and Russian aristocrats eventually murdered Rasputin in December 1916 in an attempt to save the monarchy, but by then the damage to its reputation was done [R]. Rumours, which historians now believe were false, that Rasputin and Alexandra were lovers were used as propaganda by opponents such as the Bolsheviks to turn ordinary Russians against the tsar [D]. Nicholas had also renamed St Petersburg to Petrograd in 1914 to remove its Germanic associations, a sign of how sensitive the Romanovs' German connections had become [R].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia, 1905–41**

Discuss the success of Stolypin's 'carrot and stick' approach to ruling Russia.
parts.solutionMd:
Peter Stolypin governed Russia from 1906 to 1911 using what historians call a 'carrot and stick' approach: reward loyalty, punish resistance. Whether that combination actually secured the tsarist regime is a genuine historical debate [R].

The first facet is the 'carrot': land reform aimed at the peasantry. Stolypin introduced reforms intended to increase peasant support, offering loans through the Peasant Land Bank so more peasants could buy land and become kulaks, wealthier independent farmers [R]. He reduced the power of the mirs over individual peasants and required them to reallocate vacant land within the commune [R]. This mattered because peasants made up 80% of the population, so winning their loyalty, or at least their acquiescence, was essential to any government hoping to survive [E]. Stolypin's reforms followed directly from the unrest of 1905, when peasants had set fire to landowners' properties in what became known as the Years of the Red Cockerel, so the 'carrot' was designed specifically to answer that grievance [R].

The second facet is the 'stick': repression of opponents. Stolypin harshly punished those who resisted the tsar, executing so many through military field courts that people called the noose 'Stolypin's Necktie', with over 1,000 people hanged and 20,000 exiled [R]. He also used the Okhrana, the secret police, to stop riots and investigate revolutionary movements [R]. This was significant because it demonstrated that reform under Stolypin was never intended to be a genuine transfer of power: consent was to be bought where possible and forced where it could not [E]. Stolypin's repression fell within a wider pattern set by the tsar himself, since the Fundamental Laws of 1906 had already reasserted Nicholas's right to rule by decree, so Stolypin was applying a philosophy of control that the monarchy had already committed itself to [R].

However, the land reforms achieved very little. Historians note that only a small number of peasants ever became kulaks, and poorer peasants, who could not afford the Peasant Land Bank's loans, only became poorer relative to them, deepening resentment within peasant communities rather than easing it [R]. A policy meant to create a loyal class of prosperous farmers instead created a new grievance among those left behind [A].

The repression also failed to produce lasting stability. Workers' conditions did not improve: their pay after the 1905 Revolution was lower in real terms than it had been in 1903, and strikes continued regardless of the risk of execution or exile [R]. In 1912, a year after Stolypin's own assassination, the government brutally repressed strikes at the Lena Goldfields, showing that force alone had not ended labour unrest [R]. If repression worked, such a strike, and such a violent response to it, would not have been necessary years later [A]. Trade unions remained illegal throughout the period, and the government still had no laws governing working hours, pay or conditions, so the underlying causes of labour unrest were never addressed at all, only their outward expression [R].

Stolypin's approach also could not survive contact with the tsar's own instincts. Stolypin himself recognised that Russia needed twenty years of peace to complete his reforms, yet Nicholas's government pursued an assertive foreign policy that contributed to the crisis of 1914, cutting off the time Stolypin's programme needed [R]. A long-term social policy was undermined by decisions taken entirely outside its control [A]. Stolypin was himself assassinated in 1911, three years before the war began, which meant the reforms lost their principal architect even before external events overtook them [R].

Stolypin's methods therefore secured the regime only in the short term and failed in the long term, as historians generally agree. The 'carrot' created a small class of kulaks while leaving the majority of peasants no better off, and in some cases worse, and the 'stick' suppressed individual acts of resistance without addressing why they kept recurring [A]. Neither method resolved the underlying problem that Russia's peasants and workers had genuine, unaddressed grievances, so unrest persisted after Stolypin's assassination in 1911 and resumed on a larger scale once the pressures of the First World War were added. Stolypin bought the tsarist regime time rather than security, and when that time ran out in 1914, nothing durable had been built to replace it [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study C: Russia, 1905–41**

Discuss the importance of the First World War to the downfall of Tsar Nicholas II.
parts.solutionMd:
In 1913 the Romanov dynasty appeared secure, celebrating three hundred years of rule. By March 1917 it had collapsed entirely. The First World War sits at the centre of every explanation of that collapse, and the question is how much weight it should carry alongside Russia's older problems [R].

The first facet is military failure, and its scale was extraordinary. Russia mobilised 5.3 million men within ten days, yet 800,000 lacked rifles and factories could produce only 13,000 rounds of ammunition a day [R]. Defeats at Tannenberg and Masurian Lakes in 1914 cost over 150,000 casualties between them, and by 1916 over 1.7 million Russians had died with more than a million deserting [R]. This mattered because Nicholas took personal command of the army in 1915 despite having no military experience, so every subsequent defeat attached directly to him rather than to a general who could be dismissed [E]. Even the one clear success, the Brusilov Offensive of 1916, destroyed 1.5 million Austro-Hungarian troops but cost Russia 500,000 of its own men, so it turned opinion against the war rather than reviving support for it [R].

The second facet is the economic collapse the war produced. Russia had entered the war with the largest gold reserve in Europe, but inflation reached 200%, real wages fell, and millions of conscripted peasants left farming production to collapse [R]. The railway system could not distribute what food there was, so it rotted at stations while cities starved, producing over 1,300 strikes by 1917 [R]. A population that could not eat had little reason left to remain loyal [E]. Even government support for widows and orphans of soldiers largely failed to materialise, adding a further sense of betrayal among families who had already lost the most [R].

The third facet is the vacuum in government that Nicholas created himself. By commanding the army in person he left Tsarina Alexandra in charge of Petrograd, and she relied on Rasputin's advice, dismissing ministers erratically and scandalising the Orthodox Church, one of the tsar's own 'pillars' of support [R]. Aristocrats murdered Rasputin in December 1916 to save the monarchy, but the damage to its reputation could not be undone by then [A].

However, some historians argue the war only dictated timing rather than cause. On this view Tsarist Russia had unresolvable problems regardless of the war: an economy that relied on backward peasant agriculture, a geography spanning 5,000 kilometres with only 40% of the population ethnically Russian, and a political system with no elected parliament worth the name after the Dumas were rigged [R]. These structural weaknesses would have produced a revolution eventually, and the war simply accelerated it [A].

The events of 1905 support this reading. Russia had already experienced a near-revolution over economic hardship, military humiliation and a discredited government, and Nicholas survived only through the October Manifesto and repression, both of which he later undermined by rigging the Duma [R]. A regime that had already needed rescuing once, and had wasted the rescue, was fragile before a single shot was fired in 1914 [A].

Against this, the war's specific damage is hard to explain away. The tsar's personal command of the army was his own decision, not a structural inevitability, and it directly transferred the blame for military failure onto the monarchy in a way 1905 never had [R]. Rasputin's influence, Alexandra's German background and the murder of Rasputin by the tsar's own supporters were all products of the war years specifically, and none of them existed as active grievances before 1914 [E]. Nicholas's decision to rename St Petersburg to Petrograd in 1914, distancing the dynasty from its own capital's Germanic name, shows how directly the war reshaped what Russians associated with their rulers [R].

The war was decisive, but decisive in combination with what came before it. Russia's structural weaknesses, its backward economy, its rigid social hierarchy and its rigged Duma, meant the regime had no reserves of trust or competence left to draw on once war exposed its failures [A]. The First World War did not create the fault lines in Tsarist Russia; it applied a pressure the regime's own history had already made unbearable. The war was the immediate and necessary cause of the collapse in 1917, but it succeeded only because thirty years of political failure had left nothing else standing [A].

> - The Fundamental Laws of 1906 and the rigged third and fourth Dumas are strong evidence that the regime's credibility was already damaged before 1914.

parts.problemMd:
**Radical political movements grew in Russia in the decades before 1905.**

Why did extremist political movements grow in Tsarist Russia?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that industrialisation created the conditions for radical ideas to spread. Plekhanov translated Marx's works into Russian in 1883, and by the 1890s industrialisation had produced workers' organisations, illegal trade unions and Marxist discussion circles [R]. In 1903 the Social Democrats split into the Mensheviks, led by Martov, who wanted a bourgeois revolution first, and the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, who wanted both stages together [R]. This mattered because it gave the small but growing industrial working class an organised political voice for the first time, rather than leaving discontent as scattered unrest [E].

A second reason was that the tsar's own methods of control pushed opposition towards extremism rather than defusing it. The government censored all forms of the arts, including Marx's writings, and used the Okhrana, the secret police, to investigate, arrest, torture and exile suspected revolutionaries to Siberia [R]. Earlier peaceful movements such as the Narodniks had little success, while the terrorist group 'The People's Will' had already assassinated Tsar Alexander II in 1881 [R]. This explains the rise in extremism because moderate opposition, such as through the zemstva, achieved little against an autocracy unwilling to compromise, so those who wanted change concluded that only revolutionary methods could ever succeed [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The March 1917 Revolution ended over 300 years of Romanov rule.**

Which was more important in the success of the March 1917 Revolution: popular support or military support? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The March 1917 Revolution succeeded because popular anger, an army that defected, and an organised alternative to the tsar all arrived together [R].

Popular support was genuine and widespread. The war had caused severe fuel and food shortages, and huge casualties made people less patriotic and less willing to support the tsar as head of the army [R]. Industrial workers were less religious, so belief in the tsar's divine right weakened, and more turned to Marxist parties, while Tsarina Alexandra was mockingly called the 'German Princess' [R]. This mattered because the tsar had lost legitimacy before a single soldier disobeyed an order [E].

However, popular anger alone had failed before. The 1905 Revolution also began with mass strikes and popular fury, yet Nicholas survived by using the army to suppress the general strike [A]. Popular support alone could not remove an autocrat who still controlled the means of force [A].

Military support proved decisive in 1917. Nicholas had over-relied on the army as in 1905, but the war had turned it against him, since soldiers no longer respected his leadership after the defeats he had personally commanded [R]. On 12 March soldiers ordered to stop the protests joined the strikers instead, and many joined the Soviets [R]. Without the army, the tsar lost the one tool that had saved him twelve years earlier [E].

The Petrograd Soviet then gave the revolution somewhere for power to go. It took control of supplies on 12 March, and after the abdication a system of Dual Power emerged, in which the Provisional Government needed the Soviet's influence over the army, while the Soviet needed the Government's influence over the middle classes [R]. The revolution did not simply remove the tsar; it had an organisation ready to replace him [A].

Military support was the most important factor, because it was the missing piece that had let the tsar survive an identical crisis in 1905. Popular anger created the pressure and the Soviet gave it an organised outlet, but it was the army joining the crowds on 12 March that made the tsar's position impossible [A]. Every other factor had been present in some form in 1905 and had not been enough alone.

name: Did the United States Contain the Spread of Communism?

parts.problemMd:
The United States feared that communism would keep spreading.

What was the 'domino theory'?
parts.solutionMd:
The domino theory was the American belief that if one country in a region fell to communism, the countries around it would fall one after another, like a row of dominoes toppling [1]. It was used to argue that communism had to be stopped early, even in small or distant countries that were not important to the United States in themselves [1]. President Eisenhower set the idea out publicly in 1954, when the French were losing control of Indochina [1]. It went on to become one of the main justifications for American military involvement in Vietnam [1].

parts.problemMd:
**Korea was divided at the end of the Second World War.**

Describe how Korea was divided in 1945.
parts.solutionMd:
In 1905 Japan had owned Korea, and when Japan surrendered to the Allies in 1945 the terms of that surrender included the division of Korea [1]. Soviet troops were already in the north and US troops in the south, so the Allies split the country into two equal zones along the 38th Parallel [1]. Historians believe Korea was divided in this way to prevent the USSR from taking the whole country [1]. The USSR then monitored North Korea and the USA oversaw South Korea, and each chose an unelected leader: Kim Il Sung in the north and Syngman Rhee in the south [1].

parts.problemMd:
**In October 1962 the world came close to nuclear war.**

What happened during the 'Thirteen Days' of October 1962?
parts.solutionMd:
The Thirteen Days ran from 16 to 28 October 1962, and were the closest the world had come to nuclear war [1]. On 16 October Kennedy assembled his advisory group ExComm, and on 22 October he told the American public he was imposing a blockade of Cuba [1]. Khrushchev announced on 23 October that Soviet ships would not stop at the blockade, but on 24 October twenty of them turned around [1]. Khrushchev then sent two letters, the second demanding the removal of US missiles in Turkey, and on 28 October Bobby Kennedy and the Soviet ambassador agreed a deal [1].

parts.problemMd:
**The last US troops left Vietnam in the 1970s.**

Describe the consequences of the Vietnam War for the USA.
parts.solutionMd:
Containment had failed militarily, because although the USA had stronger weapons the Viet Cong had better tactics [1]. It had failed politically, because by 1975 Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia had all become communist, giving the USSR and China new allies [1]. It had failed economically, since the war cost the USA around \$168 billion, and over 58,000 US soldiers died [1]. The use of chemical warfare and the disregard for Vietnamese civilians ruined the USA's international reputation, and the US government abandoned containment, with Nixon pursuing detente instead [1].

parts.solutionMd:
Source E, written by a CIA official historian, challenges the conclusions of the Taylor Committee's official findings in Source D. However, it does not prove them wrong entirely. Source E focuses on the circumstances in which the report was written and argues that the CIA was blamed unfairly while President Kennedy was protected [S].

Both sources acknowledge that the CIA failed at the Bay of Pigs. According to Source D, the CIA failed to 'give the project appropriate organisation, staffing and full-time direction', which resulted in disaster [S]. Source D also downplays the President's role in cancelling the second air strike, arguing that better planning and timely action by the CIA could have prevented the crisis. Source E admits that 'the CIA will continue to be blamed for the failure' [S].

Source E contradicts Source D by showing that the Taylor Committee report was prepared in haste and that several important witnesses were never interviewed. The inclusion of Robert Kennedy, the President's brother, on the Committee also raises a question about its fairness [R]. Source E therefore questions how thorough the investigation was and presents it as a politically motivated exercise to protect the President's reputation. It reverses the blame, arguing that the 'actions, or inactions, of the Kennedy Administration' were responsible for the disaster [S].

To conclude, Source E does not prove that Taylor's findings were completely wrong, but it does show that they were incomplete and shaped by political interests. It undermines the reliability of Source D not by denying the CIA's failings but by exposing the bias that stopped the Committee presenting a full account. At the same time it does not overturn Source D entirely, since it agrees that the CIA will always be blamed [R].

parts.problemMd:
The United States supported the government of South Vietnam.

Why was Diem's government unpopular in South Vietnam?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that Diem governed against the religion of most of his people [R]. He was a Catholic in a country where Buddhists were the largest faith group, and his government discriminated against them. A ruler who treats the majority of the population as outsiders cannot expect their loyalty, and the persecution gave ordinary South Vietnamese a reason to look for an alternative to Diem rather than to defend him [E].

A second reason is that his government served itself rather than the country [R]. Diem ran a corrupt administration and handed key positions to members of his own family, so posts went to relatives rather than to able people. At the same time he took land away from peasants and gave it to rich landlords. In a country where most people farmed, reversing land reform hit the majority of the population directly in their livelihoods while a small circle around the president grew wealthier. That combination of corruption at the top and hardship at the bottom pushed many South Vietnamese towards supporting the North [E].

The result was that the National Liberation Front, formed in 1960, drew in peasants from the South as well as communists from the North, and by November 1963 the United States had withdrawn its support and Diem was overthrown and assassinated in a coup.

parts.problemMd:
In October 1962 the world came close to nuclear war.

How far was Castro responsible for the Cuban Missile Crisis? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Castro carries real responsibility [R]. He overthrew Batista in January 1959 and then took the decisions that brought Soviet weapons to an island ninety miles from the American coast. In February 1960 his government signed an agreement with the Soviet Union under which Khrushchev would buy Cuban sugar and, secretly, Cuba would receive Soviet arms. He appointed communists to his government and nationalised land owned by foreign nationals despite American objections. After the Bay of Pigs he publicly announced that he was a communist and asked the USSR to help defend Cuba, and in September 1961 Khrushchev declared that the Soviet Union would supply weapons. Without those invitations there would have been no Soviet missiles on Cuba to discover [E].

Against that, American policy drove him towards Moscow [R]. The United States had propped up Batista for years because US businesses profited from his corrupt rule, and it owned Cuba's oil refineries, railways and electricity alongside its sugar trade. When Castro tried to end that control, Eisenhower cut sugar purchases in July 1960, imposed a trade embargo by October and broke off diplomatic relations by 1961. A country whose main export market has been closed has to find another buyer, and the USSR was the obvious one. The Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 then turned a trade relationship into a military one, because a leader who has just survived an American-backed invasion has every reason to want protection [E].

The superpowers also had motives of their own [R]. Khrushchev concluded from the failure at the Bay of Pigs that Kennedy was inexperienced and weak, and the crisis was ultimately settled by a superpower bargain in which the USA quietly removed its missiles from Turkey. Cuba was the location of the crisis, but the terms were negotiated over Castro's head between Washington and Moscow [E].

On balance Castro was a necessary but not a sufficient cause [A]. His revolution and his appeal for Soviet protection are what made Cuba available as a missile site, so the crisis could not have happened where it did without him. But he did not build the missiles, choose to send them, or decide how the confrontation ended.

The deeper point is that responsibility depends on the question being asked [A]. If we ask why the crisis happened in Cuba, Castro matters most. If we ask why it became a threat to world peace, the answer lies in a rivalry that had been building since 1945 between two powers with weapons capable of destroying the world, into which Cuba was drawn rather than which Cuba created [A].

> - Narrating the Thirteen Days. The events of October 1962 are the crisis itself, not its causes, and a day-by-day account will not be credited here.
> - Writing only about the Cuban Revolution. Castro coming to power is the starting point; the question is how far he caused what followed three years later.
> - Assessing who won. That is a different question, and answering it will earn nothing here.
> - Leaving Khrushchev out entirely. The missiles were Soviet, and any judgement that ignores Soviet motives is one-sided.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Castro knew about the Bay of Pigs invasion in advance and had 20,000 soldiers ready, so his own strength contributed to the humiliation that shaped what followed.
> - Kennedy had explicitly warned Khrushchev not to place nuclear weapons on Cuba, so the decision to proceed was taken in Moscow in full knowledge of the risk.
> - The immediate trigger was American, since it was a U-2 spy plane photographing the launch pads on 14 October 1962 that turned a build-up into a crisis.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Separate the two questions hidden inside this one: why the crisis happened in Cuba, and why it became so dangerous. Castro scores heavily on the first and much less on the second, and saying so is a Level 5 judgement.
> - Use the causes framework. Long-term superpower rivalry, the medium-term effect of the Bay of Pigs and the short-term discovery of the launch pads give you a ready-made structure.
> - Dates carry the argument. February 1960 for the Soviet agreement, April 1961 for the Bay of Pigs and September 1961 for the arms pledge show the sequence by which Cuba became a Soviet base.
> - Do not treat Castro as simply a victim or simply a villain. He made real choices, but he made them in response to American pressure, and the best answers hold both together.

parts.problemMd:
A cartoon published in an American newspaper, 21 April 1961

![Source C](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-history-18/the-20th-century-international-relations-from-1919/did-the-united-states-contain-the-spread-of-communism/assets/003-source-c.png)

Study Source C. What is the message of this source? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
Source C is a political cartoon published in April 1961, after the failure at the Bay of Pigs [R]. Its message is that the invasion was a hopeless failure and that Kennedy's claim to free Cuba remained an unfulfilled promise. The cartoon brings out the weakness of the invasion and establishes Castro's strength [S].

It suggests the invasion was weak, shown by the zig-zag line across the sea, and that Castro defeated it easily. The invasion effort does not even reach the fort, which shows its inherent weakness and quick collapse. Castro is shown well prepared, guarding the fort [S]. He holds a gun, symbolising a well-armed Cuba, and he watches the invasion, which shows he knew it was coming and had taken up his position well in advance. The Cuban fortress is drawn as a strong structure, safe from any damage. The weak planning of the invasion failed, and the fort remained intact [S].

Communist support for Cuba is represented by the Soviet tanks carrying the hammer and sickle [R]. The protection the Soviet Union provided kept Cuba safe from invasion across the water, and this emphasises the alliance between Cuba and the USSR [S].

The central message is that Cuba's 'Liberty' remained trapped inside the fortress and that the American claim to free it went unfulfilled. The caption, 'The Cuban people have not yet spoken their final piece', a statement by President Kennedy, is used ironically: it proved far too optimistic [R].

parts.problemMd:

![Source B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-history-18/the-20th-century-international-relations-from-1919/did-the-united-states-contain-the-spread-of-communism/assets/002-source-b.png)

Study Sources D and E. How far does Source E prove that Taylor’s findings (Source D) were wrong? Explain your answer using details of the sources and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
Both sources agree that the Bay of Pigs was a disastrous episode. However, their big messages contradict each other. Source A holds the CIA responsible for the debacle because of its 'weaknesses' and flawed planning, which became more and more 'apparent' as the operation progressed. Source B, in contrast, says it was mainly Kennedy's fault, because he wanted to bring down Castro without spending too much on the mission or being 'visible', which left the attack too weak to achieve anything [S].

Both sources agree on the cancellation of the second air strike. Source A says the 'second air strike was cancelled' by Kennedy, so the invaders received no reinforcement and could do little damage, 'leaving most of Castro's air force intact' [S]. Source B also states that Kennedy 'refused to give air force support'. Secondly, both agree that the USA tried to hide its involvement. Source A notes that the US bombers were 'painted as such that they looked like Cuban air force planes', and that Kennedy cancelled the second strike to show the USA had nothing to do with it. Source B supports this, saying the USA wanted 'minimum visibility' [S].

The sources disagree on more than they agree. Firstly, Source A mainly blames the CIA, which failed to 'keep the secret secure', chose a 'poor site for invasion' and used 'obsolete bombers'. In that account Kennedy is only partly responsible, because he cancelled the second air strike [R]. Source B pins the main responsibility on Kennedy, citing his indecision, the 'cancellation of the second strike' and his 'refusal to give air support'. Secondly, Source A highlights the inefficiency of the bombers, which 'missed many targets', so most of Castro's air force survived. Source B, by contrast, records some success for the raid, after which 'Cuba was left with only eight planes and seven pilots' [S].

To conclude, the two sources partly agree that cancelling the second air strike contributed to the failure, and that the USA did not want to be seen playing any part in the invasion. But they disagree on far more, including the CIA's planning, the casualties and how far Kennedy was responsible for the choices that were made [R].

> - **5-6 marks:** compares agreement(s) AND disagreement(s).
> - **3-4 marks:** compares agreement(s) OR disagreement(s), but not both.
> - **2 marks:** answers based on information in one source that is not in the other, or comparing the provenance or topic of the sources.
> - **1 mark:** attempts to compare but makes no valid comparison.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 7 marks include:
> 
> - Focusing on either the agreements or the disagreements and not both.
> - Using your own knowledge, or information that is not in the sources, such as Kennedy's dealings with the CIA.
> - Not quoting the sources accurately, or forgetting to quote them at all.
> - Paraphrasing in a way that changes the meaning of the big messages.

> 
> - Both sources also agree that the invasion force was trapped, that two ships were sunk and that a large number of soldiers were imprisoned. They disagree on the numbers: Source A says 1,200 invaders were captured and more than 100 killed, while Source B gives 1,197 and 67.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Use both sources to show agreements and disagreements.
> - Keep quotations short and relevant. A few words in quotation marks is enough.
> - Use separate paragraphs for agreement and disagreement.

parts.problemMd:
![Source F](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-history-18/the-20th-century-international-relations-from-1919/did-the-united-states-contain-the-spread-of-communism/assets/004-source-f.png)

Study Source F. Why did Kennedy make this speech on 20 April 1961? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
Kennedy made this speech on 20 April 1961, after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion, to limit the political damage and to convince the American public that the situation was under control. He also wanted to defend the reputation of the United States at a moment when the Cold War was intensifying [R].

According to Kennedy, the invasion was 'a struggle of Cuban patriots against a Cuban dictator'. This supported the idea that the action was not unjustified but an attempt to restore order in Cuba, where Castro was consolidating his power [S].

He also insisted that 'the armed forces of this country would not intervene in any way', which was meant to show that the United States was not responsible for the disaster. In reality the CIA had organised and trained the invaders and supplied their equipment with the approval of the US government. Kennedy wanted to protect the image of the USA as a peaceful nation, so presenting the invasion as a fight led by Cubans themselves was the safer position [S].

Kennedy also did not want to admit that the USA had broken international law by trying to overthrow the government of another country. The speech was an opportunity to portray the conflict as part of a larger struggle of 'liberty against tyranny' [S]. By drawing attention to 'communist tanks' crushing 'freedom fighters', he wanted Americans to focus on the communist threat. This was a way of uniting them behind the idea of the USA as leader of the free world, and of drawing attention away from the American failure at the Bay of Pigs [R].

In conclusion, Kennedy made this speech to influence public opinion after the failure. He wanted to protect his political and personal reputation, conceal the American role in the attack, and present the invasion as part of a worldwide struggle against communism rather than an operation backed by the USA. In the wider Cold War context, with American prestige at stake, the speech was an exercise in damage control [R].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **8 marks:** explains the speaker's purpose in the correct specific context, namely the days immediately after the failed invasion of April 1961.
> - **6-7 marks:** explains the big message of the speaker, properly explained rather than copied from the source.
> - **5 marks:** gives the specific context only, without turning it into a purpose.
> - **2-4 marks:** explains valid sub-messages, or gives only generalised context, or states a purpose without the specific context.
> - **1 mark:** makes points from the levels above but does not use them as reasons for the speech, or gives invalid reasons.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Taking the speech at face value and ignoring its historical context. Keep asking why the speech was made on 20 April 1961 in particular, rather than before or after.
> - Summarising what Kennedy said. Summary is not the same as explaining why he said it.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Kennedy declared that as president of a democracy he owed the people the truth, yet he carefully avoided any detail of US involvement, which shows how much he needed to protect his reputation after a humiliating defeat.
> - He also wanted to reassure the press and the public that his government remained committed to defending democracy abroad.
> - The speech was made to a group of newspaper editors, which shows he was trying to influence the press and shape opinion in his favour.
> - The Bay of Pigs had made the USA look weak and incompetent, which is why Kennedy focused on Castro's 'communist tanks' crushing freedom fighters, shifting attention from the defeat to the global threat of communism.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep asking 'why now?' rather than 'what does it say?'. The date in the question is doing the work.
> - Quote from the source and explain what the wording reveals about Kennedy's motives.
> - Set the speech in the Cold War context: what was at stake for American prestige, and what was Kennedy leaving out?
> - Try to give more than one purpose, since an answer built on several reads far more securely than one built on a single idea.

parts.problemMd: Study all the [sources](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2025/09/55159_June%202024-Source%20File%20-%20converted.pdf). How far do these sources provide convincing evidence that President Kennedy was to blame for the failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion? Use the sources to explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The sources provide differing views on Kennedy's responsibility for the failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion. Sources B and E support the claim, while C, D and F point the other way. Source A provides both perspectives. Overall, Kennedy had a substantial but not a sole role in the failure: poor CIA planning and Castro's strength were equally responsible for the outcome [R].

Source A says Kennedy cancelled the second air strike to hide US involvement, so the Cuban air force 'remained intact' and 'Castro could control the skies' before attacking the invaders. Source B blames Kennedy for the debacle, saying he was indecisive and 'cancelled the second air strike' [S]. He also refused air support so that the American role stayed at 'minimum visibility'. Similarly, in Source E a CIA historian blames Kennedy's 'actions, or inactions' as the main cause of failure. That source also criticises the Taylor Committee report for protecting the President by 'not interviewing some key witnesses'. Source F shows Kennedy trying to shift responsibility by painting the invasion as a fight of 'Cuban patriots' against 'a Cuban dictator', doing his best to protect his own reputation [S].

On the other hand, Source A stresses that the CIA chose 'a poor site for landing, a swampy area' that was unsuitable. It also failed to keep the plan secret and used 'outdated bombers', which made the first air strike ineffective. Source A adds that Castro knew the strike was coming and stood ready with 20,000 troops [R]. On that reading the invasion was doomed from the start, whatever Kennedy decided. The Taylor Committee report in Source D likewise argues that the CIA's poor organisation and planning were the main cause, and that the operation would have succeeded had it been 'better conceived, better organised, better staffed and better managed', without any need to escalate the issue to the President. Source E, though critical of Kennedy, admits the CIA will always be blamed [S].

To conclude, the sources suggest Kennedy should not be blamed alone, because the CIA was also incompetent. He can be blamed for cancelling the air strikes and for trying to conceal US involvement. But the sources also show that the CIA failed to plan properly or in time. Taken together, Kennedy shared a large but not the sole responsibility for the disaster [S].

**[9 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950.**

Why did the USA get involved in the Korean War?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the USA wanted to protect its economic interests in Asia. The Domino Theory held that if Korea fell to communism, its powerful neighbour Japan would be next, and Japan was an important market for US exports which the USA wanted to keep capitalist [R]. Protecting South Korea was therefore a way of protecting the wider trading system the USA had built across the Pacific, since a communist takeover in Korea threatened to spread further and close markets that had previously been open to American goods [R]. This mattered because Korea's fall would not have stayed a local defeat: it risked costing the USA its most valuable Asian trading partner and, with it, a large part of America's economic position in the whole region [E].

A second reason was that Truman had already committed himself publicly. In 1947 the Truman Doctrine declared that the USA would protect any country under threat of a communist uprising, and the US public now put pressure on the government to protect South Korea [R]. The government also believed it could win, expecting China not to react and hoping to persuade the UN to provide military support [R]. This explains the intervention because North Korea's invasion in June 1950 was the first open communist attack since the doctrine was announced, and ignoring it would have made the whole policy of containment look worthless [E].

**[6 marks]**

> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
>

>

> - Explaining only one reason will be awarded a maximum of 5 marks, where 5 marks requires the explanation to be supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them will be awarded 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification or description.
> - 1 mark will be awarded for writing about the topic without addressing the question.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Narrating the course of the Korean War instead of explaining why the USA entered it.
> - Writing about the UN's involvement. That is how the USA fought the war, not why it chose to.
> - Saying only that 'the USA wanted to stop communism' without explaining what it feared would follow if it did not.
> - Explaining only one reason and then restating it in different words.
>

> 
> Answers may include the following. This list is not exhaustive and any other valid material should be credited.
> 
> - The USA also blamed the USSR for North Korea's actions, since it had already acted aggressively in Eastern Europe and blockaded Berlin, making the invasion look like part of a wider pattern of Soviet aggression rather than a purely local dispute.
> - China had turned communist in 1949 under Mao Zedong, which made the USA fear that the whole of Asia was being lost.
> - The Long Telegram of 1946 had already advised Truman to contain communism, so the intellectual case was settled before Korea began.
> - Fear of communism at home, through the Red Scare and McCarthyism, put voters under pressure to demand action abroad.
> - North Korea had the backing of both the USSR and China, which made the invasion look like part of a coordinated communist advance rather than a local dispute.

> - Naming the Truman Doctrine and dating it to 1947 is the specific contextual knowledge that takes an explanation to the top of the level.

parts.problemMd:
**The USA attempted to overthrow Castro in 1961.**

Why did the Bay of Pigs invasion fail?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the invasion force was too weak and was deliberately left unsupported. On 17 April 1961 the US government sent 1,400 Cuban exiles to land in the Bay of Pigs, and the CIA had given them only limited military training [R]. To distance itself from the invasion, the US government then refused to send military support [R]. This was decisive because the whole plan depended on the operation looking like a counter-revolution rather than a US invasion, and that same disguise denied the exiles the firepower they needed, so they surrendered in under 24 hours [E].

A second reason was that Castro was both prepared and popular. He knew about the invasion before it began and assembled an army of 20,000 soldiers to meet the exiles as they landed [R]. Cuban citizens were also content with his government, so the invasion attracted very little support on the island [R]. This mattered because the plan assumed the Cuban people would rise up and remove Castro once the exiles arrived; since they would not, no invasion force of that size could have succeeded however well equipped it had been [E].

**[6 marks]**

>

> - Explanation - [E]
>

> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them will be awarded 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification or description.
> - 1 mark will be awarded for writing about the topic without addressing the question.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Describing the consequences of the failure rather than explaining its causes.
> - Confusing the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961 with the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
> - Saying only that 'the exiles were outnumbered' without explaining why the USA left them without support.
> - Explaining only one reason and then repeating it in different words.
>

> Answers may include the following. This list is not exhaustive and any other valid material should be credited.
> 
> - The CIA's plan assumed the landing would trigger a popular uprising which would remove Castro and allow a pro-American government to be installed.
> - Castro's soldiers had far more battle experience than the exiles, having fought a guerrilla campaign against Batista from 1956.
> - Castro had come to power on 1 January 1959 after defeating a corrupt and unpopular ruler, so he had genuine support to draw on.
> - Kennedy had only become president in January 1961 and inherited a plan he had not devised.
> - The failure led Khrushchev to conclude that Kennedy was inexperienced and weak, which shaped Soviet decisions the following year.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two points should be explained with accurate subject knowledge. One reason about the invaders and one about Castro is the clearest structure.
> - The figures do a lot of work here: 1,400 exiles against 20,000 soldiers, and a surrender in under 24 hours.
> - The strongest explanation notices that the secrecy which made the plan politically possible is exactly what made it fail militarily.

parts.problemMd:
**The USA had a huge technological advantage in Vietnam.**

Why did the USA fail to defeat the Vietcong?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Viet Cong tactics cancelled out American strength. The Viet Cong knew the USA would win in open warfare, so instead they set traps, ambushed soldiers, used Vietnam's forests to attack and hide, and dug tunnels [R]. They wore no military uniform, and many South Vietnamese citizens helped them, so US soldiers struggled to tell fighters from civilians [R]. This mattered because American advantages in firepower and technology were useless against an enemy who would not stand and fight and who could not reliably be identified [E].

A second reason was that US tactics created more enemies than they removed. Search and Destroy sent troops by helicopter to find Viet Cong bases, but the operations killed innocent villagers, while napalm and Agent Orange caused high civilian casualties [R]. Supplies also kept moving south along the Ho Chi Minh Trail despite constant US bombing [R]. This explains the failure because every operation pushed more Vietnamese towards supporting the Viet Cong, so the USA was generating opposition faster than it could destroy it [E].
