parts.problemMd:
The Treaty of Versailles left deep political scars in Germany.

Why did many Germans call the politicians who signed the Treaty of Versailles the 'November Criminals'?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that most Germans did not believe their army had actually been beaten [R]. When the armistice was signed in November 1918 there were no enemy troops on German soil and German soldiers were still holding ground in France and Belgium, so the surrender came as a shock. This made it easy for nationalists to spread the 'stab in the back' myth, which claimed that the army had been betrayed at home by politicians, socialists and Jews rather than defeated at the front. The men who signed became traitors in that story, and the label stuck to the Republic they had founded [E].

A second reason is the humiliating nature of what they signed [R]. The Treaty was a 'Diktat' that Germany was not allowed to negotiate, and Article 231 forced Germany to accept blame for causing the war. Germany lost about thirteen per cent of its territory and all of its colonies, its army was capped at 100,000 men, and it was later billed £6,600 million in reparations. Because the new Republic's leaders had put their names to these terms, opponents could argue that they had sold the nation out, and that accusation was used to justify violence against them, including the murders of Erzberger in 1921 and Rathenau in 1922 [E].

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Explanation - [E]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - 6 marks are awarded for explaining two reasons.
> - Explaining one reason is worth 4 marks, rising to 5 marks where the explanation is supported by specific contextual knowledge.
> - Identifying or describing valid reasons without explaining them is worth 2-3 marks, with one mark for each identification.
> - Writing about the topic without addressing the question is worth 1 mark.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 6 marks include:
> 
> - Listing the terms of the Treaty without linking them to the reputation of the men who signed. The question is about why those politicians were blamed, not about what the Treaty said.
> - Confusing the armistice of November 1918 with the Treaty signed in June 1919. The nickname comes from the armistice month, which is worth getting right.
> - Writing that the politicians had a choice. Germany faced invasion and a continuing blockade, so explaining that they had little alternative is good analysis but does not by itself answer why they were blamed.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - The politicians who signed the armistice were largely the new civilian democratic leaders, while the generals who had actually lost the war stepped back, which let the military escape blame.
> - Hindenburg himself gave the stab-in-the-back myth respectability by repeating it to a parliamentary committee in 1919.
> - The myth was later central to Nazi propaganda, which is why it mattered so much for the Republic's survival.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Two explained reasons is the target. A third adds nothing, so develop rather than list.
> - Every point should end by explaining the effect on how those politicians were seen. That is what turns a description into an explanation.
> - Specific detail lifts Level 3 from 4 marks to 5. Naming Erzberger or Rathenau, or giving the £6,600 million figure, is exactly the kind of contextual knowledge the mark scheme rewards.

parts.problemMd:
**Was the Treaty of Versailles fair?**

Study Sources A and B.

**SOURCE A**

Gentlemen,

This can be neither the time nor the place for superfluous words. You see before you the accredited Representatives of the Allied and Associated Powers, both small and great, which have waged without intermission for more than four years the pitiless war which was imposed on them. The hour has struck for the weighty settlement of our accounts. You asked us for peace. We are disposed to grant it to you. This volume, which the Secretary-General of the Conference will shortly hand to you, will tell you the conditions which we have fixed. Every facility which you may require for examining its text will be granted to you, including of course the usages of courtesy commonly practised among all civilized peoples.

In order to acquaint you with another aspect of my thought, I am compelled to add that this Second Peace of Versailles, which is about to become the subject of our discussion, has been too dearly bought by the peoples represented here for us not to be unanimously resolved to secure by every means in our power all the legitimate satisfactions which are our due.

*From Georges Clemenceau's speech presenting the peace terms to the German delegation, Versailles, 7 May 1919.*

**SOURCE B**

Gentlemen,

We are deeply impressed with the lofty character of the task which has brought us together with you, namely, to give the world a speedy and enduring peace. We cherish no illusions as to the extent of our defeat—the degree of our impotence. We know that the might of German arms is broken. We know the force of the hatred which confronts us here, and we have heard the passionate demand that the victors should both make us pay as vanquished and punish us as guilty.

We are required to admit that we alone are war-guilty; such an admission on my lips would be a lie. We are far from seeking to exonerate Germany from all responsibility for the fact that this world war broke out and was waged as it was. The attitude of the former German Government at the Hague Peace Conferences, their actions and omissions in the tragic twelve days of July, may have contributed to the calamity, but we emphatically combat the idea that Germany, whose people were convinced that they were waging a defensive war, should alone be laden with the guilt.

… During the last fifty years the imperialism of all European States has chronically poisoned the international situation. The policy of retaliation and that of expansion as well as disregard of the rights of peoples to self-determination, contributed to the disease of Europe, which reached its crisis in the world war.

*From Count Brockdorff-Rantzau's reply to the Allied powers on receiving the peace terms, Versailles, 7 May 1919.*

How far do these two sources agree? Explain your answer using details of the sources.
parts.solutionMd:
The big messages of the two sources are opposed. Source A treats the settlement as a bill that has fallen due: Clemenceau speaks of 'the weighty settlement of our accounts' and of terms 'we have fixed', presenting the treaty as a just reckoning after a war 'imposed on' the Allies. Source B accepts that Germany has been beaten but denies the moral basis of that reckoning, insisting that to admit sole war guilt 'would be a lie' [S].

There are real agreements. Both accept Germany's total defeat: Source A speaks as a victor dictating terms, and Source B states that 'the might of German arms is broken' [S]. Both also treat the peace as imposed rather than negotiated, Clemenceau announcing conditions 'which we have fixed' and Brockdorff-Rantzau describing 'the passionate demand that the victors should both make us pay as vanquished and punish us as guilty' [S].

They disagree on everything that follows. Clemenceau claims only 'all the legitimate satisfactions which are our due'; Brockdorff-Rantzau calls the same demands punishment driven by 'hatred', and blames 'the imperialism of all European States' rather than Germany alone [S]. So the sources agree on the facts of defeat and disagree completely on what matters, namely whether this is a debt being paid or vengeance imposed on a country that was not solely to blame. Both men spoke at the same meeting on the same afternoon, so the difference is interpretation, not information [R].

**[7 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **7 marks:** a clear, summative, overall judgement comparing the big messages of the two sources. It must be supported; an isolated point of comparison is treated as a single disagreement.
> - **5-6 marks:** compares agreement(s) AND disagreement(s).
> - **3-4 marks:** compares agreement(s) OR disagreement(s), but not both.
> - **2 marks:** answers based on information in one source that is not in the other, or comparing the provenance or topic of the sources.
> - **1 mark:** attempts to compare but makes no valid comparison.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 7 marks include:
> 
> - Writing about one source and then the other without ever comparing them
> - Comparing the provenance rather than the content, for example 'one is French and one is German, so they disagree'
> - Giving only disagreements. Both sources accept that Germany was defeated and that the terms were being imposed, and missing that caps the answer at 3-4 marks
> - Reaching the top mark without support. The big-message judgement has to be evidenced from the sources, or it is treated as a single disagreement
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Both sources are addressed to the same audience in the same room, so neither is a private document; each is performing for an audience beyond the hall
> - Brockdorff-Rantzau concedes that Germany bears some responsibility, which is a partial agreement with Clemenceau rather than a flat contradiction
> - Clemenceau offers 'the usages of courtesy commonly practised among all civilized peoples' while allowing no oral discussion, which Source B reads as the language of dictation

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Find the agreements first. They are harder to spot than the disagreements here, and an answer without them cannot pass 3-4 marks.
> - Quote briefly and often. Short phrases in quotation marks show the examiner exactly what you are comparing.
> - Aim your conclusion at the big messages, not at the details. Saying that one source treats the treaty as a debt being settled and the other as a punishment being inflicted is what reaches 7 marks.
> - Remember both men spoke at the same meeting on the same day. That means the difference between them is interpretation, not information, and saying so is a strong way to finish.

parts.problemMd:
Study Source C.

**SOURCE C**

The programme of the world's peace, therefore, is our programme; and that programme, the only possible programme, as we see it, is this:

I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view.

IV. Adequate guarantees given and taken that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety.

V. A free, open-minded, and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims, based upon a strict observance of the principle that in determining all such questions of sovereignty the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight with the equitable claims of the government whose title is to be determined.

VIII. All French territory should be freed and the invaded portions restored, and the wrong done to France by Prussia in 1871 in the matter of Alsace-Lorraine, which has unsettled the peace of the world for nearly fifty years, should be righted, in order that peace may once more be made secure in the interest of all.

XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.

*From President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, address to the United States Congress, 8 January 1918.*

Why did President Wilson set out these points in January 1918? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
Wilson set out these points in January 1918 because the war was still being fought and he wanted to fix the shape of the peace before it ended [R]. His purpose was to commit the Allies publicly to a settlement built on principle rather than on the spoils of victory, while he still had the leverage to do it [S].

He wanted first to change how peace was made. Point I demands 'Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at' and rules out 'private international understandings of any kind'. Wilson believed secret treaties had helped cause the war, and saying so publicly made it harder for his own allies to carve up territory quietly once Germany was beaten [S].

He also wanted terms Germany could accept. Point V promises an 'absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims' and Point IV offers mutual disarmament, not the disarmament of the defeated alone. Wilson believed a Germany left economically secure would trade and help rebuild Europe, while one crushed by reparations might collapse [R], so publishing such terms mid-war gave Germany a reason to seek peace on his basis. Point XIV then prepares the ground for the League, 'a general association of nations' protecting 'great and small states alike', which had to be an agreed Allied aim before the conference met [S].

The timing explains the speech. No armistice had been signed, so nothing was decided [R]. Wilson knew France wanted a harsh settlement that would be hard to resist once victory came [R], and Point VIII shows him conceding Alsace-Lorraine while framing it as righting a wrong 'in the interest of all' rather than a French prize [S].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **8 marks:** explains Wilson's purpose set in the correct specific context, namely that the war was still being fought in January 1918 and nothing had yet been settled.
> - **6-7 marks:** explains the big message of the source, properly explained rather than copied out.
> - **5 marks:** gives the specific context only, without turning it into a purpose.
> - **2-4 marks:** explains valid sub-messages, or gives only generalised context, or states a purpose without the specific context.
> - **1 mark:** makes points from the levels above but does not use them as reasons for the speech, or gives invalid reasons.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Listing what the Fourteen Points said. Summarising the source is not explaining why Wilson made it
> - Writing about the Paris Peace Conference. That began in January 1919, a full year later, and answers that drift into it lose the context the question depends on
> - Giving only general context such as 'the First World War was happening'. The mark scheme treats generalised context as 2-4 marks; the specific point is that the war was still undecided
> - Describing Wilson's character as an idealist without connecting it to what he was trying to achieve by speaking in January 1918
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Wilson wanted every nation, including Germany, to join the League, so the terms had to be ones a defeated Germany could live with
> - Setting out aims publicly appealed over the heads of Allied governments to their populations, which was itself a source of pressure
> - Point VIII concedes Alsace-Lorraine to France, which suggests Wilson was already bargaining with his allies rather than simply stating principles
> - Wilson also wanted trade barriers removed and freedom of the seas, both of which served American commercial interests as well as his ideals

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Keep asking 'why now?' rather than 'what does it say?'. The date in the question is doing the work.
> - The single most valuable fact here is that the war had not been won yet. Say it early and build the answer on it.
> - Use short quotations as evidence of purpose, not as description. 'Openly arrived at' tells you Wilson was targeting secret diplomacy, which is a motive.
> - Try to give more than one purpose. Shaping the peace, tempting Germany to the table and establishing the League are three, and an answer with several reads far more securely than one built on a single idea.

parts.problemMd:
Study Sources B and D.

**SOURCE B**

Gentlemen,

We are deeply impressed with the lofty character of the task which has brought us together with you, namely, to give the world a speedy and enduring peace. We cherish no illusions as to the extent of our defeat—the degree of our impotence. We know that the might of German arms is broken. We know the force of the hatred which confronts us here, and we have heard the passionate demand that the victors should both make us pay as vanquished and punish us as guilty.

We are required to admit that we alone are war-guilty; such an admission on my lips would be a lie. We are far from seeking to exonerate Germany from all responsibility for the fact that this world war broke out and was waged as it was. The attitude of the former German Government at the Hague Peace Conferences, their actions and omissions in the tragic twelve days of July, may have contributed to the calamity, but we emphatically combat the idea that Germany, whose people were convinced that they were waging a defensive war, should alone be laden with the guilt.

… During the last fifty years the imperialism of all European States has chronically poisoned the international situation. The policy of retaliation and that of expansion as well as disregard of the rights of peoples to self-determination, contributed to the disease of Europe, which reached its crisis in the world war.

*From Count Brockdorff-Rantzau's reply to the Allied powers on receiving the peace terms, Versailles, 7 May 1919.*

**SOURCE D**

ARTICLE 1

Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey on the one hand and Russia on the other declare that the condition of war between them has ceased. They have decided to live in peace and accord in the future.

ARTICLE 2

The contracting parties will refrain from all agitation or propaganda against the governments or all state and military institutions of the other side. Inasmuch as this obligation affects Russia, it affects also the territories occupied by the powers of the Quadruple Alliance.

ARTICLE 3

The territories lying to the west of the line determined by the contracting powers and which formerly belonged to Russia will no longer be under her sovereignty. … The precise location of this line will be worked out by a German-Russian commission.

In respect to the mentioned territories no obligations towards Russia are to be considered as issuing from their formerly having belonged to that country.

Russia gives up all interference in the internal affairs of the said territories.

*From the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, imposed by Germany on Russia, 3 March 1918. Translation transmitted by the American Consul General at Moscow.*

Does Source D make Source B surprising? Explain your answer using details of the sources and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
At first reading, Source D makes Source B very surprising. In Source B, Brockdorff-Rantzau condemns 'the policy of retaliation and that of expansion as well as disregard of the rights of peoples to self-determination' [S]. Source D shows Germany doing exactly those things fifteen months earlier: Article 3 strips Russia of territories that 'will no longer be under her sovereignty', fixes the boundary by a line 'determined by the contracting powers', and states that Russia 'gives up all interference in the internal affairs of the said territories' [S]. The populations are never consulted, yet the treaty claims the parties 'have decided to live in peace and accord' [S].

Evaluating the sources makes Source B much less surprising. Brockdorff-Rantzau's purpose was not to give a balanced account of German conduct but to resist the war-guilt clause and influence opinion beyond the room [S]. Mentioning Brest-Litovsk would have destroyed his case, so its absence is exactly what his purpose predicts. He also distances himself from the government that signed it, referring to 'the former German Government', which lets the new republic disown the old regime [S]. The situations differ too: in 1918 Germany was winning in the east and could dictate; by 1919 it was of proven 'impotence' [R].

So Source D makes the content of Source B surprising but not its existence [S]. The argument about self-determination is hard to reconcile with Brest-Litovsk, and the French used exactly that comparison to justify the treaty [R]. But once purpose is taken into account, a defeated minister making his strongest case and omitting the worst evidence against himself is entirely predictable.

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **8 marks:** compares the messages of the two sources AND evaluates at least one of them, either through its purpose or by using contextual knowledge and cross-reference to explain why it is or is not surprising.
> - **7 marks:** a contextual explanation of why Source B is or is not surprising, but with no comparison to Source D.
> - **3-6 marks:** compares the messages of the two sources to decide whether Source B is surprising.
> - **2 marks:** compares and analyses the sources appropriately but never states whether Source B is surprising, or identifies something surprising without valid explanation.
> - **1 mark:** assertions based on provenance, or a surface comparison of details.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Never answering the question. The mark scheme requires you to say whether Source B is surprising; an answer that only compares the two caps at 6 marks
> - Stopping at the contradiction. Spotting that Germany did to Russia what it complains of is the middle of the argument, not the end. The top mark needs evaluation of why Brockdorff-Rantzau spoke as he did
> - Treating the two treaties as equally harsh without evidence. Use the terms in Source D rather than asserting a comparison
> - Confusing the governments. The Germany that signed Brest-Litovsk in 1918 was the imperial regime; Brockdorff-Rantzau spoke for the new republic, and Source B distances itself from 'the former German Government'
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Brest-Litovsk was signed while Germany was still winning in the east, so the two settlements were made from opposite positions of strength
> - The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 replaced the harsher Treaty of Sevres, which shows that dictated peaces were sometimes revised and that Germany could reasonably hope for the same
> - Article 2 forbids Russia from conducting propaganda even in the territories Germany had taken, which goes beyond anything required of Germany at Versailles
> - Source B does accept some German responsibility, so it is not a blanket denial and is less surprising for that reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Answer the question in your first line. Saying clearly whether Source B is surprising, and then arguing it, keeps you out of the 2-mark trap.
> - The route to 8 marks is evaluation, not detection. Ask what Brockdorff-Rantzau was trying to achieve, and whether a man in his position would ever have mentioned Brest-Litovsk.
> - Use the dates. Fifteen months separate the two sources, and Germany's position was reversed in between.
> - A split answer is fine and often the best one. Source B can be surprising in what it argues while being entirely unsurprising as a piece of diplomacy.

parts.problemMd:
Study Source E.

**SOURCE E**

THIS chapter must be one of pessimism. The Treaty includes no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe,—nothing to make the defeated Central Empires into good neighbors, nothing to stabilize the new States of Europe, nothing to reclaim Russia; nor does it promote in any way a compact of economic solidarity amongst the Allies themselves; no arrangement was reached at Paris for restoring the disordered finances of France and Italy, or to adjust the systems of the Old World and the New.

The Council of Four paid no attention to these issues, being preoccupied with others,—Clemenceau to crush the economic life of his enemy, Lloyd George to do a deal and bring home something which would pass muster for a week, the President to do nothing that was not just and right. It is an extraordinary fact that the fundamental economic problems of a Europe starving and disintegrating before their eyes, was the one question in which it was impossible to arouse the interest of the Four. Reparation was their main excursion into the economic field, and they settled it as a problem of theology, of politics, of electoral chicane, from every point of view except that of the economic future of the States whose destiny they were handling.

*From John Maynard Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, published in 1919. Keynes was the British Treasury's official representative at the Paris Peace Conference until 7 June 1919, when he resigned because he no longer believed the draft terms would be substantially modified.*

Can Keynes's account be trusted? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
parts.solutionMd:
Keynes's account can be trusted on the economics and much less on the motives he attributes to individuals.

His strongest claim to trust is that he was there. As the British Treasury's official representative at the conference, when he says 'no arrangement was reached at Paris for restoring the disordered finances of France and Italy' he is reporting what he watched happen from inside the negotiations [S]. His central claim, that the Treaty contained no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe, is about what the document does and does not contain, so it can be checked rather than merely believed [S].

His purpose cuts the other way. Keynes resigned on 7 June 1919 because he had concluded the terms would not be modified, and wrote the book to argue the settlement was an economic disaster [S]. That is not a neutral observer but a man who had lost the argument and left, and who would naturally present the conference as ignoring the very problems he had urged it to solve.

The portraits of the Council of Four are where trust should be weakest. Calling Clemenceau's aim 'to crush the economic life of his enemy' and Lloyd George's 'to do a deal and bring home something which would pass muster for a week' is judgement of motive, not evidence of it [S]. There is knowledge behind it, since Clemenceau did want Germany too weak to invade and Lloyd George was elected on a promise to make Germany pay [R], but Keynes states as fact what he cannot have known.

So trust the observation and treat the verdicts with care [S].

**[8 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Recall - [R]
> - Source analysis - [S]
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **7-8 marks:** evaluates the source by considering Keynes's purpose in the context of the time, and uses what he is actually saying to do it.
> - **5-6 marks:** evaluates the big message of the source using cross-reference or contextual knowledge.
> - **4 marks:** evaluates details in the source by cross-reference, contextual knowledge or purpose, without reaching the big message.
> - **3 marks:** uses everyday empathy to make something of the provenance, for example that he resigned so he must have been annoyed.
> - **1-2 marks:** assertions based on provenance alone, or selects details said to be reliable or unreliable with no explanation.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable response.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 8 marks include:
> 
> - Deciding the source is untrustworthy simply because Keynes resigned. That is provenance used as assertion and sits at 1-2 marks
> - Treating 'he was there' as settling the matter. Being present makes him well informed and also makes him involved, and the best answers say both
> - Ignoring what he actually writes. The mark scheme requires you to use his own words, so quote them and test them
> - Answering whether you agree with Keynes rather than whether he can be trusted. Those are different questions
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Keynes was not a lone voice, which strengthens his credibility. Marshal Foch complained that the treaty failed to protect France, and other British politicians warned its terms would provoke another war
> - Against that, some British journalists insisted Germany could well afford to pay and some Americans thought the treaty the best available in 1919, so his verdict was contested at the time
> - The book was published in 1919, so his memory was fresh but he had no hindsight about whether the treaty would work
> - He is notably fairer to Wilson, saying the President wished 'to do nothing that was not just and right', which suggests he was not simply hostile to everyone
> - Keynes was an economist by training, which strengthens his authority on reparations and weakens it on diplomatic motive

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Split the source rather than judging it whole. Trust his account of what the treaty omitted; be wary of his account of what the leaders wanted.
> - Purpose is the route to the top band. Ask why a man who resigned in June 1919 sat down to write this book, and what he needed readers to believe.
> - Use his own phrases as evidence. Quoting 'electoral chicane' and then explaining what it reveals about his attitude is exactly what the mark scheme asks for.
> - Note the one leader he treats gently. Spotting that he spares Wilson shows you are reading the source rather than reacting to it.

ARTICLE 3

ARTICLE 231.

How far do these sources provide convincing evidence that the Treaty of Versailles was a fair settlement? Use the sources to explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Three sources support the statement and three work against it, and the balance depends on what test of fairness is applied.

Source A supports it most directly. Clemenceau presents the treaty as 'the weighty settlement of our accounts' after a war 'imposed on' the Allies, claiming only 'the legitimate satisfactions which are our due' [S]. Since the Western Front had been fought largely across France, the demand for repair was real [R]. Source F states the same case as law, Article 231 making Germany accept responsibility for 'all the loss and damage' caused by 'the aggression of Germany and her allies' [S]. Source D supports it more sharply still: Germany had imposed on Russia territories that 'will no longer be under her sovereignty' and a boundary 'determined by the contracting powers' [S], so if Versailles was unfair, Brest-Litovsk was far more so, and the French used exactly that comparison [R].

Against the statement, Source C provides the measure. Wilson had promised 'open covenants of peace, openly arrived at' and armaments 'reduced to the lowest point' for all states, yet Germany was excluded from the negotiations and disarmed alone [S]. Source B presses the same objection from the German side, conceding partial responsibility but insisting that to admit sole guilt 'would be a lie' [S]. Source E is the most damaging because it comes from inside the Allied delegation: Keynes reports 'no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe' [S], and Source F concedes his point, since Article 232 admits German resources 'are not adequate' to meet the bill the treaty imposes [S].

Overall the sources do not provide convincing evidence that the settlement was fair, though they show it was defensible [S]. On the narrow test of entitlement to compensation, A, D and F make a strong case. But fairness also means keeping the terms on which the war was ended and demanding what can be met, and on both of those C and E convict the treaty out of the Allies' own mouths, with F supplying the admission. It was justifiable as a settling of accounts and unfair as a peace [R].

parts.problemMd: 'Up to 1923, the economic consequences of the Treaty of Versailles were more important for Germany than the political consequences.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Treaty of Versailles had serious economic and political implications for Germany. There is a debate about whether economic consequences were more important than the political ones. In this essay, I will examine how the economic consequences of the Treaty of Versailles were more significant than the political consequences [R]. Firstly, the reparations amount for Germany was set in 1921 at £6.6 billion, which was too much for Germany to pay. There were significant economic losses, as it lost 16 per cent of its coal production, 48 per cent of its iron production, 15 per cent of its agricultural produce and 10 per cent of its manufacturing [R]. Secondly, Germany was unable to pay the reparations in 1922. As a result, in January 1923, 80,000 French and Belgian troops marched into the Ruhr, an industrial region of Germany, and began to confiscate goods. They sent these back to France as payment of the debts. The Weimar Republic instructed workers to go on strike and printed money to support them [E]. This led to hyperinflation, and the German currency became worthless. Prices for goods shot up, and the value of the German mark fell to 4,210,500,000,000 to the US dollar [A].

On the other hand, among the political consequences, the new German leader, Friedrich Ebert, had no choice but to sign the treaty; however, Germans took the signing to mean that the Weimar Republic agreed to all its terms [E]. This damaged the reputation of the government, and several political groups took it as an opportunity to try to overthrow the government. The Kapp Putsch, the Spartacist uprising and the Munich Putsch created political upheaval in the early years of the Weimar Republic [A].

To conclude, I strongly agree with the statement that the economic consequences of the Treaty of Versailles were more important for Germany. Most of the political consequences were rooted in economic causes. Hyperinflation, for example, led to political unrest, and the reparations failure led to the occupation of the Ruhr. The political consequences caused resentment, but the economic consequences were far-reaching and more damaging [A].

parts.problemMd:
The Big Three wanted different things from the peace settlement.

Which was more important in shaping the Treaty of Versailles: Clemenceau's demand for French security or Lloyd George's wish to protect British trade? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Clemenceau's demand for security shaped a great deal of the Treaty [R]. France had been invaded twice in fifty years and its north-east had been fought over for four years, so his aim was to leave Germany unable to attack again. The clauses that came from this aim are the ones the Treaty is remembered for: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France, the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied troops for fifteen years, the German army was capped at 100,000 men with no tanks, aircraft or submarines, France was given the output of the Saar coalfields, and Article 231 forced Germany to accept blame for the war, which then justified the reparations bill. The punitive core of the settlement is therefore French in origin [E].

Lloyd George's concern for trade was also influential, but it worked differently [R]. Germany had been Britain's second largest trading partner before the war, so a Germany reduced to poverty meant lost British exports and British unemployment. He also feared that a humiliated Germany might turn communist as Russia had. In the Fontainebleau Memorandum of March 1919 he warned that terms which crushed Germany would simply provoke another war. His influence shows up in what the Treaty did not do: Germany was not broken up, Danzig was made a free city under League control rather than handed straight to Poland, plebiscites were held in Upper Silesia and Schleswig instead of territory simply changing hands, and reparations were set lower than France wanted [E].

The two aims often pulled against each other, and where they clashed neither man simply won [A]. Clemenceau wanted the Rhineland made into a separate state permanently occupied by France; Lloyd George and Wilson refused, and the compromise was demilitarisation plus a fixed fifteen-year occupation.

On balance Clemenceau's demand for security was the more important in shaping the Treaty [A]. Lloyd George set limits on how far the settlement could go, which mattered enormously for Germany's survival as a single state, but limiting a document is not the same as shaping it. Almost every clause a student can name, from the war guilt article to the disarmament terms, exists because France wanted protection. Lloyd George's trade concern moderated the Treaty; Clemenceau's security concern wrote it.

parts.problemMd:
**The Big Three came to Paris with very different aims.**

Why did Clemenceau want a harsh treaty?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Clemenceau feared another German invasion of France. France and Germany shared a border and had already fought twice during the nineteenth century, and in those wars Germany had taken key areas from France, including Alsace-Lorraine [R]. Clemenceau therefore demanded that Germany's armed forces be disbanded, that the Rhineland come under French control and that Alsace-Lorraine be returned [R]. This explains why he pressed for harsh terms rather than moderate ones: only a Germany that had been permanently weakened would be unable to attack France a third time, so for Clemenceau the treaty was a question of national survival rather than of punishment [E].

A second reason was the damage France had suffered. The majority of the Western Front was fought on French soil, and the fighting destroyed many roads, hospitals and factories, while over two-thirds of the French Army died or were wounded [R]. Clemenceau wanted Germany to pay to repair that damage, to take responsibility for starting the war and to hand over the Saar Basin so that France could rebuild its economy [R]. This mattered because a French leader who returned from Paris with anything less would not have survived politically, so the anger of the French public pushed Clemenceau towards the harshest terms he could obtain [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The First World War ended with an armistice in November 1918.**

Why was there a need for peace treaties in 1919?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that the armistice had settled nothing beyond the fighting. Germany surrendered on 11 November 1918 and the German politicians of the new Weimar Republic signed the armistice, but this only ensured a temporary peace [R]. An official peace document was still required in which the Allies agreed the terms of defeat for Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkiye and Bulgaria, which is why five separate treaties were planned [R]. This created a need for treaties because an armistice is only an agreement to stop shooting: without a settlement, no borders, no reparations and no limits on armed forces had been fixed, and the war could simply have resumed [E].

A second reason was the scale of the destruction, which created a demand for punishment that had to be dealt with formally. Historians estimate the conflict caused around 8.5 million military deaths and around 13 million civilian casualties, and the fighting on the Western Front destroyed hundreds of factories, railways and roads in France and Belgium [R]. In Britain around 750,000 soldiers died, and Lloyd George had won the election of December 1918 on a promise to 'make Germany pay' [R]. This mattered because Allied leaders had promised their voters that Germany would be punished, and only a treaty could deliver reparations and territorial losses in a form that was legally binding on Germany [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919.**

'The Treaty of Versailles was too harsh on Germany.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Whether the treaty was too harsh depends on what it is measured against: the terms other countries had accepted, or what Germany could actually bear [R].

The military terms left Germany defenceless. Article 160 cut the army to 100,000 men, Article 181 limited the navy to six battleships and banned submarines, Article 198 forbade an air force, and Article 42 demilitarised the Rhineland [R]. This was harsh because Germany lost the ability to defend its own borders while its neighbours did not disarm at all, as the Ruhr showed in January 1923, when France occupied Germany's industrial heartland and Germany, capped at 100,000 troops by the treaty, could only respond with passive resistance, not military force [E].

The economic terms were harsher still, because Germany could not meet them. Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks, Article 45 gave France the Saar coalfields for fifteen years, costing 15% of Germany's coal, and Article 119 transferred all eleven colonies to Britain and France [R]. The treaty demanded an enormous payment while removing the resources needed to make it, which is why Germany could not pay by November 1922 [E].

However, Germany had recently imposed far worse. At Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 it forced Russia to give up around one million square miles and over a third of its population [R]. The Allies were applying a standard Germany itself had set a year earlier, so the terms were not exceptional for their time [A].

Many contemporaries thought Versailles too lenient. Some in Britain and France argued that while Germany existed at all it remained a threat, and Marshal Foch complained that the treaty did not protect France [R]. The Allies then softened it, cancelling Austria's and Hungary's reparations and reducing Germany's [R]. Authors of a crushing settlement do not spend the next decade easing it [A].

The statement is true to a large extent, but not for the usual reason. The terms were not unusually severe by the standards of 1919, and Brest-Litovsk proves it [A]. What made them too harsh was their effect: they removed the means of payment while still demanding it. A treaty is too harsh when the country it is imposed on cannot live with it [A].

parts.problemMd:
**No member of the Big Three achieved everything they wanted at Paris.**

Who was more satisfied with the Treaty of Versailles: Clemenceau or Lloyd George? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Both men left Paris having won something and lost something. The difference is that Lloyd George came looking for a compromise and Clemenceau came looking for security, and only one of those was available [R].

Clemenceau had real successes. Alsace-Lorraine was returned under Article 51, France gained the Saar coalfields for fifteen years under Article 45, Germany's army was cut to 100,000 men, and Article 231 forced Germany to accept blame, with reparations set at 132 billion gold marks [R]. These were his central demands, so on territory, blame and payment he delivered what French opinion required [E].

Yet his central aim failed. He wanted the Rhineland under French control and Germany broken into separate states; instead the Rhineland was only demilitarised, Germany remained whole, and he thought neither the army limits nor the reparations went far enough [R]. This is decisive, because his motive was preventing a third German invasion, and a demilitarised zone can be remilitarised while a divided Germany could not have been reunited [A]. Marshal Foch said openly that the treaty did not protect France [R].

Lloyd George got what he came for. Germany's navy was cut to six battleships with no submarines, restoring British naval supremacy; Britain took Germany's colonies as mandates under Article 119; and the terms were harsh enough to satisfy the voters he had promised to 'make Germany pay' [R]. Germany also survived as a trading partner, which was his other main aim [E].

His disappointments were smaller. He worried about Germans placed under French and Polish rule, and reluctantly accepted the independence of eastern European states [R]. These were concerns about the future rather than failures of his own programme, and he had deliberately positioned himself between Wilson and Clemenceau, so he never expected everything [A].

Lloyd George was therefore more satisfied. Clemenceau won more of the headline terms but lost the one that mattered to him, and said so at the time [A]. Lloyd George wanted a treaty harsh enough to please British voters and mild enough to leave Germany trading, and that is what the settlement delivered. Satisfaction must be judged against what each man was trying to achieve, and the leader who wanted the middle ground was always the likelier to accept a compromise [A].

name: Who was to Blame for the Cold War?

parts.problemMd:
There was much tension in the early years of the Cold War.

What happened in the Greek Civil War?
parts.solutionMd:
German forces withdrew from Greece in 1944, leaving no clear authority in place [1]. The Communist Liberation Front (EAM) and its military arm, the Greek People's Liberation Army (ELAS), started planning for a socialist state, while the government wanted to restore the monarchy [1]. Fighting between the communists and the government resumed in 1946 and lasted three years until 1949, and a plebiscite held in September 1946 confirmed the restoration of the monarchy [1]. ELAS was converted into the DSE, the Democratic Army of Greece, which was helped by communist states such as Yugoslavia and Albania [1]. The Greek government was supported first by Britain and later by the United States, and the DSE was eventually defeated [1].

parts.problemMd:
Relations between the wartime allies broke down after 1945.

What was the Novikov Telegram?
parts.solutionMd:
It was a report sent in September 1946 by Nikolai Novikov, the Soviet ambassador in Washington, back to Stalin [1]. It was written because the Soviet government had learned of Kennan's Long Telegram and wanted its own assessment of American intentions [1]. Novikov argued that the United States was building up its military strength in order to achieve world domination, and that after Roosevelt's death it no longer wished to cooperate with the USSR [1]. He also warned that the American people would support a war against the Soviet Union [1].

parts.problemMd:
**The Grand Alliance met at Yalta in February 1945.**

Describe what was agreed at the Yalta Conference.
parts.solutionMd:
It was agreed that Germany would be split into four occupation zones after its defeat and would pay \$20 billion in reparations, half of which would go to the USSR [1]. The USSR agreed to join the war against Japan [1]. Stalin agreed that free elections would be held in Eastern Europe, and that free elections would decide Poland's post-war government, although the USSR would gain land from Poland [1]. The three leaders also agreed to create the United Nations, with only some Soviet republics receiving individual membership [1].

parts.problemMd:
**The USSR blockaded West Berlin in June 1948.**

What was the Berlin Airlift?
parts.solutionMd:
The Berlin Airlift was the Western decision to fly supplies into West Berlin after the USSR closed the road, rail and canal links, and it ran from June 1948 to May 1949 under the codename Operation Vittles [1]. The USA and Britain flew in around 1,000 tons of supplies a day, and in January 1949 alone 170,000 tons were delivered [1]. At its peak a plane landed at Berlin-Tempelhof every 45 seconds, and the French military built a new airport at Berlin-Tegel [1]. At least 78 people were killed in air accidents, although the Soviet military caused no casualties [1].

parts.problemMd:
The United States spent heavily in Europe after the Second World War.

Why did the United States believe that economic aid would stop the spread of communism?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that Americans thought poverty was what made communism attractive [R]. Europe in 1947 was wrecked: cities had been bombed flat, food and fuel were short, and the winter of 1946 to 1947 was one of the worst on record. In those conditions the communist parties of France and Italy were polling strongly, and it seemed obvious in Washington that hungry and hopeless people would turn to whoever promised change. Marshall himself said the policy was directed not against any country but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. If prosperity could be restored, the argument ran, communism would simply lose its appeal and no troops would be needed [E].

A second reason is that recovery would produce strong allies and strong customers [R]. Roughly 13 billion dollars went to Western Europe between 1948 and 1952. Countries that recovered economically could afford to rearm and resist Soviet pressure themselves, which spared the United States from defending them directly. Recovery also created markets for American exports at a time when the United States feared sliding back into depression once wartime production ended. Aid therefore served American self-interest as well as containment, which is exactly why Stalin forbade the eastern European states from accepting it [E].

parts.problemMd: Why was Stalin worried by the introduction by Western powers of a new currency in Germany in 1948?
parts.solutionMd:
As part of the economic reform in western Germany, a new currency, the Deutschmark, was introduced across the three western zones in June 1948. The British and American zones had already been merged as Bizonia in 1947. The main aim of this move was to encourage trade and help western Germany become more independent. Stalin did not like this development, for several reasons [R].

Firstly, it would lead to economic development in the western zones controlled by Britain, France and the USA. Stalin preferred Germany to remain weak, and not to recover enough to threaten the USSR then or in the future [E]. He already suspected that the Western powers wanted to divide Germany permanently in two. That was contrary to the Potsdam Agreement, where it had been agreed that Germany would remain unified. Stalin also thought it would make capitalism appear superior to communism [E].

Secondly, in the eastern part of Germany that the USSR controlled, Stalin had deliberately devalued the old Reichsmark by printing excessive currency, leading to inflation and a weak economy. Backed by the Marshall Plan, the Deutschmark could help the German economy recover, and if it did it would attract people away from the Soviet zone and undermine Stalin's control not only in eastern Germany but across Eastern Europe [E]. The Deutschmark's success could tempt people in the Soviet zone to abandon the less stable Soviet-controlled currency and adopt the Western one, which would destroy the Soviet economic system in their zone [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The Red Army occupied much of Eastern Europe in 1945.**

Why did Stalin want control of Eastern Europe?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was security. Between 1943 and 1945 the Red Army had liberated many countries in Eastern Europe from Nazi control, and Stalin wanted to keep them as a buffer zone between the USSR and the West [R]. This became more urgent after the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, since Stalin believed the USA wanted to destroy communism [R]. This explains his determination, because the USSR had twice been invaded from the west, so a belt of friendly states bought the USSR time and distance [E].

A second reason was that a buffer zone was only useful if the countries in it obeyed him. Stalin did not want a non-communist government in Poland, so although the Grand Alliance had agreed at Yalta to free elections there, the communists took 80% of the vote in 1947 after a campaign of violence and intimidation [R]. In Hungary the communist Rakosi took control of the secret police, and in Czechoslovakia the communist Gottwald seized power in a coup in 1948 [R]. This mattered because genuinely free elections in Eastern Europe would have produced governments hostile to the USSR, so control, rather than mere influence, was the only version of the buffer zone that worked [E].

parts.problemMd:
**The USA dropped atomic bombs on Japan in August 1945.**

Why did the atomic bomb damage relations between the USA and the USSR?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason was that Truman had kept it secret from an ally and then used it as a demonstration of power. Stalin only learned that the Manhattan Project had succeeded during the Potsdam Conference in July 1945, and within weeks the USA had dropped bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August, killing roughly 120,000 Japanese civilians [R]. This damaged relations because the USSR was still formally an ally, and an ally that conceals a weapon of that scale and then displays it is not behaving like one, so Stalin concluded that the USA could not be trusted [E].

A second reason was the way the USSR responded. Stalin saw the bombing as aggressive, believed the USA wanted to destroy communism, and became willing to do whatever was needed to protect the USSR [R]. He also accelerated the Soviet atomic programme, and the USSR successfully tested its own bomb on 29 August 1949 [R]. This mattered because it produced exactly the outcome the USA feared: the bomb intended to deter Soviet expansion instead provoked it, and it began an arms race that neither side could now step back from [E].

parts.problemMd: Which was more of a threat to the Soviet Union: the Truman Doctrine or the Marshall Plan? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
After the Second World War the Soviet Union was trying to expand its influence in Eastern Europe, and its ideology was also gaining attention in some Western European countries. The Truman Doctrine promised American protection to nations that wanted to resist the spread of communism [R]. The Marshall Plan focused on economic aid to European nations to help them recover from the destruction of the war and, as a result, protect them from turning to communism. In this essay, I will explain how the Marshall Plan was a bigger threat as it could have long-lasting and deeper impacts [E].

Firstly, the Marshall Plan, or European Recovery Programme, offered 13.3 billion US dollars to 16 European nations between 1948 and 1952. It resulted in the economies of the recipient nations recovering substantially [E]. The Soviet Union and its satellite states rejected the aid, but the plan's success in Western Europe was highly visible and invited comparison. That was a direct blow to Soviet ideology and prestige [A].

Secondly, when the Marshall Plan offered aid to Eastern European countries, it alarmed Stalin. If any satellite state accepted Marshall Aid it would come under American economic influence, and communism would lose its appeal [E]. It would stop communism spreading and might even undermine it inside Eastern Europe. Stalin saw it as an American plot to destroy Soviet control over the Eastern Bloc [A].

By contrast, the impact of the Truman Doctrine remained limited. It focused on containing communism, which was never a threat to the existence of communism anywhere. The Marshall Plan, on the other hand, gave practical help designed to move countries towards capitalism [E]. This increased American influence in Europe and had a deeper effect on the countries involved. The Truman Doctrine helped countries resisting Soviet influence, but it did not directly challenge the Soviet Union's existing sphere of influence in the way the Marshall Plan did [A].

To conclude, the Marshall Plan was an ambitious programme that could redraw the map of Europe so that regions under Soviet influence might shift sides. While the Truman Doctrine focused on containment, the Marshall Plan actively built a capitalist, pro-American bloc in Western Europe. The Marshall Plan was therefore the greater threat to the Soviet Union's position in Europe [A].

parts.problemMd:
The Grand Alliance did not survive long after the defeat of the Axis powers.

Which did more to break up the Grand Alliance: the dropping of the atomic bomb or the telegrams of 1946? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The atomic bomb did serious damage [R]. Stalin learned that the Manhattan Project had succeeded while the Big Three were still at Potsdam in July 1945, and the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki the following month killed around 120,000 Japanese civilians. Alongside the official justifications for using them, the USA wanted to show the Soviet Union how technologically advanced and powerful it was, and Truman hoped this would persuade Western Europe to back the USA and encourage Eastern Europe to resist Soviet expansion. Stalin read that display as aggression and concluded that the USA meant to destroy communism, so he pressed for a buffer zone of friendly states between Germany and the USSR and accelerated the Soviet bomb programme, which tested successfully on 29 August 1949 [E].

The telegrams, though, did something different [R]. In February 1946 Kennan, the American ambassador in Moscow, sent Truman a message of around 8,000 words arguing that Stalin wanted to destroy capitalism, that peace between the two systems was impossible, and that the USA should contain the Soviet Union. In September 1946 Novikov, the Soviet ambassador in Washington, sent Stalin his own assessment: that the USA was building military strength to achieve world domination, that it had stopped wanting to cooperate after Roosevelt's death, and that the American people would support a war against the USSR. Each side already suspected the other of planning its destruction, and the telegrams confirmed those fears in writing at the highest level [E].

The decisive difference is what each produced [R]. The bomb produced fear; the telegrams produced policy. After them Truman set out to contain communism and Stalin set out to spread it through Eastern Europe, and once both governments were committed to opposing programmes there was nothing left of the alliance to rescue [E].

On balance the telegrams did more [A]. The bomb supplied the evidence, but evidence only matters once someone acts on it, and it was the telegrams that converted suspicion into strategy on both sides within seven months of each other.

It is worth questioning the premise, however [A]. Historians describe the Grand Alliance as a marriage of convenience: the USA, USSR and Britain were held together by a common enemy and were suspicious of one another throughout. Once the Axis powers were defeated in August 1945 there was nothing keeping them together. On that reading neither the bomb nor the telegrams broke up an alliance that was already finished; they determined how quickly and how bitterly the break came [A].

> - The dates are an argument in themselves. The bomb came first, in August 1945, and the telegrams followed in 1946, so you can present the telegrams as the point at which suspicion hardened into strategy.

> - Challenging the question is a high-level move here. If the alliance was only ever a marriage of convenience, then both factors sped up a collapse that was coming anyway, but you must still answer which did more.

parts.problemMd:
**Historians have long disagreed about the origins of the Cold War.**

'The USSR was to blame for the Cold War.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Both superpowers acted out of fear, so the useful test is not who was more frightened but who broke what had been agreed [R].

The strongest case against the USSR is that Stalin broke the Yalta agreement. He had accepted that free elections would be held in Eastern Europe, but the Red Army remained and communist governments were installed instead [R]. In Poland a campaign of violence and intimidation gave the communists 80% of the vote in 1947; in Hungary Rakosi seized the secret police and imprisoned opponents; in Czechoslovakia Gottwald took power by coup in 1948 [R]. These were not defences against an American threat but the destruction of governments the USSR had promised to allow [E].

The Berlin Blockade goes further. In June 1948 the USSR closed the road, rail and canal links into West Berlin, a city with only 36 days of food, to force the Western powers out of the capital [R]. Attempting to starve a city into surrender is not the behaviour of a state that merely wants to be left alone, and Stalin created the first direct confrontation [A].

However, the USA moved first and moved secretly. Truman replaced Roosevelt, took a tougher approach, concealed the Manhattan Project from an ally and used the bomb partly to demonstrate American power [R]. Kennan's Long Telegram of February 1946 already committed the USA to containment [R]. Since the satellite states were not complete until 1948, the American decision that co-operation was impossible came before the takeover it supposedly answered [A].

American policy also looked expansionist from Moscow. The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 sent \$400 million to Greece and Turkey, and the Marshall Plan gave \$13 billion to 16 countries, which Stalin called 'dollar imperialism' [R]. Trizonia followed in March 1948 and the Deutschmark that June, without Soviet agreement [R]. A rebuilt, separately governed West Germany was the exact threat the buffer zone existed to prevent [E].

The statement is true to a large extent. Both sides acted from fear, and the American atomic monopoly gave Stalin real grounds for it [A]. But the USA broke no agreement in 1945, whereas Stalin promised free elections at Yalta and then denied them, and it was the USSR that turned a quarrel into a confrontation at Berlin [A].

parts.problemMd:
**The USSR blockaded West Berlin between June 1948 and May 1949.**

How important was the Berlin Blockade in the development of the Cold War? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Berlin Blockade did not create the division of Germany, but it turned a disagreement about how to govern it into a confrontation the two sides never came back from [R].

It produced the first direct clash between the superpowers. In June 1948 the USSR closed the road, rail and canal links into West Berlin, a city with food for only 36 days and no fuel or medicine [R]. The West had three options, all bad: withdrawing handed Stalin the capital and destroyed containment, supplying by land made the West the aggressor, and only flying supplies in avoided both [R]. For the first time each side had to weigh a decision that might mean war, which no earlier quarrel had required [E].

Its consequences were long-lasting and far-reaching. NATO was created in April 1949, the Federal Republic of Germany followed in May, the German Democratic Republic in October, and the Warsaw Pact in April 1955 [R]. Germany's temporary occupation zones therefore became two states with two rival military alliances behind them, which is the shape the Cold War kept for forty years [E].

However, the division was already well advanced. Bizonia merged the British and American zones in January 1947, the Truman Doctrine followed in March, Trizonia formed in March 1948 and the Deutschmark arrived that June [R]. Stalin blockaded Berlin because of those steps, so the blockade was a reaction to a division the West had already built [A].

It also changed nothing on the ground. Stalin lifted the blockade on 12 May 1949 having gained nothing: West Berlin stayed Western, the Deutschmark stayed, and the USSR had been humiliated because it could not stop the airlift without shooting down supply planes and starting a war [R]. A crisis the aggressor abandons on the original terms has not altered the balance of power [A].

The blockade was therefore very important to a large extent, though more as a consequence rather than a root cause. It settled nothing that was in dispute in 1948 [A]. What it did was convert an argument between former allies into two armed camps with a fortified border, and make that permanent [A].

> - The blockade was possible only because West Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone and depended on East Germany for food, so geography rather than policy created the opportunity.

parts.problemMd:
American society was changing rapidly by 1919.

Who were the WASPs?
parts.solutionMd:
WASP stands for White Anglo-Saxon Protestant [1]. They were Americans descended from the settlers who had crossed the Atlantic from north-western Europe as far back as the 1600s [1]. By the start of the twentieth century they were the most powerful and influential group in the United States, dominating politics and the economy [1]. Their fears and prejudices about the millions of newer immigrants arriving from southern and eastern Europe led directly to the laws passed in the 1920s to limit migration [1].

>

>

> - Four separate points are needed for four marks. Developing a point you have already made does not earn a second mark.
> - Accept all valid responses.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 4 marks include:
> 
> - Treating WASPs and the Ku Klux Klan as the same thing. The Klan was an organisation with members; WASPs were a much larger social group, most of whom never joined it.
> - Explaining why WASPs disliked immigration. Reasons earn no credit on a recall question.
> - Writing only 'white Americans'. The Anglo-Saxon and Protestant parts of the term are doing real work, because the prejudice was directed at Catholic and Jewish immigrants as well as at people of other races.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Roughly 40 million people had emigrated to the United States between 1850 and 1914, most of them from southern and eastern Europe, which is what made WASPs feel their position was threatened.
> - WASPs were themselves descended from immigrants, which many contemporaries pointed out.
> - Their influence shows in the 1917 Immigration Law, the 1921 Emergency Quota Act and the 1924 Reed-Johnson Act, all of which favoured migrants from north-western Europe.

> - Keep each point in its own sentence so the examiner can count them.
> - Saying who they were descended from, and how powerful they had become, gives you two easy marks beyond simply decoding the acronym.

parts.problemMd:
American society was changing rapidly by 1919.

Why did life not improve for many Black Americans who moved to the northern states?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that the law changed but the attitudes did not [R]. Black Americans moved north to escape the Jim Crow Laws, which in the southern states forced them into separate schools, libraries, swimming pools and taxis and used literacy tests and voting taxes to keep them off the electoral register. There was no such legislation in the North. But racism did not exist only in the statute book, and northern employers still preferred White applicants, so Black migrants struggled to find work at all and those who did were paid less than White workers doing the same job. Escaping segregation by law turned out not to be the same as escaping discrimination in practice [E].

A second reason is that the scale of the migration made conditions worse rather than better [R]. The Black populations of both Chicago and New York doubled between 1900 and 1920, and the new arrivals were confined to the most deprived districts of those cities. Low wages meant they could not afford to move anywhere better, and prejudice meant they would not have been welcome if they could. Families who had travelled hundreds of miles looking for opportunity therefore ended up crowded into slum housing, so the material improvement they had moved for often never arrived [E].

parts.problemMd:
American society was changing rapidly by 1919.

Which did more harm to Black Americans in the 1920s: the Jim Crow Laws in the South or racist attitudes in the North? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The Jim Crow Laws did enormous harm [R]. Passed by White politicians in the southern states, they forced Black Americans into separate schools, libraries, swimming pools and taxis, and they were backed by the authority of the state itself rather than by private prejudice. Their most serious effect was political: literacy tests designed to be impossible for people who had been denied education, together with taxes on registering to vote, stripped most Black southerners of the vote. That mattered more than any single restriction, because a group that cannot vote cannot change the laws that oppress it by peaceful means [E].

The South was also more dangerous [R]. Racial tension was worst there, in the states where the great cotton and tobacco plantations had used enslaved labour, and the 1920s saw the Ku Klux Klan revive to a membership of around five million after the 1915 film The Birth of a Nation glorified it. The Klan operated in secret, with members hooded in public, and it targeted Black Americans above all. Discrimination enforced by violence is of a different order from discrimination in hiring [E].

The North was far from safe, however [R]. There were no Jim Crow Laws there, but racist attitudes were widespread. Black migrants struggled to find work at all, those who did were paid less than White workers for the same job, and they were confined to the most deprived districts of the cities. The populations of Black Chicago and New York doubled between 1900 and 1920, so this affected very large numbers of people [E].

On balance the Jim Crow Laws did more harm [A]. The North damaged Black Americans economically, and the fact that so many still went there shows how bad the South must have been. But northern discrimination left people with the vote, with the right to organise and with the legal standing to campaign, whereas the South removed all three and added the threat of Klan violence on top. Harm that is written into law and enforced by terror reaches further than harm produced by prejudice alone.

One qualification is worth making [A]. Northern racism was in one sense harder to fight, precisely because it was informal: there was no single statute to repeal and no obvious target for a campaign. That is why discrimination in northern cities long outlasted the Jim Crow Laws themselves [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the problems faced by farmers in the USA in the 1920s.
parts.solutionMd:
The 1920s were called the 'Roaring Twenties' due to the prosperity that most Americans experienced. However, it was not the case for agriculture and rural areas. While cities were progressing and blooming, agriculture faced serious problems, leading to hardship for farmers [E].

One of the major problems the American agricultural sector had to face was overproduction. During the First World War, America was exporting food crops to Europe. Demand was so high that farmers started producing more, and some of them even purchased land and modern machinery [E]. However, after the war the demand for food dropped and European countries started producing their own food again [E]. American farmers were still producing at wartime levels, which caused an excessive supply of wheat, corn and cotton. Since supply outstripped demand, prices dropped and farmers were left with unsold crops.

The immediate result of the drop in prices and sales was a fall in farmers' incomes [E]. Between 1919 and 1921, the prices of farm products decreased by 50 per cent. Farmers who had taken loans for machinery could not pay them back. There was no hope of recovery any time soon, leading to foreclosures on farms and increased poverty in rural areas [A].

Another problem added to the list was the high tariffs introduced by the US government. In 1922 the Fordney-McCumber Tariff was introduced to protect American industries [E]. Because of it, foreign countries found it harder to sell their goods in the USA. As a result, those countries began to avoid purchasing American food, which reduced farmers' incomes even further [A].

Additionally, the gap between rural and urban America was widening. City people were living a life of comfort with radios, cars and consumer goods. For rural farmers this remained out of reach, because they could not afford it [E]. Particularly in the South, farmers felt left out of the prosperity the rest of America was experiencing. Sharecroppers and Black farmers had it harder still, facing racial discrimination alongside economic problems. To conclude, while one section of American society enjoyed the growth of the Roaring Twenties, by the end of the 1920s half of American farmers were living below the poverty line [A].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of overproduction in agriculture in the USA in the 1920s
parts.solutionMd:
In the 1920s, while Americans in urban areas were experiencing prosperity in the so-called 'Roaring Twenties', the situation was deteriorating for people in rural areas. One of the reasons why farmers had to face a drop in their income was overproduction, which affected their economic, social and political life. Not only that, deep divisions between rural and urban America became visible [E].

Because of overproduction, crop prices started falling and farm incomes declined. During the First World War, Europe was purchasing food crops from America because its own territory was war-torn. Farmers in most European nations had been conscripted into the army, so very few people were available to work the land. In that situation America was the obvious solution [E]. This increased demand gave a huge boost to American food products. Many farmers saw an opportunity to make more money and started producing in abundance. Some even took loans to buy more land and modern equipment such as tractors. However, after 1918 the war came to an end and European agriculture started recovering. Farmers who had become soldiers returned to their land [A]. They no longer needed American food crops. American farmers, however, continued to produce more food than there was demand for. The natural result was a drastic drop in prices, with farm prices falling by around 50 per cent between 1919 and 1921.

Farmers who had taken loans could not repay their debts, resulting in a cycle of poverty and foreclosure. So, unlike urban industry, the agricultural sector could not benefit from the economic boom [A].

Another factor that added to farmers' grievances was that the government did not protect them. On the contrary, some tariff policies harmed them directly. While farmers were looking for buyers for their surplus, they lost prospective customers because of the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 [E]. This tariff raised import duties on manufactured goods from foreign nations. It was a protectionist measure designed to encourage American citizens to buy American products [A]. Many of the countries affected retaliated by imposing tariffs on American food exports. This reduced demand for American food further, and farmers could not find enough buyers [E]. On top of that, when bills that would have supported farmers were introduced, they were vetoed. The McNary-Haugen Bill to stabilise crop prices was vetoed twice by President Coolidge, who declared that farmers had never made much money. This exposed how little the government was willing to do for farmers compared with big business and industry [A].

Overproduction also brought out the social divisions in American society. While rural communities, especially in the South and Midwest, faced poverty, city people were enjoying consumerism, jazz and motor cars [E]. By the late 1920s half of American farmers were living below the poverty line. Sharecroppers and Black farmers were often trapped in debt and working for survival rather than profit. Crop prices remained low, so farmers earned barely enough to live on. This was in striking contrast to the glamorous image of urban America [A]. Many landless farmers were trapped in contracts with big landowners, and racism and segregation made the situation worse in the southern states [A]. Republican politicians who supported the idea of a traditional America, such as Harding, Coolidge and Hoover, became popular in this climate.

Finally, overproduction in agriculture exposed the weaknesses of the American economy. The purchasing power of millions of rural families was reduced, which in turn affected the domestic market for consumer goods [E]. Banks in rural areas were on the verge of collapse because of unpaid farm loans. These factors contributed to financial instability and eventually to the Wall Street Crash of 1929 and the Great Depression [A].

To conclude, overproduction in agriculture had severe and wide-ranging consequences. In the short term it led to falling prices, foreclosures and rural poverty; in the longer term it weakened the American economy and exposed its underlying fragility. Overproduction was arguably the most damaging feature of the 1920s, because it undermined both social stability and future economic growth [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the growth of new industries in the USA during the 1920s.
parts.solutionMd:
The industry at the centre of the 1920s boom was the motor car. Mass production made it affordable: Henry Ford's moving assembly line, first used for the Model T, meant that by the 1920s one car was being completed every ten seconds, and by 1929 there were around 23 million cars in the United States [R].

The importance of the car industry lay as much in what it pulled along behind it. Building cars required steel, glass, rubber and leather, and the firms supplying those materials expanded and took on new workers. Petrol was needed to run the vehicles, so the oil industry grew with them [R].

Construction boomed for two separate reasons. The new businesses of the decade needed offices, factories and showrooms to be built, and mass car ownership required a far larger road network than the country had possessed. American cities filled with skyscrapers, which became the visible symbol of post-war wealth [R].

The chemical industry produced entirely new products. Companies such as Dupont manufactured synthetic fabrics, including rayon, which proved highly popular with customers and took business away from the older cotton and woollen manufacturers [R].

Electricity transformed the home and created a large new consumer sector. In 1916 only 15 per cent of American homes had an electricity supply; by 1927 that had risen to 70 per cent. Americans bought the new electrical goods in enormous numbers, including refrigerators, vacuum cleaners and washing machines [R].

The fastest growth of all was in radio. In 1919 Americans owned around 60,000 sets; by 1929 that number had reached 10 million. Hundreds of radio stations came into existence, and companies sponsored programmes and bought advertising, which encouraged still more buying of consumer goods [R].

These industries reinforced one another. Mass production made goods cheap enough for ordinary families, advertising on the radio persuaded them to buy, and the profits funded further expansion. It should be remembered, however, that this growth was concentrated in the new sectors: the older industries of coal, textiles, shipbuilding and the railways were declining across the same decade, partly because of the very products that were making the new industries rich [R].
