parts.problemMd: How successful was Prohibition in the USA? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Prohibition was introduced with strong support from religious groups such as the Methodists and Baptists, who saw drinking as a sin, and from temperance campaigners such as the Anti-Saloon League and the Women's Christian Temperance Union, who blamed alcohol for poverty, crime and broken marriages [R]. This mattered because it shows prohibition responded to genuine, widely-shared concerns about the social harm alcohol was believed to cause [E].

Prohibition did reduce the overall amount of alcohol legally available and consumed compared with before 1920 [R]. For some Americans who supported the temperance movement, simply having such a law on the statute books at all was itself considered a genuine moral victory, whatever its practical effects turned out to be [E].

Bootlegging grew rapidly, and gangsters such as Al Capone became extremely rich and powerful by smuggling and distributing illegal alcohol, while corruption spread as bootleggers bribed police officers and judges to look the other way [R]. This mattered because every city in the USA developed serious problems with gang violence as a direct result [E].

By the early 1930s the government could no longer realistically afford to enforce the law, having already spent \$13.4 million on enforcement while losing out on around \$11 billion in potential tax revenue that could otherwise have been raised [R]. This mattered because the Great Depression's mass unemployment meant legalising alcohol production again offered a practical way to create jobs and much-needed tax revenue [E].

These two pictures fit together rather than contradicting each other [R]. Prohibition may have reduced overall alcohol consumption slightly, but it did so at the cost of creating a large, violent and deeply entrenched criminal industry that caused far greater harm to American society than the drinking it was meant to prevent [A].

On balance, prohibition was a clear failure. It is genuinely difficult to call a policy successful when it had to be repealed after only thirteen years, when it created the exact conditions for organised crime to flourish on a national scale, and when even the government itself eventually concluded that the costs of enforcing it clearly outweighed any benefit it might have brought. The repeal of the 18th Amendment by President Roosevelt in 1933 is itself the clearest evidence that prohibition had not achieved what it set out to do [A].

parts.problemMd:
Roosevelt had to deal with much opposition to the New Deal.

Describe how Roosevelt reacted to the Supreme Court decisions of 1935 and 1936 about the New Deal.
parts.solutionMd:
Roosevelt was furious, because these decisions put the New Deal and his plans to deal with the Depression under threat [1]. He was determined to protect the New Deal, so he decided to challenge the authority of the Supreme Court [1]. He accused the judges of being unaware of the needs of ordinary Americans and called them 'nine old men' [1]. He proposed that the number of Supreme Court judges should be increased from nine to fifteen [1].

parts.problemMd:
The New Deal did not end unemployment in the United States.

How did the Second World War help the American economy?
parts.solutionMd:
Factories that had been built to make cars were converted to produce thousands of planes, tanks and guns [1]. Farmers who had been unable to sell their crops suddenly faced a rapid rise in demand for food to feed the armed forces, and could also sell to countries such as Britain and the Soviet Union [1]. Coal and oil were needed in enormous quantities and the iron and steel industries boomed alongside them [1]. Booming industry and agriculture, combined with the numbers of men joining the armed forces, almost eliminated unemployment, which had fallen to just 670,000 by 1944 [1].

parts.problemMd:
The New Deal did not end unemployment in the United States.

Which did more to end the Depression: the New Deal or the Second World War? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The New Deal achieved a great deal [R]. When Roosevelt took office in 1933 there were 12.8 million Americans out of work, and by 1941 that had been cut to 5.6 million. That is more than seven million people back in work, and it was done through deliberate government action at a time when the previous administration had argued that government should stand back. It also changed what Americans expected of their government, and Roosevelt's re-election by a large margin in 1936 suggests that most voters thought it was working [E].

But it never finished the job [R]. Unemployment did not fall below ten per cent at any point during the 1930s, and 5.6 million people were still without work after eight years and enormous expense. The reasons were structural: many of the jobs created were short-term and insecure, improvements in manufacturing meant industry needed fewer workers, tariffs on American goods held back exports, and low wages meant people could not buy the consumer goods that would have kept factories open. That last point is the most damaging, because it shows the New Deal had not broken the cycle that caused the Depression, only softened it [E].

The war broke that cycle in a way the New Deal never had [R]. Car factories switched to producing planes, tanks and guns; farmers who could not sell their crops suddenly could not grow enough, supplying both the armed forces and countries such as Britain and the Soviet Union; and coal, oil, iron and steel all boomed. Add the millions of men taken into the armed forces and unemployment collapsed to 670,000 by 1944. The problem the New Deal had been unable to solve in eight years was gone in about three [E].

On the evidence, the Second World War did more [A]. The New Deal halved unemployment; the war effectively abolished it, and the figures make that difficult to argue with. But the comparison needs one qualification. The war worked because the government spent on an enormous scale and guaranteed demand, which is the New Deal's own approach applied without any limit on cost. In that sense the war did not disprove the New Deal so much as show what it might have achieved if Roosevelt had been willing, or politically able, to spend on the scale that only a war made acceptable [A].

parts.problemMd:
The New Deal was not popular with everybody.

Why did the US Supreme Court rule against parts of the New Deal?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason concerns the powers of the president [R]. The National Recovery Administration had set prices and wages across whole industries, but under the American constitution that authority belongs to Congress and not to the president. The Supreme Court's role is to check that each branch of government stays inside the powers the constitution gives it, and it judged that Roosevelt had taken on a job that was not his to do. It made no difference to the Court whether the policy was working; what mattered was who had the right to make it [E].

A second reason concerns the powers of the individual states [R]. The Agricultural Adjustment Administration had paid farmers not to grow food, and the Court ruled that agriculture was a matter for the state governments rather than for Washington. This was a problem the New Deal could hardly avoid, because its whole method was to attack national problems with national programmes, and doing so meant reaching into areas the states had always run for themselves. The more ambitious Roosevelt's response to the Depression became, the more likely it was to collide with the division of powers written into the constitution [E].

parts.problemMd: Why did Roosevelt do so much in the 'Hundred Days' of 1933?
parts.solutionMd:
The USA had still not recovered from the impact of the Great Depression, which is why Roosevelt decided to take urgent action after becoming President in 1933 [R]. During the first three months of his presidency he introduced a series of measures to tackle the situation. Many banks had collapsed and unemployment had risen to around 14 million by 1933. Roosevelt wanted to take concrete action to restore confidence in both the economy and his presidency. In his election campaign he had promised the American people a 'New Deal', and the Hundred Days let him prove he could deliver what he had promised [E].

Roosevelt also had the political support to pass a great many laws quickly, and through them he gave people hope that the government was finally taking responsibility. His predecessor, President Hoover, had been criticised for not doing enough to help the country recover [R]. With a Democratic majority in Congress, Roosevelt could pass legislation rapidly. Important measures such as the Emergency Banking Act, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration and the Civilian Conservation Corps were passed within weeks [E].

parts.problemMd: 'The main reason why there was opposition to the New Deal was because it interfered with business.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The New Deal received a mixed reaction in the 1930s. Some opposed it because they believed it interfered too much with business and free enterprise, while others opposed it because it did not go far enough to help American society recover from the Depression. In this essay, I will examine how the New Deal was opposed for a range of reasons, and interference in business was only a part of it [R].

Many businessmen and Republicans argued that Roosevelt was expanding government control and acting like a dictator. Rules on wages and working hours were set by agencies such as the National Recovery Administration, when businesses believed those decisions should be theirs [E]. They also argued that high taxes on the wealthy and on big companies were unfair, because investors would lose interest and economic recovery would slow. Many capitalists claimed the growth of the 1920s had come from the freedom businesses had been given [E]. Setting wages and hours by government agency struck them as close to communism. Opposition from business mattered because business was the most powerful group in the country [A].

On the other hand, a key reason people opposed the New Deal was that it did not go far enough, which is why Roosevelt had to introduce the Second New Deal [E]. Figures on the left such as Huey Long criticised it as too moderate, leaving too much wealth and power in the hands of the rich. Long's proposals for heavy taxation of the wealthy and guaranteed family incomes won mass support from people who felt the New Deal had done nothing for them. This opposition was arguably more consequential, because it could have destabilised the political system, and it was this pressure that produced the Second New Deal in 1935, with more fundamental reforms such as the Wagner Act, the Social Security Act and more aid for farmers and the poor [A].

Secondly, the cost of the New Deal caused real discontent among wealthy Americans and conservative politicians [A]. Roosevelt spent substantial government funds on public works and job creation, an approach known as deficit financing. Critics thought he was piling up government debt recklessly. Wealthy Americans and conservatives who favoured limited government disliked programmes they believed were funded by their own taxes. Roosevelt was accused of acting like a dictator, exceeding his powers and interfering in the free market. Groups such as the American Liberty League attacked the New Deal as a step towards socialism, and complained that the new alphabet agencies had created too much bureaucracy [A].

In conclusion, I do not agree that opposition to the New Deal was mainly due to its interference with business. That was one factor among several. The strongest opposition came from the belief that Roosevelt was going beyond his powers, from the cost of the programme, and from those who thought the reforms did not go far enough. Both the right and the left opposed the New Deal, and their reasons went well beyond business interests [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the measures taken by Roosevelt to help the unemployed.
parts.solutionMd:
Franklin D. Roosevelt became President of the USA in 1933, when it was grappling with the impacts of the Great Depression. His biggest challenge was to provide relief and jobs to 13 million unemployed people. The answer was his New Deal programmes [E].

He began with the First Hundred Days, in which he launched a range of emergency measures. He started by providing food, clothing and shelter for the unemployed through the Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA). This programme was run by Harry Hopkins. Under it, states received 500 million dollars from federal funds in an immediate attempt to relieve suffering [R].

His next step was to create public works programmes to provide jobs rather than just relief. The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was formed to recruit young, unemployed men to work on environmental projects. They planted trees, improved national parks and controlled soil erosion. Between 1933 and 1942, around 3 million men got jobs through the CCC [R].

In the winter of 1933 to 1934, Roosevelt set up the Civil Works Administration (CWA) to provide temporary jobs to about 4 million people. They were recruited to build schools, roads and airports. It was a well-judged programme that gave immediate relief to millions during a harsh winter [E].

Under the National Industrial Recovery Act, the Public Works Administration (PWA) was established to work on large-scale infrastructure projects. It created longer-term jobs and improved the nation's infrastructure by building dams, bridges and hospitals [E].

After 1935, Roosevelt introduced the Second New Deal, which created the Works Progress Administration (WPA). It was the largest employer of the New Deal, and it funded artists, writers and actors as well as public works projects [E].

Unemployment insurance was introduced in the USA with the Social Security Act of 1935, the first scheme of its kind in the country. It was limited in scope at first, but it became a structural reform providing longer-term protection for the unemployed [R].

Roosevelt therefore took measures to provide immediate relief as well as long-term reform [R]. Public confidence in the government was re-established and millions of people got jobs. However, it was not a complete success, because unemployment was never fully solved by the New Deal. It was the Second World War that created the jobs the programme could not [E].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the impact of the Second New Deal.
parts.solutionMd:
Roosevelt came out with the New Deal after becoming president of the USA. However, it was severely criticised. As a result, he launched the Second New Deal in 1935.

The focus of the Second New Deal was on economic recovery, social reform, political change and the role of government. However, just like the first New Deal, while it improved conditions for many groups in the short term, its effects in the long term were uneven [E].

The Social Security Act, introduced in 1935, aimed at strengthening social welfare. This act focused on old-age pensions, helping disabled and dependent children, and providing insurance for the unemployed [E]. Through this act, the federal government accepted responsibility for its citizens [E]. It was a turning point in establishing a strong bond between the government and the people, and it created a safety net that outlasted the Great Depression. However, it did not cover all sections of society: many groups, such as agricultural and domestic workers, were excluded [A].

The Works Progress Administration (WPA) became the largest employer in the USA, providing work for around two million people a year and for some 8.5 million in total across its lifetime. It covered projects in construction, infrastructure and even the arts [E]. It was not only providing jobs but also rebuilding America by constructing schools, hospitals and roads that benefited the country in the long term. It provided dignified work rather than relief or charity. However, it was criticised as costly, and unemployment still remained very high, only falling after the beginning of the Second World War [A].

Another significant aspect of the Second New Deal was labour rights. Workers gained the right to join trade unions through the Wagner Act of 1935. The National Labor Relations Board was established to protect workers from unfair practices by employers. This led to the growth of unions, whose membership increased from around 3 million in 1933 to 8 million by 1941 [E]. Because of these measures, workers could voice their concerns, gain greater protection and hold more bargaining power. However, the programme was also criticised, because many business leaders argued that the government was interfering too much in the free market. Trade unions were associated with communism, which fed American fears of a communist revolution [A].

Roosevelt also reformed the banking and utility sectors. The Federal Reserve Board gained more control over interest rates and the money supply through the Banking Act of 1935, which led to greater economic stability [E]. Farmers in rural areas benefited from electricity supply when the Rural Electrification Administration built the necessary infrastructure. This showed that Roosevelt was not limiting his projects to the cities but wanted modernisation in the countryside as well [A].

To conclude, Roosevelt's support base expanded through the Second New Deal, which was a huge political victory for him. He secured the loyalty of industrial workers, Black Americans and the poor by offering pensions, jobs and union rights. The Democrats dominated US politics for decades because of this 'Roosevelt Coalition'. However, his plans did not go unchallenged, and the Supreme Court struck down some reforms as unconstitutional. The Second New Deal was not especially successful at solving the Depression, but its impacts were far more significant in the long term [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the Second New Deal.
parts.solutionMd:
Roosevelt introduced the Second New Deal in 1935, and there were four reasons why the programme had to change. The Supreme Court had struck down parts of the first: it ruled that the National Recovery Administration had set prices and wages when only Congress could do so, and that the Agricultural Adjustment Administration had paid farmers not to grow food when that was a matter for state governments. Unemployment remained at 11 million in 1935. Business leaders complained that the programme was too expensive and interfered with their ability to trade. And a presidential election was due in 1936 [R].

The response to the Court was to replace what had been struck down. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 took the place of the NRA, encouraging workers to join trade unions and creating the National Labor Relations Board to protect their rights. Union membership passed eight million by the end of the decade, though the Republicans and many businessmen opposed the Act and some employers still refused to let their workers join. The Soil Conservation Act of 1935 replaced the AAA, subsidising farmers to plant grasses, trees or vegetables instead of crops, which tackled the soil erosion left by the Dust Bowl and reduced erosion by 65 per cent by 1939 [R].

The most far-reaching measure was the Social Security Act of 1935, which created a national welfare system providing old-age pensions, disability payments and unemployment payments, and supporting widows and orphans. This brought the United States into line with other Western countries, but the system had clear limits: pensions were only 85 dollars a month, it covered just a third of workers, and it excluded farmers and workers in private households [R].

Employment was tackled through the Works Progress Administration, which employed around two million workers a year and became the largest employer in the country. It created jobs across many professions, including acting, writing and photography, although a good deal of the work was temporary [R].

Later measures continued the pattern. The United States Housing Act of 1937 provided loans to help people buy houses, reduced rents and funded local agencies to clear or improve unsafe housing, though because the federal government left it to local authorities to decide how the money was spent, housing for Black Americans remained substandard in many areas. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 enforced a minimum wage, limited working hours and improved conditions, raising the pay of more than 700,000 workers and shortening the week for more than 1.5 million [R].

Not everything succeeded. The Resettlement Administration of 1935 set out to move 500,000 families to better land but managed to resettle only about 5,000, because many families either did not want to move or objected to where they were being sent [R].

> - The Social Security Act created the foundations of an American welfare state that long outlasted the Depression.

> - Structure the account as why it changed, then what it contained. That order makes the Supreme Court rulings do useful work rather than sitting as background.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the extent to which the New Deal solved the problem of unemployment in the USA.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is that the New Deal achieved a substantial and measurable reduction.** When Roosevelt took office in 1933 there were 12.8 million unemployed Americans; by 1941 that number had fallen to 5.6 million. The alphabet agencies created millions of jobs, the Works Progress Administration alone employed around two million workers a year and became the largest employer in the country, and the Tennessee Valley Authority created work while raising living standards in one of the poorest regions. Whatever else is said, several million people were working who would otherwise not have been [E].

**The second facet is that the problem was never actually solved.** Unemployment never fell below 10 per cent at any point during the 1930s, and 9.5 million Americans were still out of work in 1939, six years into the programme and after enormous expense. Much of the work created was short-term and insecure, and critics complained of boondoggle jobs invented for their own sake rather than because the work was needed [E].

**The third facet is that the deepest causes lay beyond the New Deal's reach.** Improvements in manufacturing meant industry needed fewer workers than before. The Depression itself meant fewer goods were bought, and tariffs on American goods depressed exports. Worst of all was the loop between wages and demand: because unemployment stayed high and wages stayed low, families had little disposable income, so sales of cars, radios, vacuum cleaners and refrigerators remained weak, so the firms that made them closed or cut staff, which pushed unemployment higher again. Job creation schemes treated the symptom while this cycle continued [E].

**The fourth facet is that the benefits were distributed unequally.** Skilled workers gained more than unskilled ones. The Civilian Conservation Corps took only young men; the WPA gave women mainly unskilled work, and the National Recovery Administration deliberately set women's wages below men's. Black Americans were paid less than white workers under the NRA and were placed in segregated CCC camps, and a third came to depend on government relief payments. Smaller farmers benefited little, and because the Agricultural Adjustment Administration paid farmers to grow less, many sharecroppers were pushed off the land and into the cities to look for work. For these groups the problem was not solved at all [E].

**The fifth facet is what actually ended mass unemployment.** The outbreak of war in 1939, and American entry in 1941, transformed the position. Factories built to make cars turned to producing planes, tanks and guns. Farmers who could not sell their crops suddenly faced heavy demand to feed the armed forces and could export to Britain and the Soviet Union. Coal, oil, iron and steel boomed, and millions joined the armed forces. By 1944 just 670,000 Americans were unemployed [E].

**Judgement.** The New Deal reduced unemployment substantially but did not solve it, and the war did what six years of policy had not [A]. That is the strongest single criticism available, because it suggests the New Deal never spent on the scale the crisis required. Yet the comparison also explains the failure: wartime spending was of an order no peacetime democracy would have accepted in 1935, and Roosevelt was already being attacked as too expensive and too interfering.

The fairer conclusion is that the question of solving unemployment is the wrong test of the New Deal [A]. Judged against it, the programme failed. Judged by whether it kept millions of people fed, housed and in work while the underlying economy remained broken, and by whether it created lasting institutions such as Social Security and the minimum wage, it succeeded considerably. The New Deal did not cure the disease, but it kept the patient alive until the war did [A].

> To help identify where credit will be awarded, the following codes have been used:
> 
> - Explanation - [E]
> - Analysis - [A]
> 
> The ladder is built around **facets**.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.
> - **6-10 marks:** attempts to address one or more facets but only by assertion. Relevant comments are undeveloped or implicit. May attempt a generalised judgement that is mostly asserted.
> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Listing the alphabet agencies. Naming the CCC, WPA and TVA is recall; each has to be tied to a claim about unemployment.
> - Concluding only that the war ended unemployment. It is true and it is essential, but on its own it is one facet and leaves the New Deal unassessed.
> - Treating all Americans alike. The evidence differs sharply for skilled and unskilled workers, for women, for Black Americans and for sharecroppers, and the best answers use that variation.
> - Confusing unemployment with poverty. Social Security and the minimum wage improved lives without necessarily creating jobs, and the distinction is worth making.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - Roosevelt won re-election by a large margin in 1936, which suggests that many Americans judged the programme a success at the time whatever the statistics showed.
> - The fireside chats restored public confidence in the banking system, which is a form of recovery not captured in unemployment figures.
> - The National Labor Relations Act pushed union membership above eight million, strengthening the position of those who did have work.
> - Roosevelt refused to support an anti-lynching bill because he needed the votes of southern Democrats, which shows the political limits on how far the New Deal could go for Black Americans.
> - Some critics argued the New Deal made people dependent on government support and undermined individual self-reliance.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Lead with the numbers and then interrogate them. From 12.8 million down to 5.6 million looks impressive until you add that unemployment never fell below 10 per cent.
> - The war is essential, but place it last and use it to test the New Deal rather than to replace your argument.
> - Break the workforce down. Showing that the answer differs for women, for Black Americans and for sharecroppers is a fast route to the top band.
> - Question the test itself. Arguing that solving unemployment is not the only fair measure of the New Deal, and then still answering the question asked, is exactly the kind of substantiated judgement Level 5 rewards.
> - Remember this debate is genuinely open. Historians still disagree, so a confident conclusion that acknowledges the other side will always read better than a one-sided verdict.

parts.problemMd:
Roosevelt introduced the New Deal immediately after becoming president in 1933.

What happened during Roosevelt's first Hundred Days in office?
parts.solutionMd:
Roosevelt closed all American banks for four days under the Emergency Banking Act, having their accounts inspected, which restored public confidence and encouraged people to reopen their accounts [1]. The Beer and Wine Revenue Act ended Prohibition for drinks with no more than 3.2% alcohol, stopping millions of dollars from going to criminals and raising tax revenue instead [1]. The Economy Act cut the wages of all government employees, including Roosevelt's own, by 15%, freeing up \$1 billion to help the unemployed [1]. Roosevelt also began broadcasting 'fireside chats' on the radio every Sunday, which more than 60 million Americans listened to [1].

parts.problemMd:
Not everyone in the USA supported the New Deal.

What criticisms did radical opponents make of the New Deal?
parts.solutionMd:
Senator Huey Long of Louisiana, a well-known radical politician, argued that the New Deal did not go far enough in helping ordinary struggling Americans [1]. He proposed that every single dollar a person owned over \$5 million should be confiscated directly by the government [1]. Long believed this confiscated money should then be redistributed fairly among ordinary American families right across the whole country [1]. He argued this radical scheme would raise more than enough money to give every single family in America a house, a radio and a car of their own [1].

parts.problemMd:
Not everyone in the USA supported the New Deal.

Why did Republican politicians oppose the New Deal?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that the New Deal went against core Republican beliefs. Republicans believed in a 'small government' that stayed out of ordinary people's lives, leaving them to succeed or fail on their own merits, and the New Deal represented the kind of large-scale, expensive government intervention that Republicans had traditionally opposed [R]. This mattered because it meant Republicans saw the New Deal as a fundamental attack on core American values, not merely as an ordinary disagreement over specific individual policies [E].

A second reason is that Republicans believed the New Deal would make Americans lazy and too dependent on government support. They feared it would encourage citizens to wait passively for government 'handouts' rather than working hard to support themselves [R]. This explains their opposition because it reflected a concern that the New Deal was undermining the self-reliance Republicans believed had made America successful in the first place, while also fearing that Roosevelt had overreached his presidential powers and was becoming unconstitutionally powerful [E].

parts.problemMd:
Not everyone in the USA supported the New Deal.

Why did wealthy Americans and business owners oppose the New Deal?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is direct taxation of the wealthy. The New Deal was an expensive programme of government spending, and to help pay for it, Roosevelt increased the amount of tax that wealthy Americans had to pay each year [R]. This mattered because wealthy Americans resented seeing their own hard-earned money spent on projects such as planting trees or giving support to homeless people, since they felt they were being made to pay for other people's problems [E].

A second, related reason is direct government interference in how private businesses were run. The National Recovery Administration forced business leaders across the country to improve working conditions, pay a legal minimum wage and set firm limits on the hours employees could work each week [R]. This explains business opposition because many business leaders, who were often Republican supporters themselves, believed these rules directly reduced how much profit they could make and how competitively they could run their companies [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Write an account of the opposition to the New Deal from the political right.
parts.solutionMd:
Although Roosevelt had been elected in a landslide victory in 1932, winning around 7 million more votes overall than Hoover, his subsequent New Deal quickly attracted fierce opposition from several distinct groups within American society, particularly from across the political right [R].

Republican politicians opposed the New Deal because it directly contradicted several core Republican political beliefs [R]. Republicans had traditionally supported 'small government' that stayed well out of ordinary people's private lives, allowing individuals to succeed or fail through their own personal efforts and merits [D]. They believed the New Deal would make Americans lazy and encourage citizens to wait passively for government 'handouts' rather than working hard to support themselves and their families, and many senior Republican politicians also believed that Roosevelt had overreached his constitutional presidential powers and was becoming unaccountably powerful within the federal government [D].

Wealthy Americans opposed the New Deal specifically because of its financial cost to them personally [R]. The whole programme was expensive to run, and to help pay for it, Roosevelt increased the amount of income tax that wealthy Americans were legally required to pay each year [D]. Many wealthy Americans resented seeing their own hard-earned money used to fund government projects such as planting trees in national parks or providing direct support to the homeless, since they felt they were being made to pay disproportionately for social problems they did not personally consider to be their own responsibility to solve [D].

Business leaders across many different industries, many of whom were themselves committed Republican supporters, opposed the New Deal because of direct government interference in how they were permitted to run their own private companies [R]. The National Recovery Administration forced businesses across many industries to improve working conditions, pay a legally mandated minimum wage, and set firm legal limits on the working hours employees could be required to work in any given week [D]. Business leaders believed these new requirements directly reduced how much overall profit they could make and how competitively they could operate against both domestic and international rivals in the same industries [D].

These three groups often overlapped in practice, since wealthy business owners were frequently also committed Republican supporters themselves, meaning their separate objections to increased taxation, industry regulation and 'big government' generally reinforced one another rather than remaining unconnected complaints [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Write an account of Roosevelt's first Hundred Days in office.
parts.solutionMd:
When Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated as president in January 1933, he faced an economic crisis so severe, with millions of Americans unemployed and thousands of banks having already failed, that he began introducing his New Deal to the American people almost immediately after taking office [R]. His policies were built around three key aims, often remembered as the 'three Rs' [R]. The first was relief, meaning providing food for people in need and implementing policies that stopped people losing their homes [D]. The second was recovery, meaning boosting the wider economy so that jobs existed for the unemployed and rebuilding both trade and industry across the country [D]. The third was reform, meaning creating a welfare state in the USA that ensured ordinary people had access to government help for unemployment, sickness, disability and old age [D]. The wide-ranging changes achieved in these early weeks of his presidency became widely known afterwards, and remain known today, as the Hundred Days [R].

One of his first actions was the Emergency Banking Act, which closed all American banks for four days while their individual accounts were inspected by government officials [R]. This decisive action restored public confidence in the wider banking system, encouraging ordinary people to reopen accounts they had emptied in panic, and it increased the money banks had available to lend to struggling businesses, since the federal government now formally backed their loans [D].

The Beer and Wine Revenue Act effectively ended Prohibition for drinks containing no more than 3.2% alcohol, well before Prohibition was formally repealed nationwide [R]. Since millions of ordinary Americans had already been openly breaking Prohibition for years, this reduced widespread law-breaking almost immediately, stopped millions of dollars from flowing to organised criminals, and raised valuable new tax revenue for the government instead [D].

The Economy Act cut the wages of all federal government employees, including Roosevelt's own presidential salary, by a full 15% [R]. While this measure created real hardship and resentment for many individual government workers, it freed up around \$1 billion that could then be redirected to help the millions of ordinary Americans who remained unemployed [D].

Roosevelt also began broadcasting his policies directly to the American people through informal radio 'fireside chats', speaking calmly and directly to the whole nation on a regular basis [R]. More than 60 million Americans are estimated to have listened to these broadcasts, a revolutionary approach to presidential communication at the time, which helped build lasting public trust and support for his wider programme of reform [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Discuss the reasons why different groups opposed the New Deal.
parts.solutionMd:
Although President Roosevelt won the 1932 election in a sweeping landslide, carrying 42 of the 48 states in total, his subsequent New Deal soon faced fierce opposition from different groups across American society, spanning the political spectrum from far right to far left [R].

The first facet, and perhaps the most institutionally powerful, is organised Republican political opposition. Republicans believed fundamentally in 'small government' that stayed well out of ordinary people's private lives, leaving individuals to succeed or fail through their own personal efforts, and they saw the New Deal as a direct attack on this long-held political principle [R]. They believed it would make Americans lazy and encourage passive dependence on government 'handouts' rather than self-reliance, and many senior Republicans also believed Roosevelt had overreached his presidential powers, becoming unconstitutionally powerful within the federal government [E].

The second facet, closely related to the first, is opposition from wealthy Americans specifically, driven primarily by increased taxation [R]. The New Deal was an expensive government programme to fund, and Roosevelt increased income taxes on wealthy Americans to help pay for it [R]. Many wealthy people resented seeing their own hard-earned money spent on government projects such as planting trees in national parks or providing direct support to the homeless, believing they were being unfairly made to fund social problems they did not personally consider to be their own responsibility to solve [E].

The third facet, more directly economic in character, is opposition from business leaders across many industries, driven by direct government interference in how their companies were permitted to operate [R]. The National Recovery Administration forced businesses to improve working conditions, pay a legally mandated minimum wage and limit working hours, and business leaders, many of whom were themselves committed Republican supporters, believed these new regulations directly reduced both their profits and their competitiveness against rivals at home and abroad [E].

The fourth and final facet is radical opposition from the opposite end of the political spectrum, led most prominently by Senator Huey Long of Louisiana [R]. Long argued the New Deal did not go nearly far enough in helping ordinary struggling Americans, proposing instead that any personal wealth over \$5 million should be confiscated by the government and redistributed fairly so that every American family could have a house, a radio and a car of their own [R]. This radical proposal appealed to millions of poorer Americans across the country who felt Roosevelt's own reforms had not gone far enough to help them [E].

These four facets are closely linked, despite emerging from opposite ends of the political spectrum. Republicans, wealthy Americans and business leaders all objected because they believed the New Deal went too far in expanding government power, spending and interference, while radicals such as Long objected for the opposite reason, that it did not go nearly far enough, meaning Roosevelt found himself paradoxically attacked from all directions for being both too radical and not radical enough by different sections of American society at the same time [A].

On balance, having weighed all four facets against one another, opposition from the political right, combining Republicans, wealthy Americans and business leaders together, was the more lasting threat to the New Deal as a whole [A]. These groups collectively held institutional power through Congress, the federal courts and their control over investment and employment across the country, giving their sustained opposition practical force that persisted throughout Roosevelt's lengthy presidency [A]. Huey Long's radical challenge was popular and concerning to Roosevelt at the time, but it was abruptly cut short by Long's assassination in September 1935, whereas organised, well-funded and institutionally embedded opposition from across the political right continued to constrain the New Deal for many years afterwards, right through to the end of Roosevelt's long presidency [A].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Discuss the reasons why unemployment remained high throughout the 1930s despite the New Deal.
parts.solutionMd:
Despite the huge overall scale, cost and ambition of Roosevelt's New Deal programme, unemployment in the USA never fell below 10% throughout the 1930s, falling only from 12.8 million unemployed Americans in 1933 to still 5.6 million by 1941, an improvement but nowhere near a full recovery [R].

The first facet, and perhaps the single most immediately visible, is that many New Deal jobs were deliberately designed to be short-term and insecure rather than permanent employment [R]. Schemes such as the Civil Works Administration created around four million individual jobs specifically intended to last only a single winter season, sometimes on so-called 'boondoggles', deliberately pointless tasks invented in order to justify paying out wages, and once these temporary schemes ended, the workers who had been employed became unemployed again almost immediately [R]. This meant that the headline New Deal job-creation figures the government publicised often masked a much less stable underlying economic reality, since many of the jobs created did not represent a lasting solution to the country's unemployment problem [E].

The second facet, more structural in nature, is that ongoing improvements in manufacturing efficiency meant that fewer individual workers were needed even as overall industrial production gradually recovered across the decade [R]. As factories across the country steadily adopted more efficient methods and modern machinery, they could produce the same or even greater overall output with far fewer individual employees than they had needed before, meaning that overall economic recovery alone did not automatically translate into falling unemployment figures in quite the way earlier generations of Americans might reasonably have expected it to [E].

The third facet, and arguably the most fundamental of all, is persistently weak consumer spending across the whole of American society [R]. Unemployment remained stubbornly high and wages generally remained low throughout the whole decade, meaning many ordinary American workers and their families lacked the disposable income needed to purchase consumer goods such as cars, radios and refrigerators [E]. This reduced consumer demand in turn caused further business closures among the companies that manufactured these consumer goods, creating a self-reinforcing economic cycle in which weak spending directly caused further unemployment, and that resulting unemployment then caused weaker consumer spending, in an ongoing and difficult-to-break downward economic spiral [A].

The fourth and final facet is the continuing damage caused by existing tariffs on American goods, which limited valuable export markets abroad and reduced overseas demand for American-made products, adding a further external economic constraint on top of the already weak domestic demand that was limiting lasting economic recovery within the USA itself [E].

Far from operating as separate, unrelated economic problems, these four facets reinforced each other. Short-term, insecure jobs failed to build the lasting consumer confidence and steady income needed to sustain regular spending, manufacturing efficiency meant that whatever consumer demand did exist required fewer workers to satisfy it, and weak export markets meant American industry could not compensate for weak domestic demand by selling its surplus abroad instead, so each individual problem worsened all of the others rather than existing in isolation from one another [A].

On balance, and having weighed all four of these facets against one another, weak consumer spending was the most fundamental of these interconnected economic problems, because it explains why the New Deal's various job-creation schemes never quite produced a self-sustaining economic recovery on their own [A]. It was ultimately not any specific New Deal policy or agency but the different circumstances of the Second World War, with its huge and sudden demand for weapons, food, raw materials and military manpower, that finally eliminated almost all American unemployment by the mid-1940s, falling to a low 670,000 unemployed Americans by 1944, showing that the New Deal alone, for all its cost and ambition, had never fully solved the underlying economic problem it had originally been designed to fix [A].

parts.problemMd: 'Weak consumer spending was the main reason unemployment remained high in the 1930s.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Unemployment stayed high and wages remained low throughout the 1930s, meaning many American workers did not have the disposable income to buy consumer goods such as cars, radios and refrigerators [R]. This mattered because demand for these goods stayed weak throughout the decade almost regardless of how many jobs the New Deal itself created elsewhere [E].

Low sales of these goods then forced many of the businesses that made them to close down or lay off workers [R]. This created a self-reinforcing cycle, since each fresh round of business closures further reduced spending power across the whole economy, which explains why weak consumer demand was never something the New Deal's relief spending alone could fix [E].

Many New Deal jobs were themselves short-term rather than permanent, and improvements in manufacturing meant fewer workers were needed even once production recovered [R]. This mattered because it meant job creation schemes rarely turned into lasting employment, so unemployment kept rising back up whenever a relief scheme wound down [E].

Tariffs on American goods also continued to damage export markets throughout the decade [R]. This explains why unemployment never fell below 10% during the 1930s, since American manufacturers lost overseas customers who might otherwise have bought their goods and supported permanent jobs [E].

The two factors reinforced each other closely rather than operating as separate problems. Short-term jobs meant workers could never build up the confidence or income to spend consistently, which kept overall consumer demand weak and gave businesses little reason to hire staff on a permanent basis [A].

On balance, this is true to a large extent: weak consumer spending was the more fundamental problem, because it explains why the New Deal's various job creation schemes never quite produced a lasting economic recovery on their own. Even when the government created millions of jobs directly, as long as ordinary Americans lacked the confidence and income to spend on consumer goods, the wider economy could not generate the kind of self-sustaining growth that would have brought unemployment down, which is precisely why it took the different circumstances of the Second World War, with its enormous demand for weapons and workers, to finally solve the problem after 1939 [A].

parts.problemMd: Which posed a greater threat to the New Deal: opposition from the Republican right or opposition from radicals such as Huey Long? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Republicans believed in 'small government' that stayed out of ordinary people's lives, feared the New Deal would make Americans lazy and too dependent on government handouts, and many believed Roosevelt had overreached his presidential powers [R]. This mattered because it reflected deep ideological opposition across the whole Republican Party [E].

Republicans backed these objections with institutional power: wealthy Americans resented the higher taxes funding the New Deal, business leaders opposed National Recovery Administration rules forcing them to pay a minimum wage and limit working hours, and the Supreme Court itself ruled that parts of the New Deal, such as the NRA, were unconstitutional [R]. This mattered because Republicans could turn these objections into obstruction in Congress and rulings in the courts, giving their opposition practical force over many years [E].

Radical opposition, led by figures such as Huey Long, argued the New Deal did not go far enough, proposing that any wealth over \$5 million should be confiscated and redistributed so every family could have a house, a radio and a car [R]. This mattered because it was a radical alternative that went far beyond anything Roosevelt himself was prepared to do [E].

This appealed directly to millions of struggling Americans who felt the New Deal had not gone nearly far enough to help them [R]. This explains the seriousness of the radical threat, since it risked drawing away Roosevelt's crucial working-class support, the voters who had originally elected him [E].

The two threats therefore pulled Roosevelt's presidency in opposite political directions at the same time. Satisfying Republican demands to reduce government intervention risked losing the poorer voters attracted by radicals like Long, while adopting radical policies of the kind Long proposed would have confirmed every fear Republicans already held about Roosevelt's dangerous use of presidential power [A].

On balance, the Republican right posed the greater threat, because it controlled institutional power through Congress and the courts, giving it the practical ability to block or weaken New Deal legislation. Huey Long's radical movement was popular, but he lacked comparable institutional power, and his influence was cut short by his assassination in 1935, whereas organised Republican opposition persisted as a coordinated political force throughout the whole of Roosevelt's lengthy presidency [A].

name: What were the Causes & Consequences of the Wall Street Crash?

parts.problemMd:
Hoover tried several measures to deal with the Depression.

What was the Smoot-Hawley tariff?
parts.solutionMd:
The Smoot-Hawley tariff was a tax introduced by Hoover's government that raised the price of goods imported into the United States [1]. Its purpose was to make foreign goods more expensive so that Americans would buy US-made products instead, protecting American jobs [1]. It did not work as intended, because other countries responded by placing their own tariffs on American goods [1]. As a result US exports collapsed and many American companies went out of business [1].

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - 1 mark for each relevant point - [1]

> 
> - Confusing a tariff with a tax on American citizens. A tariff is charged on imported goods, not on incomes or wages.
> - Listing Hoover's other measures, such as the tax cut or the road-building programme. They are creditable elsewhere but do not answer this question.
> - Writing only that it 'made things worse' without saying how. The retaliation and the collapse in exports are what earn the marks.
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> - It was one of a series of measures Hoover introduced between 1930 and 1932, alongside a tax cut of 130 million dollars and a road- and dam-building programme.
> - It is often judged to have deepened the Depression rather than eased it, because it damaged world trade at the worst possible moment.
> - Hoover's willingness to use tariffs sits oddly with his belief in rugged individualism and minimal government interference, since it was direct government intervention in the economy.

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash changed life across the United States.

Why did Hoovervilles appear in American cities?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that enormous numbers of people lost their homes [R]. As businesses closed, unemployment rose from three per cent in 1929 to twenty-five per cent by 1933, and by 1932 more than 250,000 Americans were unable to keep up their mortgage payments. Banks repossessed those houses and landlords evicted tenants who could not pay rent. Even people who kept their jobs were squeezed, because employers cut wages and lengthened hours knowing that anyone who refused could be replaced instantly. The result was a large population with nowhere to live [E].

A second reason is that there was nothing to catch them when they fell [R]. The United States had no system of social security in the 1920s, and the Republican government took the view that unemployed people should solve their own problems. Charities and local governments tried to fill the gap, but demand was so heavy that some state governments went bankrupt and could not even pay their teachers. With no state housing and no unemployment benefit, homeless families had no option but to build shelters from whatever they could find on waste ground. These settlements were nicknamed Hoovervilles as a deliberate attack on the president whose government had left people to fend for themselves [E].

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash changed life across the United States.

Which suffered more in the Depression: people in the cities or people in the countryside? Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The cities were hit very hard [R]. Unemployment rose from three per cent in 1929 to twenty-five per cent by 1933 as businesses closed, and with no social security system the unemployed were expected to look after themselves. By 1932 over 250,000 Americans could not meet their mortgage payments and were repossessed, while tenants who fell behind were evicted. The Hoovervilles that grew up on waste ground were the visible result. Even those still in work were squeezed, because employers cut wages and raised hours knowing that anyone who objected could be replaced [E].

The countryside, though, was suffering before the Crash and suffered longer afterwards [R]. Agriculture had never shared in the 1920s boom, and many farmers had already borrowed heavily to buy machinery. When food prices fell and interest rates rose between 1929 and 1933, those loans became unpayable and 750,000 farms were repossessed by the banks. On top of that came the Dust Bowl: overcultivation had stripped the soil, and from 1930 drought and high winds blew the topsoil off millions of acres of the Great Plains [E].

What happened next shows the difference [R]. A city family that lost its home stayed in the city and queued at a soup kitchen. A farming family that lost its land often lost its livelihood entirely and took to the road, heading for the citrus farms of California, where they were housed in overcrowded, unhygienic camps and resented by local labourers who believed the migrants were taking their jobs [E].

On balance the countryside suffered more [A]. Both groups faced unemployment and homelessness, but rural Americans faced them on top of an agricultural depression that pre-dated 1929 and an environmental disaster that no policy could reverse. A factory can reopen when demand returns; land whose topsoil has blown away cannot. And the rural poor had to migrate to find any work at all, which cost them their communities as well as their homes.

One group cuts across the comparison [A]. Black sharecroppers in the South were made redundant first when food prices fell, then travelled to Chicago and New York only to find few jobs and open racial discrimination, so they experienced the worst of both. That is a reminder that the sharpest divisions in the Depression were not only geographical [A].

parts.problemMd: Write an account of the Bonus Marchers.
parts.solutionMd:
By 1932 the United States was three years into the Depression, and President Hoover's response had already made him unpopular. He had believed at first that the government should not intervene and that rugged individualism would carry the country through, and in January 1930 he had told Americans that the worst had passed. It had not, and by 1932 millions were destitute [R].

Among them were veterans of the First World War. Congress had granted them a war pension, known as a bonus, but it was not due to be paid until 1945. With no work and no money, a group of around 25,000 veterans asked for their bonus to be paid immediately instead [R].

When the request was refused, they took their case to the government in person. In March 1932 they marched on Washington DC and built a Hooverville directly outside the White House, so that the president could not avoid seeing them. The name itself was a deliberate protest, since the shanty towns of the Depression had been named after Hoover as a mark of blame [R].

Hoover decided to remove them by force. The Army was sent in and used tear gas and tanks against the encampment. Two protestors and a baby were killed and more than a thousand people were injured [R].

The reaction across the country was one of shock. American society treated veterans with the utmost respect for their service, and the sight of the Army being used against men who had fought for their country was widely seen as proof that Hoover neither understood nor cared about ordinary Americans in distress. It confirmed the impression that a president who would not help the unemployed was willing to use force against them [R].

The timing made the damage worse, because 1932 was an election year. The episode hardened public determination to vote Hoover out, and in November he lost to Franklin D. Roosevelt in the largest landslide in American history, taking six states to Roosevelt's forty-two. The Bonus Marchers had not obtained their bonus, but they had helped bring down a president [R].

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of President Hoover's response to the Depression.
parts.solutionMd:
**The first facet is the initial inaction, and it is the most damaging.** Hoover believed it was wrong for government to intervene, holding that self-reliance, or rugged individualism, would carry the country through. In January 1930 he told the American people that the worst had passed. It had not, and the months in which he waited were the months in which unemployment, homelessness and bank failures accelerated. The importance of this is that it fixed an impression of a president who had misread the crisis, and no later measure ever shifted it [E].

**The second facet is that he did eventually act, which complicates the usual picture.** Between 1930 and 1932 Hoover cut taxes by 130 million dollars so that people kept more of what they earned, launched a road- and dam-building programme to employ construction workers, and made 300 million dollars available to help the unemployed. These were real interventions, and some of them anticipated what Roosevelt would later do on a far larger scale. The claim that Hoover did nothing is therefore not accurate; the fairer criticism is that he did too little, too late, and without conviction [E].

**The third facet is that one of his measures made the Depression worse.** The Smoot-Hawley Tariff raised the price of foreign imports in order to push Americans towards home-produced goods. Other countries retaliated with tariffs of their own, American exports collapsed, and companies that depended on overseas markets went out of business. This is the most consequential thing Hoover actually did, and its effect was to deepen the very crisis it was meant to relieve [E].

**The fourth facet is the Bonus Marchers, where his response destroyed him politically.** Around 25,000 First World War veterans camped outside the White House in March 1932 asking for a pension already promised to them for 1945. Hoover had the Army remove them with tear gas and tanks, and two protestors and a baby were killed with more than a thousand injured. In a society that treated veterans with particular respect, this was taken as proof that the president neither understood nor cared about American suffering [E].

**The fifth facet is what his response made possible.** In November 1932 Roosevelt won the largest landslide in American history, taking 42 states to Hoover's six with eight million more votes, on a promise of a New Deal for the forgotten man [E].

**Judgement.** Hoover's response mattered less for its effect on the economy than for its effect on what Americans expected of their government [A]. Measured purely in economic terms, the most important single element was Smoot-Hawley, because it did identifiable harm; the tax cut and the public works were too small to register against a downturn of that scale. But the lasting importance is political. Hoover's failure discredited the idea that the federal government should stand back from economic crisis, and it did so thoroughly enough that a candidate promising the opposite could sweep the country.

A qualification is needed, however [A]. The Depression was a worldwide collapse whose causes lay well beyond any president's reach, and it is doubtful that even an energetic response in 1930 could have prevented it. Hoover's real failure was one of judgement and tone rather than of economics alone: he misread how bad things were, said so publicly, and then used force against the people worst affected. That is why his response is remembered as the point at which one American political tradition lost its authority and another replaced it [A].

> - **21-25 marks:** presents more than one facet, with well-supported explanations in support of more than one facet, and reaches a clear, convincing and substantiated judgement on relative importance.
> - **16-20 marks:** presents more than one facet, with explanations that support the facets presented. May attempt a judgement that is only partially supported.
> - **11-15 marks:** presents one or more facets, but the explanation supports only one facet. May attempt a judgement that is unsupported.

> - **1-5 marks:** general knowledge of the topic, describing or identifying some points with limited focus. No attempt at judgement, or a very general and undeveloped one.
> - **0 marks:** no creditable material.
>

> 
> Common errors which prevent an answer from achieving 21-25 marks include:
> 
> - Claiming Hoover did nothing. He cut taxes, funded public works and released 300 million dollars for relief, and an answer that ignores this is factually wrong as well as one-sided.
> - Writing about the New Deal. Roosevelt's programme is what came next; this question stops at 1932.
> - Explaining the causes of the Wall Street Crash. The question is about the response to the Depression, not its origins.
> - Ending with the claim that Hoover 'was a bad president'. That is an assertion; the marks come from ranking his failures against one another and saying which mattered most.
> 
> **Alternative content**

> - His own history as a self-made millionaire made him hard for ordinary Americans to relate to, especially beside Roosevelt, who had been disabled by polio at 39.

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash of 1929 was caused partly by speculation.

What does speculation mean?
parts.solutionMd:
Speculation is when a person buys something, such as shares, with the hope that its value will increase so that it can be sold later for a profit [1]. Share prices had boomed for most of the 1920s, and many people, including working-class Americans, joined in buying shares hoping to get rich quickly [1]. Many purchased shares 'on the margin', meaning they paid only around 10% of the price themselves and borrowed the rest, expecting the shares to rise in value before the debt had to be repaid [1]. This was extremely risky, because if share prices fell instead of rising, buyers could be left in serious financial trouble [1].

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash began in October 1929.

What happened on Black Thursday, 24 October 1929?
parts.solutionMd:
On 24 October 1929, known afterwards as Black Thursday, around 13 million shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange in a single day [1]. Nearly all companies saw the value of their shares collapse suddenly on this one day [1]. Panic had built up among investors who feared the American economy was slowing down, and a trickle of people selling their shares quickly turned into a flood [1]. Many of those selling were investors who had bought shares 'on the margin' with borrowed money, and they were now forced to sell quickly because they could not afford to keep the loans if share prices kept falling [1].

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash had a serious impact on the American economy.

What impact did the Wall Street Crash have on American banks?
parts.solutionMd:
Many banks had lent money to investors so that they could buy shares 'on the margin', and once share prices suddenly collapsed these investors could no longer repay the loans they owed [1]. As a result, 659 American banks went bankrupt in 1929 alone [1]. Millions of ordinary Americans had their entire life savings held in these banks, and when the banks disappeared, their savings disappeared with them completely [1]. Fear of further collapses caused many other savers across the country to rush to withdraw their money, which made the crisis for the entire banking system even worse [1].

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash of 1929 was caused partly by speculation.

Why did share prices crash in October 1929?
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that speculation had pushed share prices far beyond what the American economy could actually support. Many Americans, including working-class investors, bought shares 'on the margin', paying only around 10% upfront and borrowing the rest, betting that prices would keep rising [R]. This mattered because once investors began to doubt the economy's underlying strength, they rushed to sell before their shares became worthless, and a small trickle of selling quickly turned into a full-scale panic that fed on itself across the whole stock market [E].

A second reason is underlying weaknesses in the American economy itself. Factories had been mass-producing more consumer goods than there were customers able to buy them, wealth was distributed very unevenly across American society, and exports were weak, partly because of tariffs [R]. This explains the crash because these underlying problems meant company profits were already under real pressure well before October 1929, giving cautious investors genuine grounds to lose confidence once they started paying closer attention to the actual economy rather than simply rising share prices [E].

parts.problemMd:
The Wall Street Crash had a serious impact on the American economy.

Why did so many American businesses go bankrupt after the Wall Street Crash?
parts.solutionMd:
One important reason is the sudden collapse in consumer demand across the country. Once the Crash wiped out the savings and confidence of millions of Americans, far fewer people had money to spend on goods, so businesses saw their sales fall sharply [R]. This mattered because industrial production fell by 45% by 1932, and car production, one of the leading industries at the centre of the whole 1920s boom, fell by an even sharper 80% over the same period, showing just how quickly and completely consumer demand collapsed across the country [E].

A second reason is the collapse of the banking system that businesses depended on. As more and more banks failed, they could no longer offer struggling businesses the loans and credit they needed to keep operating normally, pay their workers or purchase essential raw materials [R]. This explains the wave of bankruptcies because over 100,000 American businesses went bankrupt between 1929 and 1932 alone, many of them entirely unable to survive once their usual access to bank credit simply disappeared overnight [E].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Write an account of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
parts.solutionMd:
Speculation on the stock market became extremely popular and widespread across America during the 1920s [R]. Share prices had boomed almost continuously for most of the decade, and many Americans, including large numbers of working-class people who had never invested in shares before, began buying them enthusiastically in the hope of getting rich quickly [D]. Many bought shares 'on the margin', paying only around 10% of the actual price themselves and borrowing the rest from banks or brokers, confidently expecting share prices to keep rising indefinitely before the debt they had taken on ever had to be repaid in full, a widely shared assumption that had held true for most of the preceding years [D].

Beneath this widespread speculation, however, the underlying American economy was showing real signs of genuine weakness by 1929 [R]. Factories had been mass-producing far more consumer goods than there were customers actually able to buy them, wealth was distributed very unevenly across American society, and American exports remained relatively weak throughout the period, partly because of tariff barriers [D]. Some more cautious and observant investors began to notice these underlying structural problems within the wider economy and started quietly selling their shares rather than continuing to buy still more of them at inflated prices [D].

What began as a small trickle of cautious selling soon turned into an overwhelming flood as genuine panic spread rapidly among investors who suddenly feared losing everything they had invested [D]. On 24 October 1929, remembered afterwards as Black Thursday, around 13 million shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange in a single day of frantic trading, and nearly all companies listed on the exchange saw the value of their shares collapse dramatically within just a few hours [R].

Share prices continued to fall sharply in the days that immediately followed, with around 16 million shares sold on 29 October alone, a day that became known as Black Tuesday [R]. Many of those who had bought shares 'on the margin' with borrowed money were now completely unable to repay their loans, because the shares they held as security had suddenly become almost entirely worthless overnight [D].

The wider consequences spread rapidly and devastatingly beyond the stock market itself. As unpaid loans mounted rapidly across the financial system, 659 American banks collapsed entirely before the end of 1929 alone [R]. Millions of ordinary Americans who had trusted their hard-earned savings to these banks lost that money completely and permanently when the banks failed, causing severe and lasting financial ruin for many thousands of ordinary families across the country, and forcing the closure of still more American businesses that had depended entirely on those failed banks for the essential credit they needed simply to keep operating [D].

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Write an account of the impact of the Wall Street Crash on the American economy.
parts.solutionMd:
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 had an immediate, devastating and far-reaching knock-on effect right across the entire American economy in the years that immediately followed, touching businesses, banks, farmers and ordinary workers alike [R]. Businesses across the country suffered immediately and severely, as share prices continued falling for a full three years afterwards [R]. Industrial production across the USA had fallen by a striking 45% by 1932, car production, one of the great symbols of the 1920s boom, had fallen by an even more dramatic 80%, and over 100,000 American businesses went bankrupt entirely between 1929 and 1932 [R].

The banking industry was hit especially and immediately hard. Many banks had lent heavily to investors buying shares 'on the margin' in the years before the Crash, and once those loans could no longer be repaid, banks across the country began to fail in very large numbers [R]. Fearful savers then rushed in panic to withdraw their remaining money before their own local bank collapsed too, which only deepened the wider crisis further still, and the surviving banks in turn became far more unwilling to lend to already struggling businesses that badly needed the credit simply to survive month to month, deepening the wider slowdown still further [D].

Agriculture, which had never actually shared in the wider prosperity of the 1920s boom in the first place, was hit extremely hard by the Crash as well [D]. Food prices fell sharply after the Crash, and American farmers continued to struggle selling to overseas markets because of tariffs [R]. Interest rates then increased noticeably between 1929 and 1932, making existing loan repayments for already struggling farmers even more expensive at exactly the wrong possible moment, and around 750,000 farming families ultimately lost their land altogether as a direct and painful result of these several combined pressures acting together at once [R].

The impact on ordinary workers across the country was severe, sustained and genuinely widespread. The closure of so many American businesses caused a massive and rapid rise in unemployment, eventually reaching around one in four Americans, roughly 14 million people in total, by 1933 [R]. With absolutely no welfare or unemployment benefits of any kind available at the time, many people were evicted from their rented homes, or had them repossessed by the banks, simply because they could no longer afford to keep up with their rent or their monthly mortgage payments [D]. The impacts of the Depression were not felt equally across every state, which is part of why so many unemployed workers travelled from state to state searching for work and became known as 'hobos', while falling demand for coal, as factories needed less power and heating, forced many mines to close and cost still more miners their jobs [D].

**[15 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Depth study D: The USA 1919–1941**

Write an account of the 1932 presidential election.
parts.solutionMd:
By 1932 President Hoover had become deeply and widely unpopular across the whole of the United States after three long years of continuous Depression [R]. He had initially and firmly believed that the government should not intervene directly in the economy, trusting that 'rugged individualism' would allow ordinary Americans to solve their own problems without federal help, and in January 1930 he had wrongly and rather notoriously declared to the nation that the worst of the crisis had already passed [D]. Between 1930 and 1932 he did eventually introduce some genuine measures, including a \$130 million tax cut and a large road- and dam-building programme, alongside \$300 million for the unemployed, but these came too late and were too limited to change the public's growing negative impression of his presidency as a whole [R]. His subsequent use of the US Army against the Bonus Marchers in 1932, in which two protestors and a baby were tragically killed, further and severely damaged his reputation among a public that had always deeply respected its military veterans for their wartime service and sacrifice, and it made him look willing to use force against the very citizens he was meant to serve [R].

Hoover's chief opponent in the 1932 presidential election was the Democratic Party candidate Franklin D. Roosevelt [R]. Roosevelt ran an exceptionally effective and energetic campaign, travelling around 20,000 kilometres by train right across the country to deliver speeches directly to ordinary voters in person [R]. He was widely regarded as an excellent, persuasive public speaker, and he repeatedly promised that his government would help the 'forgotten man', language that resonated very deeply with millions of Americans then suffering through the Depression [D].

Roosevelt also drew considerable attention to his own personal struggles, having been left disabled by polio at the relatively young age of 39, which many ordinary Americans felt gave him genuine, first-hand understanding of hardship and suffering, in sharp contrast to Hoover's background as a self-made millionaire that many struggling voters found genuinely difficult to relate to during such hard and uncertain times for the whole country [R]. Roosevelt promised a comprehensive 'New Deal' for the American people, offering ambitious government schemes to create new jobs, revive both industry and struggling farming, help those on low incomes or entirely without work, improve worker protection, and end the now widely unpopular policy of Prohibition altogether [R].

The eventual result was a truly landslide victory for Roosevelt, the largest recorded in American history up to that point in time [R]. He won approximately 7 million more votes than Hoover overall and carried 42 of the 48 states, leaving Hoover victorious in only a small handful of six states, including Pennsylvania, Connecticut and Delaware, a scale of defeat that left no doubt about the public's verdict on his presidency [D].
